The factor that cancels the denominator at 3

Work over the completed algebraic closure of the 3-adic numbers. A discriminant-normalized period lattice has invariants g₂³ − 27g₃² = 1. Complex multiplication gives an algebraic integer j = 1728g₂³. The proof chooses a curve W with equation y² = x(x − A)(x − B) matching these invariants. Its discriminant is 16[AB(A − B)]² = 1. The bound on j gives |A² − AB + B²|₃ ≤ 1. These two conditions imply |A|₃, |B|₃ ≤ 1, so the curve has integral coefficients.

Write b₂ = a₁² + 4a₂ for the standard invariant of this integral Weierstrass equation. The formal theta calculation contains b₂/12. To see how the factor 3 disappears, take the CM endomorphism β = −1 + 2ω, where ω = (1 + √(−d))/2. Its conjugate is −β, so β² = −d and ββ̄ = d. The kernel has order d prime to 3 and its nonzero points have integral curve coordinates. Both β and β − β̄ = 2β are 3-adic units. The endomorphism identity uses the following combination.

(β² − 1)b₂/12 = −((d + 1)/3) · b₂/4.

The integer (d + 1)/3 and the 3-adic unit 4 give an integral right side. For the example with CM discriminant −23 this reads (−23 − 1)b₂/12 = −2b₂. It works for every integral b₂. The formal curve theorem combines this bound, the integral kernel coordinates and the unit β − β̄ to bound every positive derivative of the correction series φ in the additive coordinate.

Here φ is the zero-constant correction that appears on passing from the local curve parameter to the theta expansion. The scalar theta theorem starts with a lattice period whose half-period images under ω and ω̄ lie outside the lattice. Each shift is killed modulo the lattice by a positive integer N prime to 3. The half-period and the shifted half-period have orders dividing 2 and 2N. The torsion translation formula then gives integral coefficients for each translate multiplied by exp(+φ) in the curve parameter. The formal change to additive variables supplies the inverse correction exp(−φ), using the positive-derivative bounds just proved. Multiplying the two exponentials cancels the correction. The argument passes to finite sums with integral weights and to the permitted integral frames.

A Young diagram is a left-aligned array of boxes with weakly decreasing row lengths. For each column of height h in a diagram, choose h distinct output coordinates in increasing order. ΔtnG = 0   if   n > Ct = |α| − α₀ + min(α₀, β₀).

Expand each − determinant by permutations. Every term contains one factor from the top row per diagram column and |α| − α₀ factors from other rows. Thus a surviving term uses at most β₀ top-row replacements on the + side and at most α₀ on the − side. Ordinary derivatives commute, so the other row operations can be moved past the top-row operations. Compute both contractions in a two-by-two example

Take one label, two input and two output coordinates. Let α have one row of two boxes and β two rows of one box each. Choose separate output coordinates for the two height-one − minors and both coordinates for the height-two + minor. Specialize the − frame’s top row to (1,1) and the + frame to the identity. Only the term of degree two in the exponential can complete the degree-four derivative, giving G(∂)Θ(0) = −S. If vp(S) = −½, this specialized value attains the one-contraction bound. 5Lattices and the arithmetic main term

A local valuation gain becomes a positive multiple of log p after taking a lattice height. Each word in the theta construction carries an auxiliary prime level. A lower bound on the logarithm of that prime enters the lattice comparison. Expanding the bound cancels the period and auxiliary-prime terms and identifies the main term to subtract from the arithmetic prime sum.

5.1The lattices that carry the comparison

Over a number field K, an arithmetic lattice in a finite-dimensional K-vector space V is a finitely generated module over the ring of integers of K spanning V. To measure it one also needs norms at the infinite places. A basis of V and a matrix Xv at each such place give these frames. Each frame must have nonzero determinant. For such a lattice A of positive rank r over a totally complex number field, its mean slope is −(2/[K : ℚ]) log(ht(A))/r. Here ht is the lattice height in the chosen metric. The factor 2/[K : ℚ] averages over the complex places. A smaller height at fixed rank raises the mean slope. The proof obtains positivity of ht and uses [K : ℚ] = 2 times the number of infinite places.

For each choice of translation and each word u in a finite nonempty set W, the construction has a lattice Nu, a height allowance hu, and a linear map from the ambient space of Nu to the dual of the ambient space of a common lattice R. This dual consists of linear forms on that space. Its integral lattice consists of the forms taking integral values on R. The global hypotheses include an upper bound by hu for the height of each nonzero map.

Write μ for the mean slope, μmax for the maximum sublattice slope, and μmin for the minimum quotient slope. The comparison takes a mean weighted by the positive ranks ru of the word lattices. Set

s = ∑u ru(μ(Nu) − hu)/∑u ru,   bF = maxu(μmax(Nu) − hu) − s.

The latter quantity is nonnegative. For each word, its adjusted mean slope is bounded above by that word's adjusted maximum and hence by their common maximum. Averaging gives the assertion. The symbols s and bF in this chapter are real quantities at a fixed translation.

5.2What the counting bound contributes

Fix this translation. Let m be the number of successive lifts, f the positive number of place indices, and at ≥ 0 a weight at index t in the finite top set. Put A = ∑tat. Each stage j and place ρ has positive weight wjρ. Let v > 0 be the host normalization, and ℓg the logarithm of the product of the two auxiliary primes used for the host. A word has an associated prime Tu. The uniform counting estimate uses a nonnegative constant Cc, scale parameters k > 0, L and La, and the following quantities.

Ec = CcLa(1 + m²/k),   λ = ∑j (1/f) ∑ρ log(wjρv/π) + mℓg − Ec.

For every word u, the word count gives λ ≤ log Tu ≤ CcmL. It also gives |log Tu − log Tu′| ≤ Cc log k between any two words at this translation. The first inequality supplies the counting floor used in the main term. The other two control fluctuations in the slope estimate. Scalar La is log of the product of the master scale a and the root discriminant of the field E.

5.3The cancellation in the main term

Write γ for Euler's constant and d for the real logarithmic derivative at 1 of the distinguished quadratic character in this comparison. Set Ωlog = γ + log(π/v) − d. The local divisibility inequality contributes the term SD − A log Tu, where

SD = m∑t[at log at − at − atΩlog].

At zero we interpret a log a by its continuous value zero. Since A ≥ 0, subtracting A log Tu is bounded above by subtracting Aλ. The local exponent comparison contributes mAℓg with an explicit error bound. We can now calculate exactly which deterministic quantity lies under those bounds.

First expand the logarithm inside λ. Each place contributes log wjρ + log(v/π). The second summand is independent of ρ, so the mean over f places reproduces it once per stage. Thus −Aλ contributes −mA log(v/π), −mAℓg, and +AEc, as well as the weighted logarithms of w. The period term inside SD contributes +mA log(v/π), exactly cancelling the first of those terms. Adding the exponent main term +mAℓg cancels the second. Distributing A = ∑tat in the remaining place sum yields

SD − Aλ + mAℓg = M + AEc,
M = ∑j,t at[log at − 1 − γ + d − (1/f) ∑ρ log wjρ].

The plus sign of d comes from subtracting Ωlog. At m = f = 1 with a single top index and w = 1, the main term reduces to a(log a − 1 − γ + d). Doubling v adds a log 2 to SD and subtracts the same amount through −Aλ. This illustrates why a change of metric normalization in only one term would leave a linear error.

A check with two different place weights. Specialize the displayed identity to one stage, top weights 1 and 3, and place weights 2 and 8. Then A = 4 and the mean of the place logarithms is log 4. To track the cancellations, set v = 2π and write ℓg = log 15. These are values for checking the algebra. The formula for λ gives log 8 + log 15 − Ec. The period in SD contributes +4 log 2. Substitution gives

SD − 4λ + 4 log 15 = 3 log 3 − 4 − 4γ + 4d − 4 log 4 + 4Ec.

The coefficient of log 15 is zero. The surviving −4 log 4 comes from the geometric mean √(2·8) of the place weights. The count error enters with a plus sign, scaled by the total top weight 4. These three features persist for arbitrary finite sets of places and top weights.

The identification with the prime-sum expression uses specific bijections and equalities. The top indices correspond to the finite arithmetic sample, the f place indices to the chosen half of the finite group, the respective weights agree, γ agrees, and d equals the real part of the coefficient of the distinguished sign character. With these correspondences, reindex the two finite sums and take real parts. The final identification equates the weighted arithmetic prime sum to the sum over the sampled top indices and stages. Subtracting the matched main term M on both sides identifies the residual in the balance calculation.

5.4Where the slope inequality enters

Fix an upper bound H > 0 for s − μmin(R∨). Let 0 ≤ δ < 1 be the rank-deficit parameter, η ≥ 0 a frame-error parameter and 0 ≤ e ≤ 1/4 the second error parameter. The slope bound to be proved is

s − log |W| − [4bF log(1 + H/bF) + (η + 4√e)H]/(1 − δ) ≤ μ(R∨).

If bF = 0 the first product inside the brackets is zero, also its limit from positive bF. This inequality places the same dual-lattice slope appearing in the divisibility inequality on the opposite side. Combining its lower bound with divisibility's upper bound, the rank mean comparison, and the counting inequalities bounds the finite-place gain by M plus errors. The construction supplies an additional ceiling H ≤ xCHb, where x is the arithmetic scale and b its weight scale. It also supplies bounds for the error parameters, so large values of H can be multiplied by small η and √e.

5.6Why the slope bound contains a logarithm

Think of a lattice through its finite list of Harder–Narasimhan slopes, each repeated according to rank. A step in its filtration contains the directions whose slopes meet a given threshold. For a slope λ of the underlying real lattice the arithmetic normalization is 2λ + cK, with the same field constant for all words and the target. The resulting list has arithmetic mean equal to the lattice's mean slope. For the source lattices subtract each height allowance and concatenate the lists over all words. Their mean is s and every entry is at most s + bF. If a fraction p lies below s − τ, for τ ≥ 0, then the mean is at most p(s − τ) + (1 − p)(s + bF). Rearranging gives p ≤ bF/(bF + τ) when the denominator is positive. If both quantities vanish, all slopes equal s and the strict lower tail is empty. This bounds the rank lost when we discard low-slope steps in the source.

What happens to the remaining directions under the word maps? At threshold s − τ, take the sum of the images of the retained steps in R∨. A slope inequality for the maps, together with their height bounds, places this sum in the target filtration step. Bound its codimension using a matrix calculation at one infinite place. With p bounded as above, the resulting fraction of target slopes below the threshold is at most

ω(τ) = [η + 4bF/(bF + τ) + 4√e]/(1 − δ).

The matrix calculation uses bounds on traces and on Hilbert–Schmidt deviations after restriction to the selected columns. These estimates connect the dimensions of the source steps to the dimension of their combined image. Counting the target slopes below threshold now amounts to counting the dimensions missing from its filtration step.

Let ν run through the normalized target slopes with multiplicity. The lower-slope bound says ν ≥ s − H. Consequently the interval of τ in [0, H] for which ν < s − τ has length max(s − ν, 0). Average these lengths over the finite list. Their integral representation, followed by the bound above, gives

s − mean(ν) ≤ mean[max(s − ν, 0)] = ∫0H fraction{ν < s − τ} dτ ≤ ∫0H ω(τ) dτ.

For example, set s = 4 and take the three numbers 1, 3, 5 with H = 3. Two lie below 4 − τ for 0 ≤ τ < 1, and one lies below it for 1 ≤ τ < 3. The integral of the fraction is (2/3)·1 + (1/3)·2 = 4/3. This equals the average of the positive deficits 3, 1, 0. The signed mean deficit is only 1, since the last value exceeds 4. This finite list illustrates the integration step.

For bF > 0, integrating bF/(bF + τ) gives bF log(1 + H/bF). For bF = 0 this contribution vanishes. The two constant terms in ω integrate to (η + 4√e)H/(1 − δ). Since mean(ν) = μ(R∨), the calculation actually proves the bound without subtracting log |W|. The later theorem uses the displayed weaker version by subtracting the nonnegative logarithm of the number of words.

5.9Why each orbit is a product of residue groups

At each selected place the residue field has T elements. Its unit group H has T − 1 elements. The level-zero forms admit a model as complex functions on a finite set X. An element of H in one coordinate acts by a local dilation, also called a diamond operator. The operator Nv sums all these dilations in the coordinate v. Under the model, its kernel consists of functions whose sum along that coordinate is zero at every point. The ramified subspace is the intersection of these kernels.

Freeness uses arithmetic. Suppose a tuple of local multipliers fixes a level class. Represent it by an adelic element δ, whose components at the two auxiliary type primes are the identity. The power δT−1 belongs to the level subgroup, since the residues of all its multipliers have that power equal to 1. The diamond operator normalizes the level, so the same power of δκ belongs to the level for every level element κ. Fixing the class supplies a rational element γ from the double-coset relation. The admissible stabilizer gives γT−1 = 1. At each of the two distinct auxiliary primes p, the local reduction calculation kills every power of γ of order coprime to p. To see the force of having two primes, write T − 1 = pam with p ∤ m. The first condition kills γpa, whose order divides m. Now γ has order dividing pa, which is coprime to the second prime. Hence γ = 1 and δ itself lies in the level subgroup. Each local multiplier fixes a nonzero level functional killed by T. A multiplier c must therefore satisfy c ≡ 1 mod T. The tuple is the identity.

Choosing orbit representatives now identifies X with Q × Hf, where Q indexes the orbits of the function model. Its size includes the multiplicity of the value space. On each orbit a function has (T − 1)f entries before imposing any sums.

5.10Counting the independent values

Keep only the entries indexed by tuples with every coordinate different from the identity. They determine a function with vanishing line sums uniquely. To recover an entry with an identity coordinate, it must be the negative of the sum of the other entries on that line. Each of those entries has one fewer identity coordinate, so induction recovers the full table. Conversely, to extend a unit value at such a tuple a, use the product over coordinates v of (1hv=av − 1hv=1). It sums to zero along every coordinate and restricts to the unit value at a and zero at every other retained tuple. Taking linear combinations extends arbitrary data. Thus there are (T − 2)f independent values on each orbit.

dfull = |Q| (T − 1)f,   dram = |Q| (T − 2)f.

A four-by-four check. Take one orbit, T = 5 and f = 2. Order the four residues in both coordinates as 2, 3, 4, 1. Put ones on the diagonal of the first three-by-three block, zeros in its other six entries. Zero row sums force the first three entries of the last column to be −1. Zero column sums force the first three entries of the last row to be −1. Both conditions put 3 in the final corner. The nine free entries determine all sixteen. The eight row and column equations have one redundancy because summing all rows also sums all columns. The lost fraction is 7/16.

5.11From an exact count to a uniform error

For a nonzero full space and T ≥ 3, Bernoulli’s inequality gives

1 − dram/dfull = 1 − (1 − 1/(T − 1))f ≤ f/(T − 1) ≤ 2f/T.

The scale conditions give T ≥ bm/2 ≥ b, with b = exp(xε), b ≥ 3 and m ≥ 2. Thus dfull − dram ≤ de dfull for de = 2f/b. The undivided inequality also holds if the full space is zero. For each fixed family with ε > 0, one threshold works for every later x and every family index. The number f can depend on that index, but the same de works for all its words. Eventually f ≤ k ≤ x5, 2f ≤ exp(xε/2), and xε ≥ 4xε/8. Consequently √de ≤ exp(−xε/4) ≤ exp(−xε/8). Put Ex = exp(−xε/8). To obtain a bound common to all indices at this x, the proof enlarges the rank-loss cap to Ex² and the separate matrix-error cap to 2Ex². The rank term in the frame error 5σ + 3Ex now has the same value at every index. The common frame calculation supplies the diagonal and off-diagonal bounds on the full period matrices.

5.12What controls the variation of the prime level?

The comparison of two word counts uses a Vandermonde product V(z) = ∏a<b(za − zb) in the decreasing real parameters at a place. Its logarithm is a sum over pairs. For the first row a = 0 the two compared gaps are each at least 4kΔ and change by at most Δ. The variation of each logarithm is at most 1/(4k). For a ≥ 1 the gaps are at least 3(b − a)Δ and change by at most 2Δ, giving 2/[3(b − a)] per pair. Both bounds follow by integrating 1/t between the gaps. A harmonic sum over b bounds the logarithmic variation at a place by 1/4 + (2/3)k(1 + log k). Summing over f places and applying the factor 1/(fk) in the level parameter leaves variation of order log k. The shared auxiliary factor cancels when the two word windows are compared. The absolute bounds for each word also use a torus-pair estimate involving the mass, volume and formal degree.

5.13How close are the period operators to a common orthonormal frame?

Two periods can each preserve lengths and still take their values on the same line. A slope estimate that uses many words therefore needs two measurements. For a fixed family member let Pu carry the full complex space of word u, of dimension du, into one Hilbert space. Normalize by the real number cu, the product of its two unfolding volumes divided by the product of its column representation dimensions over the infinite places. The operator from the space of v to the space of u is

Kuv = (cucv)−1/2 Pu∗Pv,   Q(A) = ∑j ‖Aej‖².

Here the ej run through an orthonormal basis of the domain. For u = v we measure Q(Kuu − I). For distinct words we measure Q(Kuv), which adds the squared absolute values of all correlations between the two normalized families of columns. The estimates are for the full word dimension. The arithmetic lattice retained at the ramified level can have fewer columns. To see why correlations influence rank, collect any set of nonzero retained columns in a matrix A and put G = A*A. If its positive eigenvalues are λ₁,…,λᵣ, then (∑λᵢ)² ≤ r∑λᵢ² by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus rank(A) ≥ (tr G)²/tr(G²). For two unit columns the numerator is 4. Identical columns give denominator 4 and rank one. Orthogonal columns give denominator 2 and rank two. Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu,   Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗.

Why can a pair of words have a zero orbital term?

Fix two distinct words u and v in the selected family. Their local unitary representations have different weight parameters at every infinite place. Examine a single nonidentity term with Gram label zero in Buv. It compares a flag with a translate of the other flag. Call the pair relevant when the differentials of their two characters agree on every common infinitesimal unipotent direction. There are two ways for its orbital integral P to vanish.

If relevance fails, one direction gives unequal phases. In fact the proof rescales that direction so that, with N infinite places, the difference in the two character exponents is πi/N at each place. The product of the first character with the conjugate of the second therefore takes the value exp(πi) = −1. This character is trivial on the rational lattice. Averaging over its compact quotient in the common unipotent group gives zero, since translating the character average by that element changes its sign. The orbital integrand transforms by exactly this character, so the orbital integral vanishes.

For a relevant pair with Gram label zero, the geometric normal form gives a positive orthonormal frame perpendicular to both flag subspaces at each infinite place. Write its columns as W and the ambient Hermitian form as J, so W∗JW = I. Every M ∈ U(k) extends to a symmetry fixing those subspaces pointwise. Indeed, put

H = I + W(M − I)W∗J.   HW = WM,   Hy = y whenever W∗Jy = 0.

On the frame this map preserves the inner product because M is unitary, and on its orthogonal complement it is the identity. The other flag sees the action as CMC∗ for a fixed unitary matrix C at that place. Invariance of the orbital integral under the pointwise stabilizer gives covariance between these two actions. This uses the existence of the fundamental domain and integrability of the orbital kernel.

Choose one infinite place and let M vary only there. Fix arbitrary vectors in every other tensor factor on each side. Let Su and Sv insert a local vector into those fixed tensors. For A = Su∗PSv, covariance reads

πu(M)A = Aπv(CMC∗),   πu(M)R = Rπv(M),   R = Aπv(C).

A nonzero R would be an isomorphism. Its kernel and image are invariant, and the two finite-dimensional representations are irreducible. An isomorphism preserves the weights of the diagonal torus, including the distinguished extremal weight that determines each type. The unequal parameters rule this out. Hence R = 0 and A = 0. Varying the fixed tensors shows that every matrix coefficient of P between pure tensors vanishes. They span both spaces.

Can a scalar unitary distinguish these two types of U(2)?

On the determinant line and on Sym²(ℂ²), the scalar zI acts by z². Suppose an intertwiner sends a generator of the determinant line to a quadratic tensor w. Every diag(z,z−1) with |z| = 1 fixes w. In the basis e₁², e₁e₂, e₂², the three eigenvalues are z², 1 and z−2. Thus w is a multiple of e₁e₂. Swapping the basis vectors fixes that monomial and multiplies the determinant by −1. Equivariance gives w = −w, so w = 0.

Both cases kill each selected term individually, so their sum Buv is zero. The other terms still contribute to Kuv. The separate different-word estimate bounds the squared norm of Kuv − Buv, and substituting zero gives the bound for the full block.

How large can the surviving part of a different-word block be?

Fix distinct words u and v and put Δ = dudv/D∗. The preceding argument removes the nonidentity terms whose geometric Gram label is zero. The remaining sum, called K₀, contains the identity part and two groups of terms with nonzero label. The identity part also vanishes for this calculation. The two groups can point in the same direction in the Hilbert space of operators. The proof bounds the squared norm of each group before adding them.

Call the two groups G (generic) and N (nongeneric). Genericity tests a pair of lattice flags. Their integral span has a saturation, obtained by intersecting its field span with the ambient lattice. At primes away from the level, genericity requires that the original span already give the saturation locally. At primes dividing the level, one admissible matrix must supply the saturation using the corrected frame differences divided by the level. A term is generic when a representative passes these tests.

Each term t contributes a vector vt supported on one pair of lattices. Its row records those lattices and a finite index i. For either group S, form ai by summing its vectors with index i. In the square of that sum, terms with the same index but different lattice pairs have disjoint support. Absolute convergence permits regrouping, so only ordered pairs in the same row contribute. With Γ₁ the positive Gram normalization, the resulting energy is

Φ(S) = Γ₁ ∑i ‖ai‖² = Γ₁ ∑s,t ∈ S, same row Re ⟨vs, vt⟩.

Individual inner products can have either sign. To bound the sum, the proof groups pairs by their corank s₀ = k − dim Θ, where Θ consists of first components of vector pairs compatible with the two flags and their comparison map. On a common row with both Gram labels nonzero, s₀ ≥ 1. Among generic pairs of corank one, the scalar pairs preserve the two coefficients of the distinguished flag vectors under comparison.

The large-corank estimate bounds the sum of absolute inner products over all same-row pairs of nonzero-label terms of corank at least two by εΔ, including the factor Γ₁. Thus each group can use this bound on its own subset. In G, the nonscalar corank-one pairs cost at most another εΔ in absolute value. The signed sum of the scalar pairs is at most AΔ. In N, one signed bound ε′Δ covers all corank-one pairs. These are the only cases, giving

Φ(G) ≤ (A + 2ε)Δ,   Φ(N) ≤ (ε + ε′)Δ.

The common Gram matrix converts each energy to an upper bound on the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of its operator sum, with a factor P. The triangle inequality then gives the retained block bound

‖K₀‖² ≤ (√[P(A + 2ε)] + √[P(ε + ε′)])² Δ ≤ (1 + b−6)Δ.

Why take the square roots? Consider two contributions along one unit vector, with coefficients 1 and 1/10. Their squared norms are 1 and 1/100, but their sum has squared norm 121/100. That example illustrates only the last addition. On the selected route the kernel expansion identifies the surviving block with the full block after the zero subseries is removed. Its Hilbert–Schmidt squared norm therefore obeys the same bound used in the frame estimate.

Why does the Gram matrix cost only P, and where does b−6 come from?

For each group the squared norm is Re ∑ij Mij⟨ai, aj⟩. The supplied matrix bound says that PΓ₁I − M is positive semidefinite. Factor it as a sum of outer products wℓwℓ∗. Substituting in the difference between PΦ(S) and the squared norm gives ∑ℓ ‖∑i wℓi ai‖² ≥ 0.

Set h = b−7. Under the selected size hypotheses, b ≥ 16, the two level primes satisfy gi ≥ (kb)⁸, and k ≥ 70 log b. The full rank and density inequalities give ε, ε′ ≤ h² and A ≤ (1 + h)exp(h²). For f infinite places, the Gram factor P = (1 + 3/g₁)f(1 + 3/g₂)f is at most exp(6h). Using h ≤ 1/1000, the two radicands are at most 1 + 11h and 3h². Their square roots sum to at most 1 + 11h/2 + 7h/4. Its square is at most 1 + 16h ≤ 1 + b−6. The remaining arithmetic inputs are the absolute bounds from counting loops, the nongeneric corank-one estimate, and the main scalar-row estimate from the lattice and mass calculation.

How many flags can have the same Gram data?

Fix a row in the common frame and one Gram class Z. To count generic flags in this row, keep the part of a flag visible in the definite orthogonal space. It is a sublattice P of a fixed lattice L₀ of ambient dimension k. Its rank is k − 1. The frame determinant formula gives a bound G depending on the prescribed data. Write B for the fixed-witness bound on the number of flag classes supported by any one such P. Each contributing flag has a witness P. Summing over possible witnesses gives an upper bound even when two witnesses count the same class.

The difficulty is that P can have large index in the integral points of its own span. Set M = L₀ ∩ spanK(P), where K is the CM field. This saturation has the same field span and rank as P. It is primitive in L₀, meaning it contains every point of L₀ in that span. With the normalized determinant (the square root of the order of the dual quotient in the span), write d = det(M) and j = #(M/P). The integral, positive definite lattice and the standing CM norm hypotheses give an integer d ≥ 1. The index formula gives det(P) = j d. Hence the determinant budget G leaves room for indices only up to G/d.

For a fixed saturation let α = k + log₂[K ∶ ℚ]. The projective-module counting bound supplies at most jα submodules of index j. For x ≥ 1 there are at most ⌊x⌋ indices through x, each contributing at most xα. This accounts for the extra power in the estimate. If Cprim(L₀,n,d) counts primitive sublattices of rank n and determinant d, the total number of eligible witnesses satisfies

#{P ⊆ L₀ ∣ rank P = n, det(P) ≤ G} ≤ ∑1 ≤ d ≤ ⌊G⌋ Cprim(L₀,n,d) (G/d)α + 1.

For G < 1 there are no witnesses. For the single generic flag take n = k − 1 and multiply by B. The row weights are nonnegative, so summing first over rows or first over d yields the same upper bound. The remaining arithmetic estimate concerns the mean of the primitive counts.

Count the eight rank-one sublattices of determinant at most two by hand

Take the standard Hermitian lattice ℤ[i]². A nonzero rank-one submodule has a generator (a,b), unique up to the four units, because ℤ[i] is a principal ideal domain. The Gram entry is h = |a|² + |b|². Its dual in its own line is obtained by dividing the generator by h. The quotient has h² elements, hence the normalized determinant is h. At h = 1 the two coordinate axes are the only possibilities. At h = 2 both coordinates can be units, giving the four primitive lines generated by (1,u), u ∈ {1,−1,i,−i}. Otherwise one coordinate vanishes and the other is a unit times 1 + i. These last two submodules have index two in the coordinate axes. This lists 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 submodules. In this concrete model the primitive counts are 2 and 4, and α + 1 = 4. The general counting expression gives 2·2⁴ + 4·1⁴ = 36. Its slack comes from bounding every index by the same power.

Why a pair costs two flag counts. A loop term carries two flags and a comparison isometry. For fixed Gram classes, positive corank s and a determinant cutoff, the two flags admit a common witness P of rank k − s. Under the level and admissibility hypotheses, moving each flag by its allowed integral unipotent transformation carries the comparison isometry to the one for the new pair, by uniqueness on the orthogonal quotient. Thus the two flag classes determine the triple class. If each flag set at P has at most J classes, the ordered pair has at most J² choices. Multiply the displayed witness bound by J² and average the primitive counts in the relevant genus. The fixed-witness estimates and the primitive genus estimates enter separately in the uniform row bounds.

How many flag classes can one fixed sublattice support?

Fix a base flag, a row lattice Λ and a Gram class Z in the common frame. Let r be its isotropic rank, k the dimension of its definite complement, f the number of conjugate pairs of embeddings of the CM field E, and N = T(u)f for the base word u. Fix P inside the definite row lattice L₀, of rank k−s over E after taking its span, with 1 ≤ s ≤ k. A term flag belongs to this count if it satisfies the row and frame conditions, its cross-Gram matrix is equivalent to Z by integral triangular changes with diagonal one, and its visible lattice contains P. Count classes under the integral unipotent transformations and allowed frame changes.

The uniform theorem assumes the standing and numerical conditions on the two words, a standard base flag, an admissible row, a relevant Gram cell and Cℓ ≥ 1. For a sufficiently large height parameter C, write HZ for the prescribed height of Z. Choose Δ ≥ 1 and H with det P ≤ Δ, HZ ≤ H and Δ ≤ H³. Saturation in L₀ gives [sat(P)∶P] ≤ Δ since the saturated lattice has determinant at least one. If the flag set is nonempty, an actual term proves the Gram invariant is nonzero. The cell supplies a nonzero maximal minor of the first r rows. The proof uses Z itself as its bounded representative. The common budget Q = HZ² bounds the absolute norm of that minor, the product of the absolute values of the Gram invariant over the selected complex embeddings, and the specified different-ideal norm.

How many ways can P lift? An isometry fixing the base frame puts the row in split form and preserves the definite lattice. Every original class has a representative with exact cross-Gram matrix Z in the split calculation. A lift of P there has the form p ↦ p + φ(p), with φ valued in the isotropic lattice and the graph orthogonal to the moving frame. In one isotropic coordinate a linear form on P costs at most [sat(P)∶P] representatives beyond the restrictions of forms on its saturation. Forms on the primitive saturation contribute at most N² modulo pairings with L₀. Taking all r coordinates gives at most (N²Δ)r lift representatives. Frame-fixing integral unipotents move each graph into this list. Summing over the list gives an upper bound even if a class admits more than one graph.

What remains once the lift is fixed? Put S₀ = L₀ ∩ P⊥, a definite lattice of rank s. A nonzero ideal I of norm at most M = Δ²N² satisfies I S₀∨ ⊆ S₀, where the dual is taken in its span. Let Y be the top r rows of the exact Gram matrix and let a be its chosen nonzero maximal minor. The moving frame gives a tuple of perpendicular components w₀,…,wᵣ in S₀∨. Write y for their linear combination with the signed maximal minors of Y as coefficients. Its squared length satisfies T(u)〈y,y〉 = G, the fixed nonzero Gram invariant. For a nonzero difference in the dual lattice, integrality after multiplication by I bounds the product of its embedded squared lengths below by 1/N(I). Packing points separated in this way gives at most 9sf(MQ)s possible y. For a fixed y, the difference of two tuples has cofactor combination zero. The adjugate of the chosen submatrix expresses this difference as a combination of the rows of Y with coefficients in ((a)I)−1S₀. Reducing those r coefficients modulo S₀ costs at most (MQ)sr. The integral changes are realized by unipotents preserving the lifted graph.

With the perpendicular tuple fixed, the remaining difference is an r × (r+1) matrix x in the isotropic coordinates satisfying x*Y + Y*x = 0, where * denotes conjugate transpose. The centre acts by x ↦ x + cY for integral skew-Hermitian c. Clearing denominators with the minor a and the r-th power of the extended different bounds the number of residual representatives by Q2r². Every flag class occurs in the image of the perpendicular and isotropic representative sets. Multiplying their sizes is therefore sufficient.

A rank-one coordinate calculation over the Gaussian integers

Take S₀ = ℤ[i] with its usual norm, r = s = 1, Y = (t,0) for an integer t ≥ 1, and impose |t w₁|² = t². There are four choices for w₁, the Gaussian units. Row translations add tv to w₀, so its real and imaginary parts each give one residue modulo t. This yields exactly 4t² perpendicular classes. For integral isotropic corrections the skew equation forces x = (ij,0) with j ∈ ℤ. Integral skew scalars act by adding (itℓ,0), leaving t classes. At t = 2 this gives 16 perpendicular representatives and 2 isotropic representatives. The 32 ordered pairs describe the two coordinate equations in this model. To obtain an admissible flag one would also have to realize the pair in a single integral row with the prescribed base, Gram matrix and level.

The bound used in the row sum. Combining the graph count and the two residual counts first gives the following upper bound on the number of classes over P.

(N²Δ)r · 9sf(Δ²N²Q)s+sr · Q2r².

The standing height estimate gives N² ≤ HZ ≤ H. Since Δ ≤ H³ and Q ≤ H², the middle base is at most H6+1+2 = H⁹. The last factor is at most H4r². With H ≥ 1 one may enlarge this last exponent to 16r², obtaining

Bₛ = N2r Δr 9sf H9s + 9sr + 16r².

The generic row uses s = 1, Δ = max(G,1) for its determinant cutoff G, and H = HZ. The paired row uses a common determinant allowance and height for the two Gram classes. It applies Bₛ to each flag at the same P, then uses Bₛ² before summing over witnesses. The primitive genus mean then counts candidate witnesses of corank one. The ordered-pair estimate uses a mean allowing higher corank.

How often does a primitive hyperplane occur across the rows?

The fixed-witness estimate bounds the number of flags once their witness lattice is given. To average this bound we also need to count witnesses. After saturation the arithmetic input for one generic flag concerns primitive hyperplanes of exact determinant. Fix the frame and the word in the standing unramified CM datum. Its prime Tu is at least three and splits completely in the CM field E. The definite complement has dimension k ≥ 3. Write j = k−1 and f = [E∶ℚ]/2. For a row lattice L and an integer d ≥ 1, count the E-hyperplanes U for which the restriction to P = L ∩ U has |P∨/P| = d². Call this count Nd(L). Intersecting with the whole field hyperplane is what makes P primitive. Submodules of finite index in P have already been accounted for at saturation.

Why average over a genus? A genus collects lattices that are isometric at every completion. The count above is invariant under isometries. For a nonempty set of row representatives choose one complement lattice L₀. In its genus take one representative L per isometry class, and write a(L) = 1/|Aut(L)| and m = ∑ a(L). Apply the row-to-genus comparison first with the observable Nd, then with the constant observable one. The common row multiplicity cancels. With wΛ the row weights, the exact identity is

m ∑Λ wΛNd(LΛ) = (∑Λ wΛ) ∑[L] a(L)Nd(L).

Count the marked pairs in the other order. For a fixed lattice its finite automorphism group permutes the marked hyperplanes. Each orbit contributes its size divided by |Aut(L)|, which is the reciprocal order of the subgroup fixing the pair. This lets us first choose a rational isometry class of hyperplanes and then count the lattices meeting that hyperplane with the prescribed discriminant. The proof covers all possible marked pairs by its subspace representatives, so this second operation yields an upper bound.

Check both counts in one Gaussian lattice

Take the identity Hermitian form on ℤ[i]³. A primitive normal vector v determines U = v⊥, and four unit multiples give the same hyperplane. Put d = ⟨v,v⟩. Primitivity gives a vector w pairing to one with v. A basis of P followed by w is a basis of the full lattice. The squared length of the projection of w onto the normal line is 1/d. Factoring the Gram determinant of that basis thus gives 1 = det Gram(P)/d. The Gaussian index of the dual quotient, counted as a finite abelian group, is the absolute norm of this determinant, namely d².

At d = 3 the three coordinate norms are 1,1,1 or 0,1,2 up to permutation. In the first case the four phases per coordinate give 4³/4 = 16 hyperplanes. In the second there are 6 orders, four phases for the norm-one entry and four for the norm-two entry, giving 6·4²/4 = 24. Every integral isometry permutes the three coordinate axes and assigns a Gaussian unit to each, so the group has order 6·4³ = 384. The two stabilizers have orders 24 and 16. Counting marks at the lattice gives 40/384. Counting by orbits gives 1/24 + 1/16, the same 5/48. This example checks the change of order for one ambient lattice.

What is left when a hyperplane is fixed? Split the space orthogonally into U and a line. A lattice L gives a pair of intersections, one in each factor. Put t = Tuf. In this genus the ambient discriminant module is isomorphic over 𝒪E to 𝒪E/(Tu). One generator suffices over that ring. As an additive group it has t² elements and Tu kills every element. The hyperplane intersection has discriminant order d². The line intersection has discriminant order between 1 and d²t². For fixed intersections the line-gluing estimate permits at most t²d² ambient lattices. The count therefore uses the product of two masses, one for each factor, multiplied by this gluing allowance.

Where does the determinant gain enter? Let Mj and M₁ be the standard lattice masses of ranks j and one, and set b = log₂ f. With the supplied subspace-mass and line-mass bounds, the unnormalized marked mass is at most the following product. Its last factors come respectively from the subspace estimate, the gluing allowance and the summed line masses.

MjM₁ · dj+2+b · t²d² · (dt)2+b.

At the split prime the ambient genus mass is Mk(1 + Tu + ⋯ + Tuk−1)f. Keeping the last summand gives the lower bound Mktj. Dividing accounts for the factor (d/t)j in the row mean. The consecutive-rank mass comparison bounds Mj/Mk, and the rank-one bound contributes at most hE2f, where hE is the class number. Take a height H ≥ max(d,t). The remaining powers satisfy d4+bt²(dt)2+b ≤ H10+3b. Since H ≥ 1 the caller may use its stated exponent 11+3b. With rd(E) the root discriminant and v = rd(E)/2, the row-weighted sum is at most the sum of the row weights times

(d/t)k−1 · (eπ/(kv))kf · (2k√rd(E))f hE 2f · H11+3b.

The proof cancels the finite positive genus mass in the row identity. An empty row family satisfies the inequality directly. To return to flags, interchange the row sum and the finite determinant sum from saturation and apply this bound for each 1 ≤ d ≤ ⌊G⌋. A separate divisor-sum estimate absorbs the remaining powers and the fixed-witness allowance. For ordered pairs the possible corank is larger and the proof needs the mean for primitive sublattices of higher corank.

How many common witnesses can two flags have?

Two flags on the same row may share a witness of smaller dimension than a hyperplane. First fix its codimension s in the definite complement of dimension k. For each row we want to count the possible witnesses, with the row weights from the genus averaging identity. The saturation argument reduces this question to primitive lattices at each exact determinant. A primitive lattice here has the form P = L ∩ U for an E-subspace U. Write Ns,d(L) for the number of these subspaces with dimension j = k − s and |P∨/P| = d².

Theorem (primitive sublattices in a row genus). Fix the integral complement lattice of a row. Its Hermitian form is totally definite of rank k over a CM field E of degree 2f, unramified over its real subfield at the finite places. Its dual quotient is isomorphic over 𝒪E to 𝒪E/(T), with T ≥ 3 a rational prime splitting completely in E. Put t = Tf, and let Mr be the standard Hermitian lattice mass in rank r. The frame has a scale b ≥ 1, a rank parameter m ≥ 2, and a positive constant cl for which log rd(E) ≤ (log b)/cl. Fix any 0 < c₀ ≤ cl. The bound holds for every real C ≥ max(16, 1/c₀), every H ≥ bCm²f, every integer d ≥ 1, and every 2 ≤ s ≤ k. If mgen = ∑[L] 1/|Aut(L)| is the mass of the row genus, then

(1/mgen) ∑[L] Ns,d(L)/|Aut(L)| ≤ (d/t)k (dt)Cs + C log f Ξs.

When j ≥ 2, the remaining factor is Ξs = MsMj/Mk. When j is 0 or 1, it is (Ck)kf(Ht)Ck. The distinction comes from how we count the subspaces.

Proof for two factors of rank at least two. Mark a subspace in each lattice. A mark with orbit of size q contributes q/|Aut(L)|, the reciprocal of the order of its stabilizer. We may therefore fix the subspace first and count the compatible lattices with these weights. Put n = d², X = nt² and λ = log₂(2f). Three estimates give the count.

  1. Rational subspaces. The subspace orbit bound covers every rank-j subspace admitting an integral lattice of discriminant order n by at most n1+λ rational isometry classes.
  2. Intersections. For a fixed subspace, the fixed-discriminant mass bound in rank r is Mra(r+λ)/2 at discriminant order a ≥ 1. The intersection in U has order n. In its perpendicular space the order lies between 1 and X, since the ambient discriminant module is cyclic over 𝒪E of order t². Thus the two masses are bounded respectively by Mjn(j+λ)/2 and MsX·X(s+λ)/2. The extra X allows every possible order of the second intersection.
  3. Gluing. A lattice can strictly contain the direct sum of its two intersections. For fixed intersections of orders n and a, the gluing bound permits at most (na)2s+1 ambient lattices here. The discriminant modules on the two sides can be generated by at most s+1 and s elements, respectively. An ambient lattice gives an intermediate submodule between the sum of the intersections and the sum of their duals. Here is the finite-module count. If a finite module Q over the ring of integers has g generators, each of its submodules also has at most g. At each prime supporting Q, lift the submodule to the free module of rank g over the discrete valuation ring. Its preimage is free of rank at most g, so its images generate the submodule locally. Pad each list with zeros and combine corresponding entries across the primary components by the Chinese remainder theorem. Hence every submodule is generated by some ordered g-tuple in Q, and there are at most |Q|g of them. The Stacks Project, Lemma 15.22.11 on modules over a discrete valuation ring[5] · Lemma 10.15.4 on simultaneous residues[6]. Finally a ≤ X bounds its base by nX.

Multiply the three estimates. Keep nj/2, replace the remaining factors of n by X, and use (nX)2s+1 ≤ X4s+2. The exponent of X is (1+λ) + λ/2 + 1 + (s+λ)/2 + 4s+2. Consequently the unnormalized marked mass is at most

MjMs dj(dt)9s+8+4λ.

The split-prime genus mass is at least Mktk−1. Dividing leaves a numerator djt over tk. Increase dj to dk and absorb t in one further power of dt. Since λ ≤ 1 + 2 log f, we have 9s+9+4λ ≤ Cs+C log f for s ≥ 2 and C ≥ 16. This gives the stated mean.

Proof for a line or the zero space. There is at most one zero subspace. On a line of discriminant order n, the rank-one short-vector bound supplies a nonzero lattice vector whose squared length at every embedding is at most B = rd(E)n1/(2f), where rd is the root discriminant. The vector determines the line. The ambient short-vector bound gives at most (1+2√B)2kf choices, hence at most (9 rd(E))kfdk because B ≥ 1. This bound holds for each lattice. Indeed f log rd(E) ≤ (f/c₀) log b ≤ Cm²f log b ≤ log H, so rd(E)f ≤ H. Factoring out (d/t)k leaves at most the announced Ξs.

Count the first two determinants in a four-dimensional Gaussian lattice

Use the identity Hermitian form on ℤ[i]⁴. A saturated plane has a Gaussian basis u, v. Put pab = uavb − ubva. Its Gram determinant d is the sum of the six squared absolute values of these minors, by Cauchy–Binet. The dual quotient has order d². A single nonzero minor forces the field plane to be the corresponding coordinate plane, whose saturated lattice has determinant 1. There are six such planes. Andrew Putman, The Cauchy–Binet formula, Theorem 0.1[7]

At determinant 2, precisely two minors must therefore be units. Their index pairs share an index, since expanding the definitions gives p₁₂p₃₄ − p₁₃p₂₄ + p₁₄p₂₃ = 0. Disjoint pairs would leave a single nonzero product. With common index a, the plane is spanned by ea and eb + εec with b < c and ε one of the four Gaussian units. The two coefficients of value one along a and b show that these vectors already generate the whole intersection. There are 4 choices of a, 3 unordered pairs {b,c}, and 4 phases, or 48 planes. They form a single orbit under the 4!·4⁴ = 6,144 coordinate isometries, so their contribution for this lattice is 48/6,144 = 1/128. This calculation illustrates the marked mass for one lattice. The genus theorem uses the split-prime hypotheses stated above.

Theorems used. Cauchy–Binet for a Gram determinant

From one primitive count to a pair of flags. Fix two relevant Gram labels and let H be the product of their heights. Fix the cutoff exponent α and take 1 ≤ Δ ≤ Hα. Let K be the uniform bound for one flag over a given witness. An ordered pair costs at most K² over that same witness. By saturation, a primitive determinant d contributes with multiplicity at most (Δ/d)k+λ+1. The comparison of row weights with genus weights applies to each exact determinant, so we may average the primitive counts first. The primitive mean has a fixed constant C₁. Once the pair constant satisfies C ≥ C₁, the first label height is at least bC₁m²f and the second is at least one. Their product H meets the same height condition for every d in the sum. If A(d) denotes the right-hand side of the genus theorem, the resulting mean number of pairs is bounded by

K² ∑1≤d≤⌊Δ⌋ (Δ/d)k+λ+1A(d).

In every summand, (Δ/d)k(d/t)k equals (Δ/t)k. For instance, in the scalar identity take k = 4, Δ = 4 and t = 5. At d = 1 the product is 4⁴(1/5)⁴. At d = 2 it is 2⁴(2/5)⁴. Both are 256/625. The costs of gluing and of choosing the two flags still have to be paid. Only this fourth power is common to all the terms of the sum. Write e = C₁(s + log f) for the exponent from the primitive mean. The remaining powers satisfy (Δ/d)λ+1 ≤ Δλ+1 and (dt)e ≤ (Δt)e. At most ⌊Δ⌋ terms occur, so Δλ+2 suffices for these multiplicities. The pair estimate allows Δλ+4, then absorbs it and the fixed-witness cost using the two label heights. Here the primitive-mean constant C₁ is fixed first. The final pair estimate uses a sufficiently large constant C ≥ C₁. Taking two independent genus means would lose the condition that both flags have the same witness.

What replaces vanishing when the two words coincide?

The subseries Buu still excludes the identity and has geometric Gram label zero. Now the two infinite-place representations agree. An intertwiner from a representation to itself can be a nonzero scalar. The goal is to control the size of the surviving sum. Write Q for the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm, du for the full word dimension, k for the weight parameter and f for the number of infinite places in the product. We will obtain Q(Buu) ≤ du exp(−kf log k). The other diagonal contribution, Kuu − Buu − I, has its own estimate.

Each orbital term involves two flags. Call their distinguished subspaces X and X′, each of dimension r. Group terms by the dimension lost in their intersection, j = r − dim(X ∩ X′), and by a list δ of leading minors of their pairing matrix through size j. This j belongs to one term. The corank used for two terms on a common row in the preceding argument compares different data. Terms whose characters disagree on the common stabilizer vanish. For the remaining terms in this subseries, the geometric input gives 1 ≤ j ≤ r. This lower bound matters. At j = 0 the power that pays for summing the terms would disappear.

Where does the half-power of the last minor come from?

Keep one nonidentity term t that survives the character test in the diagonal subseries. Its two flags determine a positive rank j and an arithmetic list of minors δ. Consider the last minor of that list at each of the f infinite places. In the coordinates adapted to the flags, let Dτ be its positive normalized absolute size. The comparison of Gram minors identifies the local factor in the normalized ideal norm Δ of the last minor with Dτ². Consequently the product P of the Dτ is positive and Δ = P². The local amplitude bound contains one inverse power of the absolute size for each of the k − 1 − j occurrences. Multiplication over the places gives

∏τ Dτ−(k−1−j) = P−(k−1−j) = Δ−(k−1−j)/2.

A sufficient numerical threshold is (16C + C³²)m⁶L ≤ k log k, with C ≥ 1 and f ≥ 1. It ensures k ≥ 8, k ≥ m and k ≥ C¹⁶. Since (j − 1)(k − 2 − j) ≥ 0, every exponent j(k − 1 − j) is at least k − 2. 5.15How many rows can the period maps share?

All the word maps take values in the same target. Its dimension D counts the independent ways the chosen archimedean representation occurs in automorphic L² after applying the finite-place projector e. The main term M for this integer is a real number. If dv is the formal degree at the real place v and V is the Haar volume of a fundamental domain F, then M = c0V, where c0 = (∏v dv) Re e(1). Why should this expression approximate a dimension? Both arise from one kernel.

Let φ be the product of the normalized archimedean matrix coefficients, their formal degrees and the finite-place function e, with the archimedean coefficients conjugated. Summing φ(x⁻¹γz) over rational group elements γ gives a kernel K(x,z). It represents an orthogonal projection of rank D. Choose continuous representatives F1, …, FD of an orthonormal basis of the range. The geometric kernel and the basis expansion give the same action on compactly supported test functions. Continuity and uniqueness of the automorphic representatives identify the two kernels pointwise. In particular,

Re K(x,x) = ∑j |Fj(x)|² ≥ 0,   ∫F Re K(x,x) dμ = D.

Each basis vector contributes one to the integral. On the geometric side the identity γ = 1 gives the constant c0 on the diagonal. Its integral is M. The real parts of the remaining summands can have either sign.

Write n for the unitary rank, f for the number of real places, and put U = nf log n, α = exp(−U/4), δ = exp(−n²f). The indefinite count divides F according to the infimum of the normalized sizes of nonzero sublattices at x. On the moderate part this size meets a prescribed threshold. There the integral of |Re K(x,x) − c0| costs at most αM from near nonidentity summands and δM from far summands. Here “near” tests the conjugated rational element at every archimedean place. On the deep part, below the threshold, the rare-flag estimate bounds the volume by αV, so the identity term there costs at most αM. A separate concentration bound gives ∫deep Re K ≤ δD. Positivity of the full diagonal lets the last two bounds control the absolute value of their difference. Thus

|D − M| ≤ (2α + δ)M + δD.

For a two-point illustration, take counting measure and project onto the unit vector (2,1)/√5. The diagonal is (4/5, 1/5) and its sum is 1. Compare with the constant 3/5 on each point. The two local differences are +1/5 and −2/5, even though both diagonal entries are positive. Their sum −1/5 is precisely the rank minus the reference mass. This illustrates the sign in the trace subtraction. The exponential estimates come from the arithmetic of the unitary quotient.

The bound still contains the unknown D on the right. Write X = |D − M|. Since D ≤ M + X, we get (1 − δ)X ≤ (2α + 2δ)M. The threshold on n ensures n ≥ exp(15). With f ≥ 1 the proof gets α, δ ≤ exp(−U/16)/8 and δ ≤ 1/2. Hence X ≤ exp(−U/16)M. For each fixed level-growth exponent, the counting theorem chooses its rank and spectral-gap thresholds before the row data vary. The definite case has an exact identity. The family has q = m/2 ≥ 1 negative directions, so it uses the estimate just derived.

The comparison of the automorphic model with the family identifies (D, M, n) with (Dall, D∗, r). The count bounds the difference in both directions. The frame proof takes its upper inequality, Dall ≤ (1 + exp(−rf log r/16))D∗, to bound the number of common target rows. The Gram estimates separately control the entries obtained by pairing the word maps.

5.18Counting matrices at one prime

Let q be either auxiliary prime. The number of invertible n-by-n matrices over the field of q elements is qn²Πn(q), where Πn(q) = ∏j=1n(1 − q−j). Choose the columns in order. Once i independent columns have been chosen, their span excludes precisely qi out of the qn choices for the next column. An index divides this count by the number of allowed level matrices. On the column side, these are upper triangular with diagonal entries 1. The strictly upper triangle has k(k − 1)/2 free entries.

The row has a central block of size k + 1 flanked by (m/2 − 1) singleton blocks on each side. Between different blocks all entries above the diagonal are free. Within the central block the first k positions have a free strictly upper triangle. Its final column has zeros in all k positions above its diagonal within that block. Thus the whole row matrix has r(r − 1)/2 − k free entries. Every choice has determinant one. Subtract the exponents of q in the two indices. The difference is r(r + 1)/2 + k − k(k + 1)/2 = A, where A = mk + m(m − 1)/2. The first k factors of Π cancel.

row index / column index = qA P(q),   P(q) = ∏j=k+1r(1 − q−j).

Check at q = 2, k = m = 2. The two invertible groups have orders (4 − 1)(4 − 2) = 6 and (8 − 1)(8 − 2)(8 − 4) = 168. Each level subgroup has one free binary entry, so its order is 2. The quotient of indices is 84/3 = 28, exactly 25(1 − 2−3). This checks the local identity in small ranks. The estimates for the full family use m ≥ 44.

5.20How a volume becomes a sum over lattice classes

The formula for the word scale uses the volume of a unitary group on the row side and a Hermitian genus mass on the column side. To compare ranks, we need both in the same units. A genus consists of lattices isometric at every finite place. Its mass is the sum of 1/|Aut(Λ)| over its global isometry classes. The proof starts in positive definite rank two, where the automorphism groups are finite.

Let Γ be the rational unitary group, G its adelic group and K the subgroup preserving the completed lattice at finite places and unrestricted at infinity. In the definite case the prescribed archimedean measures are probabilities. Applying the product normalization to the whole compact group at each infinite place gives μ(K) = 1. Pick representatives gi of the finite double quotient Γ∖G/K. In the class of gi, exactly |Γ ∩ giKgi−1| translates of a point by Γ land in giK. Weight that coset’s indicator by the reciprocal. Its sum over Γ is one on that class. Integrating the weighted indicators over G now gives the volume of a fundamental domain. The stabilizers are the lattice automorphism groups, so the result is the genus mass.

A finite model. Take G = S₃ and Γ = K = {1, (12)}. The two double cosets have representatives 1 and (13), with stabilizer orders 2 and 1. Their weights add to 3/2. Directly, μ(K) = 1 gives mass 1/2 to each element and a Γ-fundamental domain has three elements. This explains the inverse stabilizer in the formula. A deeper finite level K′ ⊂ K has measure 1/[K:K′]. Renormalizing that subgroup to measure one therefore multiplies the covolume by its index. In the word count the row uses its own index and the column uses its own, so their quotient is row index divided by column index.

5.21Why adjacent ranks have a predictable mass ratio

Write M for the new rank, f for the number of conjugate pairs of complex embeddings of the CM field, and v for half its root discriminant. The quadratic extension of its totally real subfield is unramified at every finite prime. For a totally positive definite integral Hermitian lattice Λ, count vectors whose squared lengths are at most j² at every embedding. Sum these counts over the genus using the reciprocal automorphism weights above. The zero vector contributes the mass μΛ. Grouping the other vectors by their represented value gives the same sum, now expressed through representation counts. Divide by j2fM and let j grow. The two ways of counting give

μΛ (πM/M!)f / (vfM δ) = (cM−1 λΛ/δ) M−f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

On the left, πM/M! is the volume of a unit ball in ℂM, and δ is the positive square root of the absolute norm of the lattice discriminant ideal. On the right, cM−1 is the mass constant for the preceding rank, λΛ is a product of local lattice corrections, and Lη(M) is the Euler product of the CM field. This second limit uses the representation-density formula and the asymptotic sum of its local factors. The zero vector’s separate contribution tends to zero after division. Cancel δ and use M!/M = (M − 1)!. For a lattice with an orthonormal integral basis every local lattice correction is one. The two standard masses consequently satisfy the following identity for the ranks M ≥ 3 used here.

massM / massM−1 = [((M − 1)!)(v/π)M]f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

For instance, take M = 3 and a finite prime of the totally real subfield of residue size 2. If it is inert, the unique prime above it has norm 4 and its Euler factor is (1 + 2−3)−1 = 8/9. If it splits, its two primes of norm 2 each contribute (1 − 2−3)−1/2, giving 8/7 together. These are factors at a single prime. Across the rank increments, the same positive rank-one constant occurs in both standard masses and cancels in their ratio.

To reach the indefinite row, the normalized unit-vector unfolding supplies the same ratio for a space and the orthogonal complement of a vector of norm +1 or −1. From definite rank two, use +1 to compare successive positive definite ranks. For a constant signature (P, Q) with P ≥ 2, induction on Q uses a −1 vector, whose complement has signature (P, Q − 1). The two inductions identify the row volume with the standard mass of its rank r. In the word-scale formula the column mass then cancels the common ranks, leaving exactly the increments M = k + 1, …, r. These are the factors estimated in the lower bound for each word.

5.23What survives in the quotient of dimensions?

Fix a place. Write its row as λ = (c0, …, ck−2, −b0, …, −bm−1) of length r = k + m − 1. Its first block is nonnegative and decreases in steps of at least one. The bj are positive and increase in steps of at least one. The column u0 > ⋯ > uk−1 belonging to the word interlaces the first block, with ui > ci > ui+1. Write V(y) = ∏i<j(yi − yj). Each cross-block gap ci + bj is at least bj, and each gap within the negative block is at least one. This proves the first inequality below.

V(λ) ≥ V(c)∏j bjk−1,   V(u) ≤ D2k−3V(c),   D = 8xeL.

For the second inequality, the column has k − 1 gaps touching its first entry and another k − 2 touching its last. Each is at most D. Each remaining gap ui − uj is bounded by the distinct gap ci−1 − cj. The unused adjacent gaps of c are at least one. Dividing the inequalities now cancels the factor V(c). For a small check take c = (4, 0), u = (6, 2, −1) and b = (3, 5). The row has gap product 7,560, the column has gap product 84, and their ratio is 90. This example illustrates the interlacing calculation alone.

The local factor in the mass identity is dρFr/V(u), with formal degree dρ and Fr = ∏h=0r−1h!. At the required separation between parameters of opposite signature, the discrete-series estimate with tolerance 1/3 gives dρ ≥ (2/3)V(λ)/Fr by Weyl’s dimension formula. Thus the row factorials cancel as well. The source allows a logarithmic loss of 2k log D + 2k(1 + log k) in the Vandermonde comparison. At the family threshold, 2(log 8 + 1 + log x) ≤ L and log(2k) ≤ L, so this loss is at most 5kL.

5.24Adding the losses in the mass identity

The geometric weights satisfy 0 < bj < wjρ ≤ (1 + 1/x)bj and wjρ ≤ 2eL. Then k log w − (k − 1) log b = log w + (k − 1) log(w/b) ≤ 2L + k/x. Each rank increment M = k + 1, …, r contributes a positive mass Euler product Lη(M). Group its local logarithms by the rational prime p. A prime ideal of residue degree d above p contributes at most (d/2)[−log(1 − p−M)] in absolute value. The residue degrees above p sum to at most the field degree 2f. Summing over p gives |log Lη(M)| ≤ f log ζ(M) ≤ f, since M ≥ 2. Averaging over the f places leaves a total cost at most m − 1 for the r − k rank increments.

Subtract S + mG from log Xu and multiply by k. In the mass identity the surplus m(m − 1)[log(v/π) + G]/2 is nonnegative. The two remaining discriminant terms cost at most kL + (m − 1)L/2, using 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and log(2v) ≤ L. The two auxiliary primes together cost at most 2. Add these amounts to the place and Euler losses.

8kL + (m − 1)L/2 + m + 2 + k ≤ 11kL,   log Xu ≥ S + mG − 11L.

Indeed, (m − 1)L/2 ≤ kL/2 and m + 2 + k ≤ 5kL/2 because 44 ≤ m ≤ k and L ≥ 1. For fixed family and constants ε > 0, C0, CY, a single threshold works for every admissible scale above it, every family index, every choice of spacing and weights satisfying the stated data, and every word. The later transfer from Xu to the chosen prime level has its own window loss.

5.25Why a real-place degree has the size of a Vandermonde product

The placewise mass estimate compares a row with the column belonging to a word. The row supplies a discrete series of the real unitary group U(p, q), an irreducible unitary representation σ with square-integrable matrix coefficients. For a nonzero vector w, its formal degree is ‖w‖4 divided by the integral of |⟨w, σ(g)w⟩|2. Multiplying the Haar measure by a positive number divides the degree by that number. The numerical comparison therefore requires a specific measure.

Let N = p + q with both signs present. The parameter λ has strictly decreasing entries indexed from 0, with λi − (N−1)/2 integral. Each index carries a sign, with p positive and q negative. Write Fn = ∏0≤a<na! and V(λ) = ∏i<j(λi − λj). On the normalized measure one has the following equality for the large-gap parameters used here.

d(λ) = V(λ)/FN,   FN = ∏i<j(j−i).

5.26How an integral fixes the missing constant

Imagine moving λ by integer steps. When an admissible step raises one coordinate by one, the degree and the Vandermonde change by exactly the same ratio. Along λi(t) = λi + t(N−1−i), for integers t ≥ 0, the steps can be ordered so that decreasing order and the gap survive. Thus d(λ(t))/V(λ(t)) stays constant. To find its value, let Tt be the lowest compact type, the finite-dimensional representation of U(p) × U(q) selected by the weight λ(t). Form Yt = tpq dim(Tt)/d(λ(t)).

Put A = ∏(j−i) over opposite-sign pairs i<j. On the algebraic side the compact Weyl dimension formula cancels the same-sign factors of the moving Vandermonde up to ratios tending to one. Indeed, if the moving gap is g, its ratio is (g+b)/g, where b counts opposite signs strictly between the indices. Each opposite-sign pair leaves t/[λi−λj+t(j−i)], tending to 1/(j−i).

On the analytic side, polar coordinates use probability measure on the compact group and one complex coordinate per opposite-sign pair. The Haar density includes the constant c = FN/(πpqFpFq). Rescaling each complex coordinate by 1/√t absorbs tpq. The limiting squared coefficient has a Gaussian factor exp(−(j−i)|z|²) in each coordinate, whose plane integral is π/(j−i). The coefficient supplies a lower limit and an integrable upper bound supplies the matching upper limit. Comparing the two values of the same limit gives the stated degree.

V(λ)/[d(λ)FpFqA] = lim Yt = cπpq/A = FN/(FpFqA).

  • The coefficient of log(v/π) is f[(m − 1)k + m(m − 1)/2]. Since 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and m ≤ k, the normalized contribution is at most 3/2. The term in −log(2v) is nonpositive.

For the last inequality even the looser k ≥ 5 suffices. The constants independent of CY sum to at most 3/2 + 1/45 + 4/3 + 12 = 1337/90, strictly below 15. 5.30Which changes of scale cancel?

Let K0 be the imaginary quadratic host field of discriminant −dK, and E the extension used in the host. Take a nonzero integral ideal 𝔠 of K0 with norm prime to 2dK. If Δ is the discriminant of its embedded elliptic lattice and δ12 = Δ, the rescaled lattice Λ = δ·φ0(𝔠) has discriminant one. Take any number field M inside ℂ containing the specified images of E and the Weierstrass invariants g2(Λ), g3(Λ). For each embedding ρ of M, transport those two invariants and let Aρ > 0 be the area of the corresponding period lattice.

Fix a host embedding label τ. The source spans the vectors of conjugates of elements of the host fractional ideal and intersects the resulting module with the τ-coordinate line. Write ℓτ for the resulting module inside M and DM = [M : ℚ]. For a nonzero s in ℓτ, put I(s) = [ℓτ : 𝒪Ms]. The measured quantity is

mρ(s) = log(π |ρ(s)|² / Aρ),   Ω̄τ = (2 log I(s) − ∑ρ mρ(s)) / DM.

When ℓτ has generator a, every such s has form ca with 0 ≠ c ∈ 𝒪M. The index is |NM/ℚ(c)|. Meanwhile each local logarithm increases by 2 log |ρ(c)|. Their sum increases by twice the logarithm of precisely that index. Thus Ω̄τ equals the average of −mρ(a). For a small check, take the free line ℤ[i] and use the test element s = 1 + i. Its multiples form a sublattice of index 2. Each of the two embeddings contributes an extra log 2, cancelling the finite contribution 2 log 2. This example checks the normalization in a free line.

Set B equal to the absolute norm of the relative different. Its half-different identity gives b² = B. The discriminant tower formula gives |disc(E)| = B(dK)h. Since rd(E) = |disc(E)|1/n, the correction (2/n) log b equals log rd(E) − log √dK.

For the area term the proof compares the conjugate lattices with a family indexed by ideal classes. Over a common extension their homotheties give 6 log Aoriginal = 6 log Afamily + log |ρ(u)|, with u a discriminant unit. The unit contributes zero to the sum over embeddings. Averaging over the extension gives the same mean as over M, because each embedding occurs with the same multiplicity. The Chowla–Selberg class-sum formula then evaluates the area mean as γ + log(2π/√dK) − dχ, where dχ = Re(L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ)) for the host quadratic character. This dχ is the scalar denoted d in the main-term calculation above. Subtracting the correction cancels log √dK. For every compatible M and every τ this gives

Ω̄τ = γ + log(2π/rd(E)) − dχ = Ωlog.

This identifies the scalar that occurs earlier with v = rd(E)/2. The calculation uses the CM family of period lattices, the Chowla–Selberg evaluation and the ideal-index formula as inputs.

6Theta lifts, local factors and the Galois input

How can a theorem attaching Galois representations in odd dimension give one in even dimension? Lift the same automorphic representation twice to a larger odd rank, adding different character lists each time. The shared part can then be recovered. Both global theta integrals must produce a nonzero form for this argument to start.

What is being lifted? · Two parallel lifts · Recovering the even-dimensional row · The iterated chain · Whittaker factors · Split and inert places · The finite test vector · Real places · Continuation · Split lattice calculation · Inert cell calculation

6.1What is being lifted?

A Hermitian form measures lengths using both a field and its conjugation. On two complex coordinates the example is ⟨x,y⟩ = x₁y₁ + x₂y₂. Its unitary group consists of the changes of coordinates preserving this pairing. For a number field we can make such a change at each place. An adelic group element collects these choices, integral at almost every finite place. A rational change of coordinates gives the same change simultaneously in all completions.

An automorphic form here is a function on the adelic group, invariant under those rational changes on the left and satisfying additional finiteness and regularity conditions. Translating its argument on the right produces a space of functions carrying a group action. The irreducible space being lifted is U, and φ is one vector in it. A theta kernel converts φ into a function on another group by integration. To show that this conversion retains some information, one proves that a resulting vector has positive squared norm. At a good finite prime the commuting Hecke operators then provide a list of spectral parameters, with multiplicities, which can be compared on the two sides.

6.2Two parallel lifts to odd rank

Let E be a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of its totally real subfield F. The version used here assumes that E/F is unramified at all finite places, that E contains a square root of a negative rational integer, and that [F : ℚ] is even. At every nonsplit finite place the underlying prime of F has odd residue characteristic, norm greater than three and does not divide the absolute different of F. Take an even rank n ≥ 1 and an automorphic representation U of the definite unitary group of rank n. Fix its highest weights λ at the complex embeddings and a finite split place w₀ of E.

For a Hermitian source with identity Gram matrix and signature (n, 0), the lifting theorem gives a rank threshold d₀. The proof chooses t = 2(d₀ + n) + 1. Both targets are definite skew-Hermitian models of rank D = n + t, an odd integer above the threshold. Each lift uses its own compatible pair of splitting Hecke characters. The proof takes a common lower bound b for the components of λ at the chosen complex embedding above each real place and chooses their target exponents so that mW,j(v) ≤ 2b − D. Thus every required archimedean inequality D + mW,j(v) ≤ 2λv,k holds. Applying the same rank theorem once for each pair produces U₁ and U₂.

There is one common algebraic Hecke character κ, and two lists ψj,h of t algebraic Hecke characters. No character from the first list equals any character from the second as a global character. At a split place w where κ and list j are unramified and U has a Satake multiset, write B(w) for its algebraically normalized eigenvalues. Unramified means the character is trivial on local units. Its value at a uniformizer is then well defined. The target eigenvalues obey the following multiset identity, with multiplicities retained.

Bj(w) = κ(w)−1B(w) ⊔ {ψj,h(w) ∣ 0 ≤ h < t}.

At infinity the target weight jumps are the union of the original jumps shifted by the weight of κ and the negatives of the weights of the added characters. At the chosen w₀ the construction specifically guarantees that κ and every member of list 1 are unramified. Distinct global characters can agree in value at an individual prime. The proof compares their associated global Galois characters.

6.3Why each global theta lift is nonzero

The lifting theorem first obtains a real threshold L for integrability of a height power against Haar measure. Taking an integer N > 2L and d₀ = max(N, 2n) gives both D ≥ 2n and L < D/2. For splitting characters with the prescribed restrictions and archimedean exponents, the real-place pairing supplies a nonzero vector f∞ in the Weil model and a nonzero automorphic form φ with matching type. The outstanding choice is the finite-place Schwartz vector ffin.

Let ω be the Weil representation of the source and target adelic unitary groups on test functions on adelic n-by-D matrices over F. For a source group element g and a target element h, its theta kernel sums the translated test function over rational matrices, diagonally embedded into the adeles. With DX the model’s source integration domain, the lift of φ is the function of h given by

Θ(Φ, φ)(h) = ∫DX (∑ξ∈Matn×D(F) [ω(g, h)Φ](ξ)) φ(g) dμ(g).

This convention conjugates the source form. The matrix coefficient used to test nonvanishing pairs ω(g, 1)Φ with Φ using additive Haar measure on the adelic matrix space. The source coefficient pairs the right translate of φ with φ on DX.

Set Φ = f∞ ⊗ ffin. Write cΦ(g) for the Weil matrix coefficient and mφ(g) for the source matrix coefficient. The Rallis input says the following integral converges and must vanish if the theta transform of (Φ, φ) is identically zero.

I(Φ, φ) = ∫ cΦ(g) mφ(g) dg.

Choose a finite set S containing enough places to control the level of φ, the ramification and the tail estimate. Use a local bump vector at each place of S and the model's vacuum vector elsewhere. The proof decomposes the integral into archimedean, finite-in-S and outside-S factors. The Schur calculation supplies a nonzero scalar and the chosen coefficient is nonzero at the identity. A compact open set of positive measure supplies the main contribution. A bound on the outside-S tail gives the strict estimate that prevents cancellation. This proves I(Φ, φ) ≠ 0 for the chosen data. The resulting theta transform is an automorphic form. An equivariant projection onto an automorphic constituent preserves a nonzero component, yielding a target representation to which the weight and local-parameter statements apply. The finite vectors may be chosen separately for the two lifts.

More explicitly, after integrating the archimedean and selected finite-place factors, the last integral has an integrand equal to a constant r > 0 on a compact open subgroup K. Its norm away from K is bounded by r times a nonnegative function w. The tail choice makes ∫Kᶜ w dμ < μ(K). Thus the contribution from K has absolute value rμ(K), strictly larger than the maximum possible contribution from its complement. The other factors are a positive Haar volume and a nonzero scalar.

6.4Recovering the even-dimensional representation

To see the danger in subtracting eigenvalues at just one prime, take the cyclic group of order four generated by g. The two characters taking g to 1 and −1 agree at g². A list of values at g² cannot tell which character was added. Once two semisimple representations have been identified as representations of the entire group, one can compare the multiplicities of each irreducible constituent and subtract known character lines. The argument below explains how the good primes supply that global comparison.

Apply the available odd-rank Galois theorem twice, each time in dimension D. It attaches continuous semisimple ℓ-adic representations ρ₁ and ρ₂ to U₁ and U₂. Let χj,h be the ℓ-adic character attached to ψj,h, and Pj(g, X) the characteristic polynomial of ρj(g). Injectivity of the Hecke-to-Galois character map preserves disjointness across the two lists. Comparing normalized Frobenius data at good split places and using density gives, for every Galois element g,

P₁(g, X) ∏h(X − χ2,h(g)) = P₂(g, X) ∏h(X − χ1,h(g)).

The representations ρ₁ ⊕ ⨁χ2,h and ρ₂ ⊕ ⨁χ1,h consequently have the same characteristic polynomials. The proof uses semisimplicity and a one-character splitting theorem to separate a line χ1,h from ρ₁ and retain a comparison identity for the complement. Induction removes all t lines, preserving continuity, semisimplicity and the required local conditions. The remaining dimension is D − t = n. Tensoring with the ℓ-adic character of κ restores the original normalization. Given a source Satake multiset at w₀, unramifiedness of the first list supplies the local conclusion there. Repeating the construction at each split place gives weakly compatible representations. Their isomorphism transports the local conclusions to a common representation.

The strong local–global statement attaches a continuous semisimple ℓ-adic representation of dimension a to regular algebraic polarized cuspidal data on GLa over a CM field. It includes comparisons away from ℓ and Hodge–Tate data above ℓ. Its closing proof supplies the global theta-lift theorem to the geometry construction. The intervening proof combines the two-lift input with odd-rank geometry, congruence and a limiting argument, then passes to the local–global statement.

A separate calculation in the long-chain application concerns a single row and its adjoint. It has its own rank variables and its own hypothesis ensuring that the lifted row survives.

6.5The row and its adjoint

An automorphic form is a function on an arithmetic quotient of a group with specified transformation and regularity properties. A theta lift uses an integral kernel to carry such functions between groups. In the part of the proof examined here, the relevant spaces of forms at fixed level and weight are presented as finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. This allows a precise question about nonvanishing before any local representation is identified.

Fix an index i. It specifies a row number j and a tuple of character data μ. Suppress these two subscripts. Write M for the row space and V for the target space. There is a linear map P from V to M. Its adjoint T goes from M to V. The row space has designated subspaces Mσ for its types σ. A type here labels a component of the space of forms. The target has subspaces Vπ for target types π.

The required Gram hypothesis says that PT acts by a real scalar λσ on Mσ, strictly positive whenever Mσ is nonzero. For every f in that subspace the adjoint identity gives

‖Tf‖2 = Re ⟨f, PTf⟩ = λσ ‖f‖2.

Thus a nonzero row vector survives the upward map. Positive semidefiniteness, which is automatic for an operator times its adjoint, would only yield λσ ≥ 0. Strict positivity is a genuine arithmetic input. The point-condition construction gets the local scalars from its linked isotropy and scalar hypotheses before calling the pairing theorem.
