6.6Locating one target type

Call σ and π paired if there are f ∈ Mσ and v ∈ Vπ with ⟨v, Tf⟩ ≠ 0. Assume that the target subspaces span V, are pairwise orthogonal, and that for each σ at most one π can pair with it. The uniqueness property is the upward form of Howe duality in this argument.

Choose nonzero f in Mσ. If every target component were orthogonal to Tf, their span would also be orthogonal to it. This would force ⟨Tf, Tf⟩ = 0, contrary to the Gram identity. Some π therefore pairs with σ. Now take any g in the same row subspace. A nonzero inner product of Tg with a different component would supply a second paired type, contrary to uniqueness. Since the orthogonal components span V, Tg lies in Vπ. The entire image T(Mσ) is a nonzero subspace of Vπ.

6.7Reading the parameter at a split place

Work with a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real number field. At a finite place of the real field which splits into two places in the CM field, the relevant unitary groups have local descriptions by general linear groups. Write K for the local field at the chosen place. The source rank is r = k + m − 1 and the target rank is r + t. The rank data impose r + 5 ≤ t. In particular r < t, the inequality used in the local classification theorem. These are dimensions of underlying linear groups. The spaces of automorphic forms in the Gram calculation can have different dimensions.

A representation assigns an invertible linear action to each group element. A smooth representation of a group over K is one in which each vector is fixed by an open subgroup. An irreducible representation has no proper nonzero invariant subspace. Unitarisability asks for an invariant positive inner product. The classification step takes a smooth, irreducible, unitarisable representation τ of GLr(K), a smooth irreducible representation Π of GLr+t(K), and a smooth unitary character μ of K×. Its pairing hypothesis asks for a nonzero equivariant bilinear map on test functions and vectors. The test functions are locally constant and compactly supported on the space of (r + t)-by-r matrices. Equivariance says that acting on the function and the target vector is compatible with the source group action. The actual comparison applies this condition to a determinant twist of the target representation.

Given the stated inputs on finiteness and irreducibility of induced representations, the local theorem identifies Π with the parabolically induced product of τ and μ ∘ det on GLt(K). Parabolic induction here uses the subgroup of upper block triangular matrices, with diagonal blocks of sizes r and t. These blocks act on the tensor product of the two input representations. The construction extends this action to the full group by induction. In the application, Π is the twisted target and the comparison removes the twist afterward.

What information survives on the Galois side? A local parameter records the local representation in a form with well-defined direct sums and twists by characters. At each split place w, let Aw denote the source parameter and μw the parameter of the character. Write μw[b] for its real-power twist with exponent b. Let ηw−1 denote the final inverse character in this normalization. The paired target has parameter

(Aw ⊕ ⨁0≤h<t μw[(t − 1)/2 − h]) ⊗ ηw−1.

There are t one-dimensional terms. Their exponents decrease by one from (t − 1)/2 to −(t − 1)/2. They account for the entire increase in rank. The parameter-translation laws turn the induced product into a sum, identify the segment for μ ∘ det, and then remove the determinant twist to give η⁻¹ on the full sum.

A rank check. If k = 6, m = 2 and t = 13, the rank formula gives r = 7 and target rank 20. The extra block has 13 character terms with exponents 6, 5, …, −6. This is an example of the rank arithmetic. Choosing the three integers supplies none of the automorphic forms or nonzero pairings needed by the theorem.

6.9Why a nonzero vector survives the iterated lifts

The parallel arrows above recover a Galois representation. The following successive arrows serve a different purpose. One needs a downward map onto an entire space of functions. Nonvanishing on a basis alone is insufficient. For the map (x,y) ↦ x + y, both coordinate vectors survive and their difference dies. The proof must also distinguish the images of different labels. That distinction gives injectivity in the upward direction and hence surjectivity for its finite-dimensional adjoint.

At stage j, the Hermitian space Yj has rank r + jt, where r = k + m − 1. For 0 ≤ j < m, the next lift adds t dimensions. Write Cj for the multiplicity space at the prescribed level and archimedean type. Its elements turn test vectors into automorphic functions. There is a downward map pj from Cj+1 to Cj. The upward construction finds the adjoint image of a Hecke eigenvector and proves it is nonzero. This lets that vector enter the next lift.

Fix a nonzero eigenvector u at stage j with local parameter family B. Write S for the excluded finite places. With polynomial test data φ and a finite-type vector v, put F = u(v). The upward integral uses the conjugate theta kernel against F. A local zeta nonvanishing theorem supplies φ and v for which an integral I of Weil and source matrix coefficients, over elements integral outside S, is nonzero. This already forces F ≠ 0. Let L₀ be the holomorphic value at s = t/2 of the partial, twisted function LS(s + ½). The Hecke form of the doubling identity gives the Petersson square of the conjugate upward lift.

⟨ΘφF, ΘφF⟩ = vol(Yj+1) · L₀ · I / dS(t/2).

The volume of the target quotient is positive. The partial normalizing factor dS(t/2) is nonzero. Once L₀ ≠ 0, all factors on the right are nonzero. A zero lift would give a zero Petersson square.

Why L₀ is nonzero at this step. The proof starts from the parameter family at stage zero with the prescribed half-rank bound. It twists that family by a unitary character. Its Euler product converges and is nonzero at (t + 1)/2 because t ≥ r + 5. Each previous step also contributed a length-t segment. For its index a, with 1 ≤ a ≤ j, the corresponding quotient character is μa μj+1−1. The proof uses the distinct infinity exponents of these characters to obtain an entire partial L-function nonzero at every integer from 1 through t. At the desired point the segment arguments are

t/2 + ½ + (t − 1)/2 − h = t − h,   0 ≤ h < t.

Thus the last segment factor is evaluated at 1, where absolute Euler-product convergence alone would leave a gap. The quotient-character theorem covers that endpoint. Multiplying the twisted initial factor by the finite product of segment factors gives a holomorphic continuation near t/2 with nonzero value L₀. At stage zero the segment product is empty.

Finite-dimensionality and the positive Hermitian metric now give x ∈ Cj+1 satisfying ⟨y, x⟩j+1 = ⟨pjy, u⟩j for all y. The span of target evaluations and the adjoint pairing identify the nonzero lift above with an actual evaluation x(w₀). Consequently x ≠ 0. Local transfer identifies its parameter family outside S. With α and β the source and target character values at a place w, it multiplies each member of B(w) by α/β and appends the multiset of t terms α qw(t−1)/2−h. Here qw is the residue-field size. The induction applies the same argument to x with this new family.

For each chain of length at most m satisfying these hypotheses, the downward composite maps onto C₀. Write a possible kernel vector as a sum of simultaneous eigenvectors and group the terms whose parameters agree outside the excluded places. Inside one group the sum again has those eigenvalues. If that sum is nonzero, the nonvanishing theorem applies to the sum itself, even if its eigenspace has dimension greater than one. Across different groups the parameter update is injective and the resulting eigenspaces are linearly independent. Their images can add to zero only if every grouped component was zero. This proves injectivity of the adjoint. The following sections compute the local factors, choose the test vector and continue the doubled integral to the point used in this argument. The span step also uses the stated representation-theoretic inputs.

6.11Where the quotient volume comes from

Doubling puts the two copies of the source in a single hyperbolic space. There is a test vector Δ(Φ₁, Φ₂) on the doubled space whose kernel on the embedded pair (g₁, g₂) recovers the product of the original kernels. In the source’s orientation this product is χB(det g₂) times the doubled kernel. The Siegel–Weil section of Δ restricted to (g,1) gives W(g). Extending the section by the height contributes exactly h(g)s−s₀. The determinant character explains the inverse twist in the doubling integral.

Siegel–Weil identifies the normalized mean of the doubled theta kernel with an Eisenstein value at s₀. For b ≤ 2a the proof invokes the convergent-range theorem with a + w < b, where w is the dimension of a maximal totally isotropic subspace of B. For b > 2a, the series identity applies in the convergence region s₀ > a/2. When the two source integrals are paired, the squared norm of each kernel on the target grows at most polynomially. Cuspidal rapid decay makes the absolute triple integral finite, so the target pairing can be performed first. Converting the normalized target mean into the Petersson integral multiplies it by vol([H]). This produces a holomorphic continuation value of the full doubling integral. The proof first works at the frame lattice, then transfers it to the given self-dual lattice.

On the theta side, integrate the doubled kernel over the target quotient [H] and divide by its volume. Its second conclusion identifies the holomorphic value of the Eisenstein family at s₀.

E(g,s₀) = vol([H])−1 ∫[H] θφ(g,h) dh,   s₀ = (b − a)/2.

The chain uses ranks 1 ≤ a < b. Its hypotheses require the Witt index w of the target to be zero or satisfy a + w < b. Its convergence and the region of absolute convergence of the Eisenstein series are two different statements.

Construct the section and move between models. At s₀ the section f is built from the translate of φ by g. Restrict that function to pairs (v,−v) and integrate over a fundamental region for the rational lattice in v. For example, at the identity, the doubled test function Δ(Φ₁,Φ₂) restricts to Φ₁(v) Φ₂(v). Thus its section value there is the original inner product. The Levi action contributes χB−1(det M) and the normalized absolute determinant to the power s₀ + a/2 = b/2. The compact translates of the Fock vector span a finite-dimensional space. Applying the linear section map to that space gives the same finiteness for the compact translates of f. To move away from s₀, multiply f(g) by the positive Siegel height h(g)s−s₀. It equals one as a multiplier on the compact subgroup, and increases the determinant exponent to s + a/2.

In the range b ≤ 2a the proof changes coordinates to a standard Schrödinger model, in which the theta kernel is a sum of a Schwartz–Bruhat function over rational vectors. The chart and a translation put the chosen compact data into standard position and carry the Fock polynomial to a polynomial Gaussian at infinity. The individual theta kernels then agree at the corresponding group arguments, hence so do their means. The chart also identifies the rational parabolic cosets. The two choices of height give a factor Ds₀−s in the comparison of the flat sections, where D is a fixed positive absolute determinant. Where does the strict half-plane come from?

At the identity, let hγ be the positive height of a representative of a rational Siegel coset. The spherical section to be summed has magnitude hγT, with T = Re s + a/2. Arithmetic reduction assigns to each coset a tuple j of a nonnegative integers. For a base B > 1 and a constant C, its height is at most C B−∑j. For any fixed tuple the number of cosets in any finite sample with this label is at most C Ba∑j. Multiplying those bounds gives a bound for the whole label.

∑γ with label j hγT ≤ C1+T (Ba−T)∑j.

For T > a, summing over the tuple gives a product of a geometric series with common ratio Ba−T < 1. This bounds every finite subsum, establishing summability of the nonnegative spherical majorant. Iwasawa decomposition and the bound for the section on the compact subgroup transfer convergence to the flat section and its translates. The terms vary holomorphically in s through powers of positive heights. Choose a small vertical strip around the point, with both edges inside the half-plane. Each term is bounded in absolute value throughout the strip by the sum of its absolute values at the two endpoint real parts, since a positive height raised to a real exponent is monotone in that exponent. Both endpoint majorants are summable. The holomorphic terms therefore converge locally uniformly.

Their Gram determinant is the determinant for an integral lattice basis times the square of the sublattice index. Comparing this identity with the product bound on the selected row lengths controls the index and keeps the dyadically rescaled row matrix away from singularity. Each nonzero rational entry has a nonzero infinite component, while the dilates tend uniformly to zero there. Its jth successive minimum λj is the smallest radius of a closed ball about zero containing j linearly independent lattice vectors. Discreteness gives vectors attaining these radii in a nested sequence of spans. Orthogonalize the resulting real basis. Scale the new orthogonal direction at step j by 1/λj, obtaining a linear map T. If the last nonzero orthogonal coordinate of a lattice vector x is its jth, then x lies outside the previous span. To allow for tied minima, let k be the first index with λk = λj. If x were shorter, it and the first k − 1 vectors would give k independent vectors shorter than λk. Thus ‖x‖ ≥ λj. Every nonzero coordinate of x is scaled by at least 1/λj. Thus ‖Tx‖ ≥ 1.

The inverse image of the open unit ball under T contains no nonzero lattice point. Its volume is vol(ball)·∏λj. By the symmetric convex body bound this is at most 2rcovol(L). To see the volume threshold, shrink the body by one half. If it had more volume than a fundamental cell of L, two of its translates into that cell would overlap. The difference of the two original points would be a nonzero lattice vector in the original body, by convexity and symmetry. The unit ball contains the open cube of side 2/√r, in orthonormal coordinates. For r ≥ 1 these observations give

λ₁ ⋯ λr ≤ rr/2 covol(L).

The covolume is taken in the real span of L. For an integral basis u with image under the row map φ, it is √det Gram(φu).

A rational relation between the lifts would, after clearing denominators, be an integral relation between the independent images. At least one lift therefore lies outside the previous field span. Choose it as the next row wi+1. Since the minima increase, the first radius in each block, raised to the power D, is bounded by the product of the D radii in that block. Consequently

∏i=1n ‖φwi‖D ≤ ∏k=0n−1 λDk+1D ≤ λ₁ ⋯ λr.

Here φ is only required to be additive and ℤ-linear. It sends a row to its archimedean coordinates after the given change of variables. The dimension argument takes place over E before applying φ.

Choose a dyadic scale ai with ‖φwi‖ ≤ ai < 2‖φwi‖. Dividing each row by its scale bounds every entry of the resulting matrix c. Take all D integral-basis multiples of each of the n selected rows. They span a full-rank sublattice of the original row lattice, of index m ≥ 1. Its squared volume is m² det Gram(φu). Each of the D real rows coming from wi carries the same scale ai. With G(c) the Gram determinant of all the rescaled rows, we get

The product of the scales is bounded in the form ∏ aiD ≤ 2rrr/2 covol(L). Cancel the covolume. This bounds m² by a constant times G(c). Since m ≥ 1, it also bounds G(c) away from zero. The upper bound gives a uniform bound for the integer m. Taking the factorial of an integer upper bound makes one integer M divisible by every possible m. Multiplication by M therefore puts every original row in the module generated by the selected rows.

Rounding leaves an error of size at most 2−k. The finite component stays in a fixed compact set. Across the d real places the number of scalar centres is bounded by C₀ bk, where b = 2d, C₀ = (2R + 1)d and B = b².

Choose δ in E with conjugate −δ so that (1,δ) is an F-basis. A skew-Hermitian matrix S can be described by n² scalar adelic coordinates tij. Its (i,j) entry is (tij−tji) + δ(tij+tji). On the diagonal this is 2δtii. Off the diagonal the two ordered entries share two scalar coordinates. Cover tij at depth μi+μj. Its error then carries the factor corresponding to the left and right diagonal scalings. Combining the coordinate choices writes S as a rational matrix plus a centre y plus DμωDμ, where Dμ = diag(sμᵢ) and the entries of ω lie in a fixed compact set. The finite set Yμ of centres is the image of the product of the scalar grids. Its size is at most the number of grid tuples.

|Yμ| ≤ ∏i,j C₀ bμᵢ+μⱼ = C₀n² b2n∑μᵢ = C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ.

A rank-two count. Take one real place, a scalar grid with R = 1 and label μ = (1,0). The four ordered depths are 2, 1, 1 and 0. The corresponding lists of integer numerators have 9, 5, 5 and 3 entries. Their product gives 675 tuples. The formula above permits 3⁴·4² = 1,296. These numbers count candidates and bound their image. Counting rational cosets still requires the multiplicity argument.

Why a centre has bounded multiplicity. Subtract the rational unipotent term and put the compact error into a matrix w(q). In the Cayley coordinates the proof obtains a rational invertible matrix Z(q) = z(μ,y)w(q), with w(q) in a fixed compact set. The map q ↦ Z(q) is injective. In fact, equality of two such matrices makes the original rational representatives differ on the left by an element stabilizing the diagonal subspace. They represent the same Siegel coset.

Fix μ and a centre y. For a nonempty finite collection of cosets using them, choose one member q₀. Multiplying by Z(q₀)−1 cancels the common left factor z(μ,y). The relative matrices w(q₀)−1w(q) are rational and belong to a fixed compact set, independent of μ, y and q₀. Each matrix entry belongs to a finite set of rational points, so there are at most N possible relative matrices. Left multiplication preserves injectivity. Each chosen centre can therefore account for at most N cosets. Summing over all available centres gives an upper bound even when some centres are unused and others occur for multiple cosets.

#{q ∈ A with label μ} ≤ N |Yμ| ≤ N C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ   for every finite sample A.

A uniform finite bound on all finite samples also bounds the full fibre, since a larger fibre would contain a finite sample exceeding it. The summability proof uses exactly the finite-sample statement. Multiplication by the height bound raised to the power T gives the geometric decay when T > n.

How do the Fourier coefficients recover the theta mean?

Consider the lower range of the Siegel–Weil formula. Write n for the source rank and m for the dimension of the target Hermitian space V over the quadratic extension E/F. Thus n < m ≤ 2n and n + w < m, where w is the Witt index of V. The evaluation point s₀ = (m − n)/2 can lie on the boundary of absolute convergence or to its left. Take a test function Φ in the global Fock subspace of the Schrödinger model. With this input we can compare one frequency of the two sides at a time. The frequencies are rational Hermitian n × n matrices β. A frequency is nondegenerate when det β ≠ 0.

For an automorphic function F, move g by the upper unipotent matrix u(b) with diagonal blocks 1 and upper right block b. Invariance under rational unipotent translations makes this function of b periodic. Its domain is the Hermitian adelic matrices modulo the rational ones. Use a fundamental region 𝒟 of volume one. Put ⟨β,b⟩ = ½ TrE/F(tr(βb)), with rational entries embedded in the adeles and the field trace extended to the adeles.

Cβ(F)(g) = ∫𝒟 F(u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

On the theta side, a frequency selects a Gram matrix. Write φ = ω(g)Φ for the translated test function. A rational tuple x of n vectors of V contributes φ(h−1x) to the theta kernel. Translating by u(b) multiplies this summand by ψ(⟨Gram(x),b⟩). The target action of h preserves the Gram matrix. After weighting by the inverse β-character, integration gives 1 if Gram(x) = β and 0 otherwise. Absolute theta convergence justifies grouping tuples by Gram matrix, averaging over [U(V)] and integrating the resulting character series. When det β ≠ 0, every tuple in that fibre has rank n, since rank(x∗Gram(V)x) ≤ rank(x). Thus Cβ(I)(g) is the normalized average of the sum over precisely these full-rank tuples, where I is the theta mean.

On the Eisenstein side, the same frequency selects the open cell. For Re z > n/2 the coset sum has a summable bound on a compact set of representatives. This permits integration of the sum by cells. On each other cell, when det β ≠ 0, there is a translation preserving its contribution and multiplying its character by a scalar different from 1. Its integral is therefore zero. The open-cell cosets are indexed by rational Hermitian translations. Their translates of 𝒟 cover the full adelic Hermitian space, giving the integral below. Here w is the Weyl element interchanging the two isotropic coordinate spaces and fz is the flat section.

Cβ(E(·,z))(g) = ∫Hermn(𝔸) fz(w u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

The Weyl action is a Fourier transform. Evaluating it at zero integrates the translated test function against the Gram character. Consequently the section in this integral is the Gram-character integral of φ times the height H(w u(b)g)z−s₀. This identifies the unfolded family on the right half-plane with the Whittaker integral for β. Its holomorphic value at s₀ is the same full-rank fibre average computed on the theta side. The input used here combines finite-place factors, the unramified Gram-density calculation, a real-place computation, global factorization and a low-rank density identity. Finite linear combination treats the compact argument, then the Iwasawa decomposition transports the identity to arbitrary g.

What can be invisible to all the nondegenerate coefficients?

Take the additive group of symmetric 2 × 2 matrices over the field of three elements. This finite example has 27 elements. Set ζ = exp(2πi/3), T = diag(1,0) and F(B) = ζB₁₁. The normalized β-coefficient is the average of ζtr((T−β)B). At β = T all 27 terms are 1. For β ≠ T, at least one of the three matrix coordinates has a nonzero coefficient in this linear form. Its sum is 1 + ζ + ζ² = 0. The off-diagonal entry appears with multiplier 2, which is invertible in this field. Hence every invertible β has coefficient zero, although F(0) = 1. The missing information sits at the rank-one frequency T.

How does the proof rule out such a discrepancy? At a real place selected using the Witt-index inequality, choose a compactly supported test function η whose Fourier transform vanishes on singular Hermitian matrices. Suppose a continuous automorphic function F has zero full-rank coefficients for all g. Integrate its unipotent translates against η. The β-coefficient of this convolution factors into the β-coefficient of F and the transform of η at the associated local frequency. For invertible β the first factor is zero. For singular β the associated local matrix is singular too, so the second factor is zero. All Fourier coefficients of the convolution now vanish, so Fourier uniqueness on the compact Hermitian quotient makes the convolution zero. Density and continuity give the same vanishing with a group translation on either side of the unipotent argument.

Removing a possible pole and computing the value

At this real place, first take the Gaussian Fock vector (the constant polynomial 1). The local signature condition gives a choice of η and of the two translations for which a compact-group average defines an operator T with nonzero scalar c(0) on the theta mean of this vector. On the corresponding regularized Eisenstein family the scalar is c(z−s₀). Meanwhile, the convolution argument shows that T kills every automorphic discrepancy with zero full-rank coefficients. On a discrepancy with eigenvalue c(0), this forces the discrepancy itself to vanish.

To see where holomorphy enters, write the continued Eisenstein family as A(z)/d(z) with holomorphic numerator and polynomial denominator. Factor d(z) = (z−s₀)kd₁(z) with d₁(s₀) ≠ 0. The full-rank coefficient identities ensure that while a power remains in the denominator, the regularized numerator at the point has zero full-rank coefficients. Its eigenvalue forces that value to vanish, so one can divide the numerator by z−s₀ holomorphically and repeat. After k divisions, the difference between the resulting numerator at s₀ and d₁(s₀)I is killed by T and has eigenvalue c(0). It is zero. Division by d₁ now gives the required value.

What does a full-rank Whittaker factor count at a good finite place?

The open-cell integral compares a Fourier coefficient of the Eisenstein series with the mean of tuples of vectors having Gram matrix T. At a good finite place v, this comparison has a concrete arithmetic content. Count the tuples whose Gram matrix agrees with T modulo increasing powers of a uniformizer. Once the measures are fixed, the normalized count gives the local Whittaker value at z₀ = (M−n)/2, where M is the dimension of the Hermitian space and n is the number of vectors.

Write q for the size of the residue field of Fv. At the places treated here, 2 is a unit, the local quadratic algebra is unramified, the forms J and T are integral with unit determinant, and the scalar character ψv has conductor the valuation ring. The integral lattice is trace-self-dual. Set ε = −1 when the quadratic algebra is the unramified field, and ε = +1 when it splits. The Schwartz function is the characteristic function of the integral M × n matrix lattice. A nonzero rational det T gives this unit condition at almost all places.

Count one Gram fibre. Let Nk be the number of distinct matrices X modulo ϖk satisfying X∗JX ≡ T. Here ∗ is conjugate transpose. There are q2kMn possible input matrices and qkn² Hermitian targets. The density compares the proportion of matrices in this fibre with the proportion one would obtain if every target occurred equally often.

αk(J,T) = Nk · qkn²/q2kMn = ∏j=0n−1 (1 − (ε/q)M−j),   k ≥ 1,   n ≤ M.

At level one a change of basis reduces the unimodular target to the identity. Solutions are orthonormal frames over the residue algebra. Choose one vector of norm one, then choose the next in its orthogonal complement. In dimension r, the norm-one count is q2r−1(1−(ε/q)r). The successive dimensions M, …, M−n+1 give the product above after normalization.

Why does the density stay constant at deeper levels?

Lift a solution modulo ϖk by writing its next representative as X+ϖkY. For k ≥ 1 the quadratic term in Y disappears modulo ϖk+1. The correction must solve the linear equation Y∗JX+X∗JY = H in the residue algebra, with H Hermitian. It is solvable for every H. For instance, since 2 and T are invertible here, take Y = ½XT−1H. The linear map has a domain with q2Mn elements and a codomain with qn² elements. Every fibre has q2Mn−n² elements. Thus Nk+1 gains exactly the factor cancelled by the next density normalization.

A Gram fibre over nine elements. Take ℚ(i) over ℚ at the inert prime 3, J = I₃ and T = I₂. Then q = 3 and ε = −1. In 𝔽₉ the norm of a+bi is a²+b² in 𝔽₃. There are 252 choices for a norm-one column of length three. For each, its two-dimensional orthogonal complement has 24 norm-one columns. This gives 6,048 frames among 9⁶ matrices at the first level. The normalized density is 6,048/3⁸ = 224/243 = (1+3−3)(1−3−2). Each frame has 3⁸ lifts to level two.

Which integral gives this number? Use the self-dual Haar measure on the matrix space for its Weil pairing and the self-dual Haar measure on the Hermitian matrices for their trace pairing. Write ⟨T,b⟩ for half the quadratic-algebra trace of tr(Tb). The source integrates the following expression in b. Inside it the character has positive Gram phase, and the Fourier projection contributes the negative target phase. The height is h(b) = vol(L+bL)/vol(L) for the standard column lattice L. The auxiliary Haar measure in this ratio cancels.

Wv(z) = ∫ h(b)−(z−z₀) ψv(−⟨T,b⟩) (∫integral X ψv(⟨b,X∗JX⟩) dX) db,   Re z > n².

At a good place the Hermitian integral lattice has volume one. Grouping by its cosets rewrites the integral as a sum. The cosets appear in increasing finite sets indexed by a level k. With t = εMq−(2z+n), their sums of absolute values have a geometric majorant because qn²|t| < 1 in the stated half-plane. Each positive-level sum is the same polynomial in t.

How do congruence counts determine a polynomial?

At each positive level the finite Fourier sum is a polynomial Pk(t) whose terms are weighted by the level character at the negative target, and by a nonnegative lattice-index exponent of t. Evaluate it at t = (ε/q)m for each auxiliary rank m ≥ n. Finite Fourier orthogonality and the Gaussian sums identify that evaluation with the density of T for the identity form in dimension m. The counting formula just proved gives ∏j(1−(ε/q)m−j). This equals the evaluation of ∏j(1−t(εq)j) at the same point. Those points have distinct absolute values, so the two polynomials agree everywhere. The auxiliary rank varies only in this interpolation step.

Wv(z) = ∏j=0n−1 (1−εM+jq−(2z+n−j)),   Wv(z₀) = α₁(J,T).

The product extends to an entire function of z. Substituting 2z₀ = M−n gives exactly the density, since εM+j = εM−j. In the example z₀ = ½, while the integral theorem assumes Re z > 4. The continued value is therefore obtained by evaluating the explicit product.

From places to the global coefficient. The pure adelic datum is standard outside a finite set. The global construction multiplies the real factor, the finitely many exceptional factors and the product of the explicit good factors. The last product is holomorphic on Re z > 0. Agreement on a sufficiently far right half-plane identifies the continuation of the global integral. Since n < M, z₀ lies in this positive half-plane. The remaining identification with the theta coefficient uses the global density theorem equating the product of the real and finite densities at T with the normalized mean of the rational Gram fibre. The comparison then returns through Iwasawa decomposition and the open-cell identity to the coefficient at every group argument.

Apply the strict-rank theorem with the extra range assumption n+2 ≤ M or anisotropy of J, and with an integrability hypothesis on a right half-plane. Its general statement also has an implication imposing a Gaussian vacuum condition if a flag is true. In this branch the flag is false, so that particular implication is automatic. The congruence counts, the Whittaker integral and the density-to-mean identity all enter separately. For the example with M = 3 and n = 2 the positive-definite identity form over ℚ(i) is anisotropic over that field.

What replaces the good-place formula at an exceptional finite place?

The good-place count assumes a particular test function, the indicator of the full matrix lattice. A test supported on just one residue class can change the answer even at an unramified prime. The local argument works at every finite place and gives an entire function of the complex parameter z. Its value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 is the density of the chosen test at the target Gram matrix. The global application has n < M.

Fix the local quadratic algebra Ev = Fv ⊗F E, the local component ψv of the adelic additive character, a nondegenerate Hermitian form J of rank M, and a Hermitian target T of size n whose determinant is invertible in Ev. This allows determinants of nonzero valuation. A test Φ is a locally constant, compactly supported function of the M × n matrix X. Use the self-dual measures μ on the matrix space and ν on the Hermitian space for their respective pairings. For a Haar measure λ on Evn and two compact open additive subgroups L₁, L₂, put r(b) = λ(L₁+bL₂)/λ(L₁). It is at least one. Write ⟨b,S⟩ for half the field-algebra trace of the matrix trace of bS. The opposite signs single out the fibre X∗JX = T.

u(b) = ∫ Φ(X) ψv(⟨b,X∗JX−T⟩) dμ(X),   Wv(z) = ∫ r(b)−(z−s₀) u(b) dν(b)   for Re z sufficiently large.

Why can one compact ball determine an entire function? On a shell R < ‖b‖ ≤ 2R, change variables by b ↦ (1+x)∗b(1+x), with x in a small additive matrix ball of radius C/R. These changes preserve the shell, its Haar measure, the lattice index and the integral containing the positive Gram phase. The negative target phase acquires a term linear in x and a term quadratic in x. The latter has norm bounded by a constant times R(C/R)², so the character is trivial on it for large R. Invertibility of T lets one choose C so that at every b in the shell the linear term gives a nontrivial character of the x-ball. Its Haar integral is zero. Averaging the change of variables therefore kills the shell integral for every z, with one cutoff valid for all z. At a singular target the linear term can lose this oscillation, and the stated density hypothesis covers only the regular set.

Choose a ball B₀ beyond that cutoff and double its radius successively. Adding any of the resulting shells leaves the integral over B₀ unchanged. On B₀ the index and its logarithm are bounded, so one can differentiate the compact integral with respect to z. This gives an entire Wv, with no poles. A separate absolute estimate identifies it with the original integral on a right half-plane. For radii growing by a fixed local dilation, the jth outer shell has r(b) ≥ 2j and volume at most a constant times κj. Thus the integral of the absolute value has a geometric majorant when Re z is large. The statement requires existence of a real threshold depending on the data.

How does the test enter the value? Let g be the supplied continuous density of the pushforward of Φ dμ by X ↦ X∗JX on the open set of invertible targets. At z = s₀ the lattice weight is one. Integrating over a large additive ball Λ in b retains those X whose Gram matrix belongs to T+Λ⊥. Indeed, the average of the phase on Λ is one when the difference annihilates Λ and zero otherwise. The annihilator shrinks into the regular set around T, and self-duality gives ν(Λ)ν(Λ⊥) = 1. The integral is therefore an average of g near T. By continuity it approaches g(T). Every sufficiently large ball already gives Wv(s₀).

∫Λ u(b) dν(b) = (1/ν(Λ⊥)) ∫T+Λ⊥ g(S) dν(S)   ⟶   g(T) = Wv(s₀).
Compute the entire factor for one residue class at 3

Take E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ and the inert prime 3. Let J be the two-dimensional identity, n = 1, T = 1 and L₁ = L₂ = 𝒪Eᵥ. Use a character of conductor ℤ₃. The standard integral lattices have self-dual volume one here. Let Φ be the indicator of X ≡ (1,0) modulo 3. There are four scalar coordinates over ℤ₃, so this class has mass 1/81. Its Gram value N(X₁)+N(X₂) belongs to 1+3ℤ₃. For each lift to the next power of 3, the derivative in the real coordinate of X₁ is 2 modulo 3. For each choice of the other three digits, exactly one digit of this coordinate gives the required next Gram digit. Thus the mass is uniform on 1+3ℤ₃, a set of volume 1/3, and the density there is 1/27.

Integration of the character on this coset, including the negative target phase, gives u(b) = (1/81) · 𝟙3⁻¹ℤ₃(b). On ℤ₃ the lattice index is one. On the shell 3⁻¹ℤ₃ ∖ ℤ₃, of volume two, its value is nine because the residue field of Ev has nine elements. In this example the original integral has compact support and converges at every z.

W₃(z) = (1 + 2 · 9−(z−1/2))/81,   W₃(1/2) = 1/27.

Now keep J = I₂ and T = 1, and restore the full-lattice test. There are 24 norm-one columns modulo 3. At every such column at least one scalar derivative of the norm is nonzero modulo 3, so each residue class contributes the same density 1/27. Summing the 24 contributions gives 24/27 = 8/9, the good-place answer in these same dimensions.

Which domain reaches the global coefficient? The local proof uses no rank inequality to construct the entire function once a density is given. The global theorem supplies these densities from the normalized Gram mean when n < M and either n+2 ≤ M or J is anisotropic. It chooses a finite set S outside which the forms, measures, lattices and test meet the good-place conditions. On Re z > 0 multiply the archimedean function, the finitely many entire factors Wv for v ∈ S, and the convergent good-place product. Farther right this equals the adelic integral for the full-rank Fourier coefficient. The point s₀ lies inside the global half-plane by the strict rank inequality. Substituting the local density values gives the normalized Gram mean there. The resulting global continuation is holomorphic on Re z > 0.

Why is the archimedean Whittaker factor entire at a nonsingular target?

At infinity the Fourier variable ranges over Hermitian matrices. For a target with nonzero determinant, integration by parts trades oscillation in this variable for extra decay. Repeating this operation reaches every complex parameter. The value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 recovers the density of the test on the target Gram fibre, as in the finite-place calculation.

Start at one real place. A frame identifies the Hermitian form with J = diag(1p,−1q), with p+q = M. The character on ℝ is u ↦ exp(2πiℓu) for a real ℓ ≠ 0. Set t = 2πℓ and c = 2π|ℓ|. In these coordinates the test on a complex M × n matrix X is a polynomial P in the entries of X and their conjugates, multiplied by exp(−c∑|Xᵢⱼ|²). Define A(Y) by integrating this test against the positive phase exp(it tr(YX∗JX)). The Whittaker coefficient uses the negative phase at the target B. Write D(Y) = det(I+Y²) and w = z−s₀. The integration measure here is Lebesgue measure in the n² real coordinates yᵢⱼ = Re Yᵢⱼ + Im Yᵢⱼ.

W(w) = ∫ D(Y)−w A(Y) exp(−it tr(BY)) dY   for Re w sufficiently large.

One determinant derivative moves the convergence line. Put s = sign(ℓ). Gaussian integration gives A as a polynomial in the entries of (I−isY)−1 and (I+isY)−1, multiplied by the determinants of those inverses to powers p and q respectively. Let Δ be the determinant of the matrix of first derivatives in Hermitian coordinates. Integration by parts shows that the negative Fourier transform of Δf is (it)ndet(B) times that of f, whenever the derivatives are integrable. As det(B) ≠ 0, one can divide by this scalar.

For the decay estimate, diagonalize Y with real eigenvalues λj. Cauchy's derivative estimate uses a radius proportional to √((1+|λi|)(1+|λj|)) in matrix entry (i,j). Each determinant term differentiates once in every row and column. The product of the reciprocal radii thus supplies a factor proportional to ∏j(1+|λj|)−1 ≤ D(Y)−1/2. After N determinants, differentiating the weight D−w leaves that weight times a polynomial in w of degree at most nN with coefficient functions of Y. At integer weights 0 through nN one can absorb the weight into the two determinant powers. Polynomial interpolation transfers the same decay bound to the coefficient functions. On compact parameter sets the differentiated amplitude is bounded by a constant times D(Y)−Re w−(M+N)/2.

Where does the determinant come from in two rows?

Write the diagonal entries of the Hermitian integration variable as x,y and its upper-right entry as u+iv. For a Hermitian target with diagonal a,b and upper-right entry c+id, the trace pairing is ax + by + 2cu + 2dv. Its negative Fourier phase is the exponential of this expression times −it. In these unscaled entry coordinates the determinant derivative is ∂x∂y − (∂u² + ∂v²)/4. Applying it to the phase gives (it)²(ab − c² − d²) times the same phase. Integration by parts twice transfers the derivative to the amplitude with positive sign.

For diagonal entries 2 and 3 and upper-right entry 1 + i, the multiplier is −4t², which we may divide out. For the matrix with every entry equal to one it is zero, although the target itself is nonzero. This is why the hypothesis concerns the determinant. In the derivative estimate the two permutations also have the same decay. The mixed diagonal derivative costs one inverse radius for each diagonal entry, while two off-diagonal derivatives each cost the inverse geometric mean of those radii.

Two complex Gaussian variables and one real Fourier variable

Take n = 1, M = 2, signature (1,1), ℓ = 1, and P = 1 in the one-place Lebesgue model. Then s₀ = 1/2. The Gram value is |x₁|²−|x₂|². Since ∫ℂexp(−a|x|²) dx = π/a for Re a > 0, the two rows give factors 1/[2(1−iy)] and 1/[2(1+iy)]. Thus A(y) = 1/[4(1+y²)]. The absolute integral converges exactly for Re w > −1/2.

In radial coordinates u = |x₁|² and v = |x₂|² the measure is π² exp(−2π(u+v)) du dv. Integrating along u−v = B gives g(B) = (π/4) exp(−2π|B|). For B ≠ 0 this equals W(0). Differentiating the scalar Fourier transform of 1/(a²+y²) with respect to a at a = 1 gives W(1) = (π/8)(1+2π|B|)exp(−2π|B|). At w = −1 the weighted amplitude is the constant 1/4. Its second derivative vanishes, and −1 belongs to U₂, so the continued value is zero. At the singular target B = 0, the phase is constant. As real w decreases to −1/2 the positive integral tends to infinity, since its limiting tail is proportional to 1/|y|. This is where the invertibility hypothesis matters.

Why does a product of local Gram densities give a global mean?

At one finite place a density measures how often a tuple has a prescribed Gram matrix. A rational tuple must satisfy the same equations at every place. To bring these two descriptions together the proof averages over all adelic isometries of a single rational Hermitian space. Let E/F be the CM extension, J the nondegenerate Hermitian form on EM, and T a rational nonsingular Hermitian matrix of size n. The theorem assumes n < M, with either n+2 ≤ M or J anisotropic over E. Anisotropic means that a rational vector of norm zero must itself be zero. The test Φ has a Schwartz factor at infinity and locally constant, compactly supported factors at finite places. Almost all finite factors are the characteristic function of the standard lattice. At every place the two Hermitian matrices come from these same rational forms, and each local additive character comes from one global character.

Let H = U(J), and choose a fundamental domain 𝒟 for its rational points in its adelic group. For each h sum Φ(h−1X) over the rational solutions of X∗JX = T. Replacing h by γh for a rational isometry γ permutes these solutions by X ↦ γ−1X. The sum therefore defines a function on the quotient. Integrate it over 𝒟 using Haar measure and divide by vol(𝒟). Equivalently one can first add the measures obtained by moving each rational tuple under h ↦ h−1X, normalizing their sum by the same volume, then integrate Φ. Countability of the rational tuples and integrability justify this equivalence.

vol(𝒟)−1 ∫𝒟 ∑X rational, X∗JX=T Φ(h−1X) dh = g∞(T) ∏v finite gv(T).
Why can grouping the terms change their weights?

A finite group makes the Haar weights visible. Take H to be the six permutations of three letters and put Γ = K = {id,(12)}. A function constant on ΓhK has just two values. The class of the identity contains two permutations. The class of (13) contains the remaining four. Indeed the size of ΓhK is |Γ||K|/|Γ ∩ hKh−1|, and the two intersection sizes are 2 and 1. If the function takes values 2 and 5, the normalized Haar average is (2·2 + 4·5)/6 = 4. Giving both classes weight ½ would give 3½. The same issue arises when a quotient integral is grouped into classes, whose weights come from their volumes. The definition above keeps that weighting by integrating on a fundamental domain.

Build the global measure one vector at a time. A tuple with no columns has one possible value. For a positive number of columns choose a rational vector of nonzero length t in the target form T. A change of basis writes T as the orthogonal sum of the line ⟨t⟩ and a nonsingular form T₁. If J represents t over E, choose such a vector and split J into the same line and a complement J₁. After fixing the first vector, the remaining columns lie in its orthogonal complement and have Gram matrix T₁. Both dimensions have dropped by one. This preserves the gap M−n. In the boundary case M = n+1 the complement of an anisotropic form is still anisotropic.

The local measures admit the same integration in stages. First integrate the test on the complement fibre, keeping the first vector fixed. This gives a test on the one-vector fibre, where the one-vector mean formula applies. At finitely many exceptional places the proof retains the actual integrals and their change-of-measure constants. Outside them the standard-lattice masses of the two stages multiply. This makes the global average factor with constant one.

If J fails to represent t rationally, the global fibre is empty. To show that the product also vanishes, the proof applies the one-vector measure identity to that empty fibre. It obtains a zero fibre measure at infinity or at some finite place. The projection onto the first column forces the full local fibre there to have zero measure as well. For example, over ℚ(i) take J = I₂ and T = (−1). The sum of two complex squared absolute values cannot be −1 at the real place. Even the congruence at 3 has a solution, given by the column (1,1) since 2 ≡ −1 mod 3. A solution at this one finite place cannot make the global mean positive.

What fixes the constant in the one-vector mass formula?

Fix a nonzero scalar β ∈ F× and consider vectors of Gram value β in a nondegenerate Hermitian space of dimension M ≥ 3 over a CM extension E/F. In the induction on Gram fibres, invariance, support on the fibre and local finiteness identify the normalized theta measure with a scalar c times an Euler product. If a local fibre measure vanishes, both sides are zero even when the product is assigned constant one. Suppose now that all the fibre measures are nonzero. The proof determines c by enlarging just the finite-place test.

An upper bound for the discrepancy. Put d = [F ∶ ℚ]. At infinity choose a strictly positive Gaussian test Φ and denote its integral over the fibre at β by w. It is finite and strictly positive. At a finite place v, take the indicator of a−1Λv for a positive integer a. Let I(a) be the normalized global integral with these tests, and let P(a) be the convergent product of their finite local fibre masses at β, using the reference coordinate measures. The trace form expresses the same global count as a Fourier coefficient of a theta average. Its comparison with the corresponding Eisenstein coefficient yields

|I(a) − w P(a)| ≤ C adM   for every integer a ≥ 1.

Where does the exponent come from? For the indicator of the original lattice the weighted difference between the averaged theta function and the Eisenstein series is bounded after reduction to a Siegel domain. The dilation replaces the real upper-half-plane variable x+i by (x+i)/a². Its imaginary part is a−2 at each of the d real places. The product of the local weights (Im τ)M/2 is therefore a−dM. Removing that weight gives the bound above since integration against the unit-modulus Fourier character costs at most the volume subsequently divided out.

A lower bound for the finite local product. Write αv(t) for the mass of the undilated lattice at target t and qᵥ for the residue cardinality of Fᵥ. Multiplication by a sends the fibre at β to the fibre at a²β. The Jacobian has local exponent 2M, and in the single scalar target it has exponent two. Disintegration therefore gives qᵥordv(a)(2M−2)αv(a²β) for the dilated-lattice mass at β. The product of the explicit powers is ad(2M−2).

Choose an integer N clearing the denominator of β and large enough that the dilated test has positive mass at each exceptional place. Take the integer p = 1 + ∏v exceptionalqᵥ, so every place dividing p is good. Along a = Npk, the masses αv(a²β) away from p agree with those at N²β because p is a local unit. They are positive and their deviations from one are absolutely summable, hence their product is positive. At the finitely many places dividing p, the good-place bound |αv(t)−1| ≤ 2/qᵥM−1 gives αv(a²β) ≥ 1/2. This produces a fixed κ > 0.

P(a) ≥ κ ad(2M−2)   along an unbounded sequence of integers a.
Check the local power at the inert prime 3

For E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ, J = I₃ and β = 1, normalize the standard coordinate lattices to volume one. Modulo 3 each of three complex coordinates contributes a sum of two squares. Counting the 729 vectors gives 252 of norm 1 and 225 of norm 0. Of the latter, 224 are nonzero. Each nonzero solution has one independent scalar Gram condition on its six next digits, giving 3⁵ lifts for each prescribed next target digit. Thus primitive vectors contribute 224/3⁵ at target 9. For the vectors divisible by 3, put X = 3Y. The six source coordinates contribute a volume factor 3−6, the scalar target contributes 3−2, and the new target is 1, of density 252/3⁵. Consequently α₃(9) = (224+3−4·252)/3⁵ = 2044/2187. The mass on 3−1Λ₃ at target 1 is 3⁴α₃(9) = 2044/27.

Return to the unknown scalar. The exact measure factorization gives I(a) = c w P(a) for the same test. Combining the two estimates along the selected sequence gives |c−1| ≤ (C/(wκ)) a−d(M−2). The right side tends to zero. At F = ℚ and M = 3, the comparison is already between a cubic error and quartic growth. Dimension two gives no exponent gap, and the anisotropic binary case has its own normalization argument.

How is the scalar fixed in an anisotropic plane?

One vector in an anisotropic binary space needs a different normalization argument. The proof combines local mass and compactness estimates with a representation principle and invariance under similitudes. A rational similitude transports a common scalar κ across the represented nonzero lengths. A counting theorem compares two limits for a test of volume V with 0 < V < ∞ and gives V = κV. Thus κ = 1. A second binary result supplies a bound on the error in the local lattice masses. In higher rank the resulting bound outside finitely many places is |massv−1| ≤ C/qv², where qv is the residue size. The sum of these errors converges, which controls the Euler product of the standard-lattice masses.

Why can two spheres of different lengths have the same mass coefficient?

Fix a CM extension E/F with conjugation, and an anisotropic Hermitian plane with nonsingular matrix J. Write Q(x) = x*Jx, where * means conjugate transpose. For β ∈ F×, the rational sphere consists of x ∈ E² with Q(x) = β. Average its rational points over the adelic unitary quotient to obtain a measure Θβ. The first mass formula for this length supplies a nonnegative number κ such that, on product tests, Θβ integrates as κ times the product of the local Gram-fibre integrals. A separate choice of κ for each β would leave an unknown weight inside the sum over lengths. A rational change of variables makes the same κ work throughout that sum.

Build the change of variables from two points. Suppose Q(x) = β and Q(x′) = β′, both nonzero. If x*J = (r₀,r₁), put y = (−r₁,r₀)t and take the two columns of Pₓ to be x and y. Then x*Jy = 0 and det Pₓ = r₀x₀ + r₁x₁ = β. Taking determinants in its diagonal Gram matrix gives βQ(y) = β² det J. Thus the two frames give the same diagonal form up to their respective lengths.

Pₓ*JPₓ = β diag(1, det J),   γ = Pₓ′Pₓ−1,   γ*Jγ = λJ,   λ = β′/β.

In particular γx = x′. Its entries belong to E and its multiplier λ belongs to F. This one matrix bijects all rational points of the first sphere with those of the second. On the group used in the average, put h′ = γhγ−1. It is unitary and γ(h−1x) = (h′)−1γx. Pull back the Haar measure and the fundamental domain together under this conjugation. The volume dividing the average is preserved. Reindexing the sum and changing variables gives γ∗Θβ = Θβ′ because the normalized theta measure is independent of these auxiliary choices.

Compute what happens on a fibre. At a place v, write dX for ambient additive Haar measure and db for Haar measure on the scalar length coordinate. The Gram-fibre measures mᵥ(b) recover the ambient integral by integrating over b on the regular locus. Define the positive factors aᵥ and bᵥ by γ∗dX = aᵥ dX and (multiplication by λ)∗db = bᵥ db. Since Q(γX) = λQ(X), the changed family must reconstruct aᵥ dX using bᵥ db. Uniqueness of the normalized fibre measures fixes the quotient, including its direction. Combine all infinite places in F∞.

γ∗mᵥ(β) = (aᵥ/bᵥ) mᵥ(β′),   (a∞/b∞) ∏v finite (aᵥ/bᵥ) = 1.

For the first product formula the proof expresses γ as a linear map in F-coordinates. For the second, scalar congruence on a one-by-one Hermitian matrix acts by λ². Its Haar factor is the square of the positive factor for multiplication by λ, so taking square roots gives the required product formula on lengths. Outside finitely many places the factors are one and γ and its inverse preserve the standard lattice. On a product test enlarge its finite set of places to include these exceptions. All local changes of measure then cancel in the product, leaving exactly the original κ in the formula for Θβ′.

Follow the factor at infinity and at 2 for a sphere of length two

Over ℚ(i)/ℚ take J = I₂, x = (1,0)t and x′ = (1,i)t. Their lengths are 1 and 2. The frame gives γ with rows (1,i), (i,1). Multiplication gives γ*γ = 2I₂ and detℚ(i)γ = 2. In the four rational coordinates its determinant is the norm of 2, hence 4. A pushforward measures the inverse image of a set. At infinity its factor on vectors is therefore 1/4, and on lengths it is 1/2. The fibre factor is (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2. At 2 the absolute values are |4|₂ = 1/4 and |2|₂ = 1/2, giving pushforward factors 4 and 2 and fibre factor 2. At every odd prime the factors are one. Thus the product of the fibre factors is (1/2)·2 = 1, although the real fibre measure alone changes. This computes the transport of a mass formula without evaluating either sphere’s individual mass.

Which lengths reach the counting theorem? Start with the coefficient supplied for a fixed β ≠ 0. If the infinite fibre measure or any finite fibre measure is zero, its factorization forces Θβ = 0. The local finiteness and summability already supplied let one write the zero factorization with coefficient 1 directly. Otherwise the binary representation theorem gives a rational vector of length β from the nonzero infinite fibre measure. Now consider every β′ ≠ 0. A represented β′ receives the same κ by the preceding argument. For an unrepresented β′ the rational sum is empty, and the contrapositive of that representation theorem gives zero infinite fibre measure. Apply the individual mass formula for β′ to obtain its finiteness and summability conditions. Its zero factorization now holds with the chosen κ as well. For example, length −1 is empty over the reals in the positive definite plane above. The degree-one Gram matrix at β = 0 is singular, and anisotropy leaves only the zero rational vector there. The counting theorem uses precisely the nonzero lengths. Having a common κ on all of them permits the positive-volume comparison that gives κ = 1.

Why does the infinite fibre detect a rational point in this plane?

For a proposed nonzero length t, compare J with diag(t, t det J). Their determinants differ by t², the norm of t from E to F. At an indefinite real place both planes have one positive and one negative direction. At a definite place representing the sign of t makes their signatures agree there too. With all signatures equal, Landherr’s classification gives a rational isometry of the two Hermitian forms. The image of the first basis vector then has length t. Consequently a missing rational length has the wrong sign at some definite real place. The infinite fibre is empty there and its supported measure vanishes. The archive obtains the classification result used here from a quadratic Hasse norm theorem.

Why can we integrate the paired kernels in either order?

Let X = [G] be the source quotient and Y = [H] the target quotient, with their quotient Haar measures μ and ν. Each is the space of adelic points modulo rational changes of basis. To use the doubling identity we need the reverse order, pairing the two kernels on Y before integrating over the two source variables. What keeps the new integral finite?

At (g,g), the doubling identity identifies |K(g,h)|² with the absolute value of that doubled kernel, because the determinant character has modulus one. The Siegel–Weil theorem on these data supplies integrability in h. Its regular Eisenstein value bounds the absolute value of the normalized target mean by a power of the doubled height. The height at (g,g) is at most a constant times a power of the height at g. Multiplying the mean by ν(Y) therefore gives a polynomial bound for ∫Y |K(g,y)|² dν(y). This step uses the rank and Witt-index assumptions of the global formula.

At every fixed y, the kernel also grows at most polynomially in x. The same decay proves that each defining lift integral exists there. Continuity and invariance in both rational variables give measurable kernels on the quotients.

The remaining bound separates into a function of x and a function of x′. Tonelli’s theorem applies to |F| because it is nonnegative, giving the absolute bound below. With equal kernels and equal inputs this bound also gives Θi ∈ L²(Y). We can now use Fubini for the complex integrand itself.

∫X²×Y |F| ≤ M₁M₂ < ∞.
⟨Θ₁,Θ₂⟩Y = ∫X² ⟨K₁(x,·),K₂(x′,·)⟩Y u₁(x) u₂(x′) dμ(x) dμ(x′).

The Petersson pairing here conjugates the second factor. If g₁ and g₂ represent x and x′, the mixed doubling identity makes the inner pairing the normalized doubled theta mean times ν(Y) and χB(det g₂). The preceding Siegel–Weil step supplies the normalized mean, including its own convergence conditions.

Try the two orders on an infinite sum. Give X = {1,2,…} counting measure and Y = {+1,−1} equal probabilities. Let K(n,y) = n yn−1, u₁(n) = 21−n and u₂(n) = (z/2)n−1 with |z| = 1. 6.12At an unramified finite place

For v outside S, put volume one on the local lattice stabilizer Kv. The spherical section φ on the doubled group has φ(1) = 1 and inducing character χB−1. Let c be a bounded spherical matrix coefficient with the specified Hecke parameters. At a split place the bounds on each parameter and its inverse follow from all integral Hecke sums. For Re s > a the integral of φ((g,1)) c(g) over the local group is

c(1) · Lv(s + ½) / dv(s).

The restriction to the compact stabilizer would contribute just c(1), since the integrand is constant there and its volume is one. Freeing the local variable multiplies that contribution by the displayed quotient. The denominator therefore enters once each time a good place is freed.

The numerator runs over every CM place w above v and every Satake parameter β there. Its factor is (1 − β χB(w)−1 Nw−(s+½))−1, where χB(w) denotes the unramified character value. If η is the quadratic character of the CM extension, the denominator is ∏0≤i<a Lv(2s + a − i, ηb+i). The source gives the local η-factor as a singleton parameter at an unramified place, with value +1 at split places and (−1)b+i at inert places. Every argument of this denominator has real part greater than one when Re s > 0. The resulting dS = ∏v∉S dv is holomorphic and nonzero there. At s₀ the local denominator takes arguments t + 1 through t + a.

Split places. The two places above v have equal residue norms. Their parameter multisets are related by inversion, and their character values multiply to one. Identifying the local unitary group with GLa transports the spherical section to the graph used by the GL doubling calculation. The lattice-fixed source vector and the spherical section make the integrand constant on right Kv-cosets. The sum of these values is the Haar integral because every coset has volume one. Evaluating the GL sum gives exactly the two-place numerator and the split denominator above. The split lattice calculation below derives the required complex sum from the unramified GL doubling theorem.

Inert places. Let q be the residue size at v. The CM residue size is q². Write ε for the value of the inverse target character at a uniformizer and α₁,…,α⌊a/2⌋ for the unitary parameters. Put X = ε q−(2s+a) and y = ε q−(2s+1). For a zonal coefficient normalized to one at the identity the closed expression is

∏h=0a−1 (1 − (−q)hX)   ∏i=1⌊a/2⌋ [(1 − yαi)(1 − y/αi)]−1,

with the additional factor (1 − y)−1 for odd a. To see the source of the powers of X, assign a matrix the lattice length obtained from its elementary divisors. The graph section takes the value X to that length. Summing over the unitary Iwasawa cells uses counts for their unipotent radicals and geometric series for their Levi factors. Pairing each α with its inverse gives the second product. In odd rank the base-change parameters also contain 1. The character restriction gives ε = (−1)b, which converts the first product to the reciprocal of dv. For Re s > a, the half-rank bounds on α and its inverse and |y| = q−(2 Re s+1) place all series in their convergence domain when the coefficient at 1 is nonzero. The adelic comparison restores the factor c(1).

For a local rank-one check take a = 1, b = 8, and set the spherical parameters and twist equal to one. Write x = q−(s+½). At a split place the numerator is (1 − x)−2, while the denominator is (1 − x²)−1. Their quotient is (1 + x)/(1 − x). At an inert place the single CM norm q² gives numerator (1 − x²)−1, hence quotient 1. For |x| < 1 the split answer also reads 1 + 2∑n≥1 xn. To see the cancellation, expand (1 − x)−2 as a sum over pairs of nonnegative integers (u,v). Adding one to both entries preserves their difference and multiplies the term by x². Multiplying by 1 − x² leaves precisely the pairs with one entry zero. This explains the denominator in this rank-one example. Actual chains in this chapter begin at r = k + m − 1 with m ≥ 2 and k ≥ m + 3.

The inert cell calculation derives the two geometric series and their cancellation. To follow the global argument, continue with the places inside S.

6.13The part that stays inside the integral

For each admissible chain step and each additive measure and fundamental domain of covolume one, choose one polynomial datum φ and one finite-type test vector v. They work for every nonzero vector u of the stage multiplicity space. The order matters. These choices give a nonzero JS(s₀) already before choosing a Hecke eigenvalue. Write F = u(v) and K for the prescribed finite adelic level. We compute the integrand W(g) · pet(R(g)F, F), with R the right translation.

Two restrictions on the finite datum enter the support proof. Its matrix must lie in the summand selected by the split-place idempotent and be integral in the chosen frames. At every selected CM place its top square block must reduce to an invertible block triangular matrix, and the family of upper-left blocks must meet the given subgroup condition. If both a matrix and its translate have nonzero test value, these unit top blocks recover integrality of the transformation in the selected summand. Self-duality gives the conjugate summand, and the two reductions give the required level of the finite transformation. Away from the selected places this already follows from g ∈ U(S). Thus a transformation outside the level moves the support off itself.

For the Weil matrix coefficient one must still transfer this disjointness to the theta vector. A finite sum of additive characters is one on the support and zero on its translate. The corresponding sum of Heisenberg operators fixes the datum. After conjugating the coefficients, transporting by g−1, and reversing the translations, it kills the same datum. The operators commute with the polynomial Fock construction at infinity. Moving the finite sum from one entry of the Hermitian pairing to the other therefore shows W(g) = 0.

On the remaining subgroup, write g = b∞ κ with κ ∈ K. The Weil coefficient acquires the level character χK(κ). The Petersson coefficient acquires the same character before conjugation. Their product contains |χK(κ)|² = 1. The Petersson coefficient also contributes the scalar ⟨u,u⟩ and a product of real discrete-series matrix coefficients. Pushing the restricted adelic Haar measure forward along the projection to the real group gives a Haar measure m∞. Its normalization includes the finite-level volume. If Z∞ denotes the remaining Weil coefficient times the conjugate of that product of real coefficients, the result is

JS(s₀) = ⟨u,u⟩ · ∫ Z∞(b∞) dm∞.

The finite-level computation controls the entire restricted integral, including any relation between the block reductions at the selected places.

6.14A positive contribution at each real place

The actual step vector starts with a nonzero Fock vacuum f. Let I₀ be its squared norm in the chosen covolume-one pairing. At each selected real place τ the gap and weight comparisons allow a polynomial Φτ jointly of highest weight for the two compact groups. Choose a smooth, compact-finite unit highest-weight vector wτ of the source. Glue the Φτ and tensor the wτ to obtain the test data above. On the discrete-series cover, the integral of a Fock coefficient against a conjugate highest-weight coefficient is a positive multiple of a squared norm divided by formal degree. The norm is that of the coefficient projector applied to the normalized joint vector. Its nonvanishing on that vector and positivity of the formal degree make the result strictly positive. Pullback to the cover introduces a positive Haar constant, and the unitary phase cancels against its conjugate. Denote the resulting local value by rτ > 0.

Why the real-place projection has positive mass

Fix one real place τ of a step of the iterated theta chain. Its integral pairs a Weil matrix coefficient with the conjugate of a discrete-series coefficient. Even when both vectors have norm one, the integral can vanish if the two coefficients detect different parts of the representation. Here the Fock model realizes vectors using polynomials with a Gaussian inner product. Restricting a representation to a compact subgroup breaks it into finite-dimensional types. A joint highest-weight polynomial selects a specific type for each of the two compact groups. We must show that this choice survives projection onto the component detected by the source vector. The chain chooses a polynomial Φ of the prescribed highest weights for both compact groups and a unit source vector of its prescribed highest weight. Its real-place comparison identifies the polynomial with a vector in the Fock model of the oscillator representation.

Build the projection. Let G̃ be the double cover of the real unitary group U(p,q) with Haar measure ν. Let σ be the source discrete series on this cover, v its chosen unit vector, and dσ its formal degree for ν. We use the inner product linear in its second entry. Write mv(g) = ⟨v,σ(g)v⟩. For unit v, Schur orthogonality gives ∫ |mv(g)|² dν(g) = 1/dσ. This fixes the scalar that makes the projector send v to itself in σ. For any unitary representation π of the cover define the operator

Pvx = dσ ∫G̃ mv(g) π(g)x dν(g).

The chain’s gap condition ensures absolute integrability of the kernel. The estimate used here requires every pair of source parameters in opposite signature blocks to differ in absolute value by at least 120(p+q)min(p,q)3/2. In polar coordinates the discrete-series decay then pays for the growth of Haar measure. The joint-vector theorem additionally uses the admissible pair of parameters, their matching compact weights and the chain’s further gap and Casimir conditions.

Schur orthogonality gives Pvx = ⟨v,x⟩v in σ itself. In any π, inversion gives Pv* = Pv. Convolving the same kernel on both sides of a translate gives Pvπ(g)Pv = mv(g)Pv. At the identity mv(1) = 1, proving idempotence. Its range is the closed span of the vectors T v for continuous intertwiners T from σ to π. In the Fock representation let η be the normalized joint polynomial vector. Testing the integral operator against η and using η − Pvη ⟂ Pvη gives

∫G̃ ⟨η,π(g)η⟩ mv(g) dν(g) = ⟨η,Pvη⟩/dσ = ‖Pvη‖²/dσ.

The Fock coefficient has absolute value at most one by unitarity, so the same integrability estimate justifies this pairing.

A circle calculation that isolates what the projector measures

Give U(1) Haar mass one and take σ(z) = z, of formal degree one. On ℂ² put π(z) = diag(z,z²) and η = (1,2)/√5. The product of coefficients is ((z + 4z²)/5)z = (1 + 4z)/5. Its integral is 1/5. The operator gives the same answer by sending η to (1,0)/√5. Choosing η = (0,1) would give zero. This calculation checks the conjugation and the squared norm. In the theta chain the following argument supplies the nonzero component.

Why the joint vector survives. Suppose Pvη = 0. Testing against every Fock vector would make every integral ∫⟨z,π(g)η⟩ mv(g) dν vanish. The two source-side highest vectors η and v have the same compact highest weight. Their pair generates a finite-dimensional irreducible representation E of the maximal compact subgroup. Write j₁ and j₂ for its maps to the Fock and discrete-series spaces and give E the norm induced by the injective j₂. Compact translation and irreducibility propagate the assumed vanishing to the integrals of all mixed matrix entries from E.

To see the contradiction, compress π(g) and σ(g) to E, writing A(g) = j₁*π(g)j₁ and B(g) = j₂*σ(g)j₂. In an orthonormal basis, F(g) = tr(B(g)*A(g)) is the sum of exactly those mixed entries, so its integral would vanish. Left compact translation changes the common basis and preserves F. On the noncompact Cartan directions g = exp Y, positivity of the Fock joint harmonics and of the lowest compact type of σ makes both compressed operators positive semidefinite. Diagonalizing one shows tr(B*A) ≥ 0. Since each g is a compact translate of some exp Y, this proves F ≥ 0 everywhere. At the identity B(1) = 1 and F(1) = ∑j ‖j₁ej‖² > 0 because η belongs to the image. Continuity and positive Haar measure on open sets contradict a zero integral. Thus Pvη ≠ 0. When the partner is definite, the stronger local theorem gives Pvη = η and the cover integral equals 1/dσ.

Return to the real integral. Let the cover map send ν to c₀μ for the measure μ chosen on the real group. Let CF > 0 compare the theta pairing with the Fock inner product, and write η = n · ι(κΦ), where κ puts the polynomial in local model coordinates, ι embeds it in Fock space and n = 1/‖ι(κΦ)‖. The original Weil coefficient thus contributes CF/n² times the normalized Fock coefficient. On the cover, both the Weil and discrete-series coefficients carry the same unit-modulus splitting character. Complex conjugation on the discrete-series factor cancels that phase. Passing from ν back to μ therefore gives the positive value

rτ = CF ‖Pvη‖² / (c₀ n² dσ).

The chain uses this number at one real place for its chosen test data. The product over the real places also carries the vacuum normalization and a product-measure constant. The finite-place integrals, the continued L-value and the global Siegel–Weil identity enter separately in the theta norm. The local positivity proof uses discrete-series orthogonality, decay and positivity of its lowest compact type, the Fock positivity on joint harmonics and Cartan decomposition. Its conclusion gives strict positivity for these data, with magnitude depending on the projection and the measures.

The Weil coefficient splits as I₀ times a product, with each real factor divided by I₀. Comparing m∞ with the product of the local Haar measures introduces one constant cHaar > 0. Thus

∫ Z∞ dm∞ = I₀ · cHaar · ∏τ (rτ / I₀) ≠ 0.

The same data supply the convergence assumption to the left of s₀. For each allowed majorant frame, the product h∞ of archimedean heights lies in (0,1]. The norm of the Weil coefficient is bounded by a constant times h∞b/2, and the product of the discrete-series coefficients is integrable. At s₁ = 0, multiplication by h∞−t/2 leaves the nonnegative exponent (b − t)/2 = a/2. At finite places the local height equals one on the level. Inserting a new good place v in S removes its lattice-stabilizer restriction. Write an element of U(S) as an element whose v-component is 1 times an embedded element of Kv. At the real special point, the normalizing Euler factors have the form (1 − ηb+i(v) q−(t+a−i))−1. Their signs inside the parentheses may differ, but every factor is positive. The exponent is at least t + 1, so the logarithms are absolutely summable and the product is positive. The twisted numerator is a different matter. Its characters can take complex values, and the argument in the preceding chain section proves nonvanishing of the continued special value. On the diagonal the full Petersson pairing is a squared norm.

The integrable height bound at s₁ makes JS holomorphic on Re s > s₁. Uniqueness of meromorphic continuation matches the product just computed to the full doubling integral at s₀, using the supplied holomorphic value L₀ and the nonvanishing of dS. For example, at the second lift a = r + t, so s₀ = t/2 lies even to the left of a/2. Substitution in the far-right Euler identity alone would miss this step. Combining the continued identity with the positive volume, the nonzero residual integral, and the special value proved above forces the chosen lift to survive.

6.16Summing the split local integral one lattice at a time

At a split place, the unitary group can be written as GLa over the local field. A matrix takes the standard lattice to a new lattice, and two matrices give the same lattice exactly when they differ on the right by its stabilizer K. Give K Haar volume one. The local integral is now a sum over lattices. We need to know both what each lattice contributes and whether this infinite sum converges at the complex parameter used by the lift.

Choose a uniformizer ϖ, an element of valuation one, and write q for the residue-field size. The elementary divisors of a lattice give a unique weakly decreasing tuple of integers d = (d₁,…,da). Choosing integral bases separately in the source and the target makes the matrix diagonal with entries ϖdᵢ. Let Sd be the finite set of lattices with that tuple. Two integers extracted from it enter the kernel. The signed sum D = ∑dᵢ gives the determinant valuation and the twist zD, with |z| = 1. The sum k = ∑|dᵢ| measures the total displacement. For d = (1,−1), the twist is one although the displacement is two. With X = q−(a/2+s), the spherical section gives zDXk on every lattice in the cell.

Let v be the spherical vector and write its matrix coefficient as c(g) = λ(π(g)v). By the Hecke eigenvector equation, summing π(g)v over this cell gives a scalar hd times v. Applying λ gives hdc(1). Thus all the information from the representations in this part of the sum fits into a single scalar per tuple. Write Ad = zDhdc(1). If |c(g)| ≤ C, then |Ad| ≤ C |Sd| by the triangle inequality.

Count the first two shells in rank two

Take residue-field size 3 and the trivial coefficient and twist. The two tuples of displacement one are (1,0) and (0,−1). In the first cell, the sublattices of index 3 correspond to the four lines in the two-dimensional residue space. Multiplication by ϖ identifies the second cell with the first. The coefficient of X is therefore 8.

At displacement two the tuples (1,1) and (−1,−1) give one lattice each. The other three are (2,0), (1,−1) and (0,−2), all equivalent by central scaling for the purpose of counting. A lattice of type (2,0) is the kernel of a surjection onto the quotient of the local integer ring by (ϖ²). There are 9² − 3² primitive pairs of coefficients for such a map. Two maps have the same kernel precisely when a unit of the quotient relates them, and there are 9 − 3 such units. Each of the three cells has 72/6 = 12 elements. The counting series begins 1 + 8X + 38X². For the constant coefficient 1 of the trivial representation, the two Satake parameters here are √3 and 1/√3. Thus the product below becomes (1 − X²)(1 − 3X²)/[(1 − 3X)²(1 − X)²]. Its coefficients bound the absolute sum at this one place. To obtain a nonzero norm for a step in the chain, the proof also needs the continued global value and the residual integral.
