Take U to be the triples (x,y,2z) with z ∈ 𝔽₂. Its eight characters have the form ax + by + cz. The four fixed characters have a = b and take value c on σ². The orbit count gives an upper bound on the number of generators of the dyadic module. One generator can still yield a quotient of infinite length, as ℤ₂/(1−1)ℤ₂ shows. To compute the length at a finite layer, we next determine which ℚℓ/ℤℓ-valued characters of the infinite kernel extend to locally trivial cocycles with the prescribed twist. Dualizing that description gives the quotient whose length is needed.

8.9Why restriction recovers the locally trivial classes

Fix a field F in one of these towers. Let G be its absolute Galois group, χ its cyclotomic character, U = ker χ, and e a nonzero integer. The coefficient module A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ carries the action ρ(g) = χ(g)−e. For a class in degree one, inflate to G and restrict a cocycle z to U. Since U acts trivially, z restricts to an additive character φ, and every coboundary restricts to zero. Conjugation of the cocycle identity gives φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u). Local triviality forces φ to vanish on inertia and on decomposition groups above ℓ, in each case after intersection with U. We will recover exactly the equivariant characters with these vanishing conditions.

For injectivity, suppose φ = 0. The cocycle then factors through the cyclotomic quotient. In our fields this quotient is procyclic. Choose g whose image topologically generates it. The value χ(g)−e − 1 is nonzero. Indeed the cyclotomic degrees over a fixed number field grow without bound, whereas the ℓ-adic roots of a fixed nonzero power are finite. Multiplication by this nonzero scalar is surjective on A, so choose a with (ρ(g) − 1)a = z(g). Subtract its coboundary. The resulting cocycle vanishes on g, hence by the cocycle rule on all its powers, and by continuity on the quotient. This is where the condition e ≠ 0 enters.

For surjectivity let φ be one of the equivariant characters. Write C for the closure of the powers of a lift of a cyclotomic generator. Its compact image surjects onto χ(G), so G = CU. The character φ vanishes on C ∩ U. In group-theoretic terms the pro-ℓ part of the procyclic group C maps onto an infinite pro-ℓ group. That part is ℤℓ, and all its nonzero closed subgroups have finite index. Its kernel is therefore zero. The intersection has only prime-to-ℓ finite quotients, so its continuous characters into ℓ-primary torsion vanish. The code proves this vanishing directly by congruences in finite quotients. We may consequently define

z(cu) = ρ(c)φ(u),   c ∈ C,   u ∈ U.

Two decompositions differ by an element of the intersection, making the formula independent of the choice. Equivariance gives the cocycle identity on multiplying two decompositions. Continuity follows because C × U → G is a continuous surjection of compact Hausdorff spaces, hence a quotient map. Away from ℓ, inertia already lies in the cyclotomic kernel, where φ vanishes. Above ℓ, the restricted cocycle vanishes on the kernel of the local cyclotomic character. Its image on the decomposition group is open in ℤℓ×, and the allowed roots of unity give the same procyclic condition. The preceding generator argument therefore subtracts a local coboundary. Inflation from the group unramified outside ℓ now supplies a locally trivial class, whose restriction is φ.

How does a character on the infinite kernel extend across the cyclotomic direction?

Let G be the absolute Galois group of a number field F, χ its ℓ-adic cyclotomic character, U = ker χ and A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ with action ρ = χ−e. A character φ on U in the restriction theorem is locally constant, additive on products and satisfies φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u). It vanishes on the intersections of U with finite inertia groups and with decomposition groups over ℓ. We assume e ≠ 0. At odd ℓ the generator condition holds for the cyclotomic image of any number field. At 2 the theorem assumes χ ≡ 1 modulo 4 throughout G, as happens when F contains a primitive fourth root of unity.

What happens if two lifts give the same element? Choose γ lifting a topological generator of χ(G), and write C for the closure of its integer powers. Its image is compact, contains all powers of χ(γ) and hence equals χ(G). Thus G = CU. To define a cocycle vanishing on C and restricting to φ on U, the two prescriptions must agree on C ∩ U. Here is the congruence calculation that forces agreement.

Fix x in this intersection. Local constancy at the identity gives an open subgroup H of G with φ = 0 on H ∩ U. The finite coset space of H gives a positive integer d with γd in H. Write d = ℓab, with ℓ coprime to b. The unit w = χ(γ) has infinite order. The orders of its reductions modulo ℓj therefore contain arbitrarily large powers of ℓ. Indeed each reduced order divides (ℓ − 1)ℓj−1 for j ≥ 1. If their ℓ-parts were bounded by ℓa, every reduction of w(ℓ−1)ℓa would equal 1, forcing the same equality in ℤℓ. Choose j so that wk ≡ 1 modulo ℓj implies ℓa+1 divides k.

A power γk can approximate x simultaneously in the coset xH and in its cyclotomic residue class modulo ℓj. Since χ(x) = 1, we have ℓa ∣ k and hence d ∣ kb. Thus γkb belongs to H. Also x−1γk belongs to H. The elements x and γ commute because x lies in the closure of the powers of γ. Taking the bth power in this last relation gives xb ∈ H ∩ U. Now bφ(x) = 0 and φ(x) has ℓ-power order. Coprimality forces φ(x) = 0. Only the finite coset space of H was needed to choose d.

For two expressions cu = c′u′, the element c′−1c = u′u−1 is in the intersection. It has zero φ-value and acts trivially on A. Consequently the formula below is independent of the expression. Multiplying two expressions gives (cu)(dv) = cd(d−1ud)v. Equivariance of φ gives the displayed cocycle rule. The product map C × U → G is a continuous surjection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, so continuity descends from the formula on the product.

z(cu) = ρ(c)φ(u),   z(gh) = z(g) + ρ(g)z(h).

How do the restrictions survive passage to the unramified quotient? Let S be the places over ℓ and N the closed normal subgroup of G generated by all inertia groups away from S. The cyclotomic character χ, and hence its twist, factors through GS = G/N. In particular, all such inertia groups lie in U and z vanishes there. Inside N the zero set of z is a closed subgroup, since N acts trivially on the coefficients. It is normal in G by the cocycle rule, which gives z(gng−1) = ρ(g)z(n) for n in N. It therefore contains all of N. Now z(gn) = z(g) gives the continuous quotient cocycle.

For a prolongation over a place in S, let D be its decomposition group. The restriction of z kills D ∩ U. Choose a lift γD of a generator of the open local cyclotomic image. Since e ≠ 0, the scalar ρ(γD) − 1 is nonzero. Multiplication by it on A is surjective. Choose a with (ρ(γD) − 1)a = z(γD). Subtracting δa, where δa(d) = ρ(d)a − a, gives zero on the local kernel and on every generator power, hence on D by continuity. The same argument on the global quotient proves injectivity of restriction on H¹.

A different prolongation changes D to gDg−1. For d in D, the cocycle rule gives z(gdg−1) = z(g) + ρ(g)z(d) − ρ(gdg−1)z(g). Substitution of δa gives the new local primitive below. Thus the class descends with its local conditions. Choosing another global cocycle in the same class changes it by a coboundary, whose restriction to U is zero. The tower argument uses injectivity and precisely this description of the image to identify the locally trivial H¹ with its equivariant characters.

z|D = δa   ⇒   z|gDg−1 = δ(ρ(g)a − z(g)).
Two decompositions and a conjugate subgroup in a group of order 54

Use triples (n,k,ε) with coordinates modulo 9, 3 and 2 respectively. Give the first coordinate of a product (n,k,ε)(m,j,η) the value n + 7km modulo 9, and add the other coordinates. This defines a group since 7³ ≡ 1 modulo 9. Take the finite character χ = 4k modulo 9 and let ρ = χ−1 act on ℤ/9. Here U consists of the triples with k = 0 and C is generated by γ = (0,1,1) of order six. Their intersection is generated by γ³ = (0,0,1), which any homomorphism into ℤ/9 kills. The equivariant character φ(n,0,ε) = n extends to z(n,k,ε) = n.

The two expressions γ(8,0,1) and γ⁴(8,0,0) both represent (2,1,0). Each gives 7 · 8 ≡ 2 modulo 9. Multiplying this element by (4,2,1) gives cocycle value 2 + 7 · 4 ≡ 3. Finally z vanishes on C. 8.10The inverse action and the Tate twist

Return to the base field L0 and one of its cyclotomic layers Lm of relative degree ℓm, embedded in the same algebraic closure. The two fields have the same infinite cyclotomic kernel. Write c for the largest exponent such that L0 contains a primitive ℓcth root. Under the roots-of-unity hypothesis its cyclotomic image is 1 + ℓcℤℓ. The subgroup for the layer has image 1 + ℓc+mℤℓ. Choose γ in the base Galois group lifting a generator of its cyclotomic image. The valuation of χ(γ) − 1 is exactly c, and b = γℓm generates the image for that layer. In these statements “generator” refers to the closure of powers in the cyclotomic image.

On the common character module D = Dℓ the action is (de(g)φ)(u) = χ(g)−eφ(g−1ug). Equivariance says that φ is fixed by the layer group. It suffices to require it fixed by b, equivalently by b−1. Indeed each character is killed by a power of ℓ and its conjugation action is locally constant on a sufficiently high congruence subgroup. Powers of χ(b) meet every needed open coset. Thus the kernel of de(b−1) − 1 is the entire invariant group just identified with Sha.

The linear dual X = Homℤℓ(D, A) carries the contragredient action xe(g)f = f ∘ de(g−1). Consequently its scalar factor is χ(g)+e. Put T = de(b−1) − 1. Restriction X → Hom(ker T, A) is onto by injectivity of A. Its kernel consists exactly of the maps f ∘ T. Indeed a functional vanishing on ker T factors through the image of T and extends from there to D. This identifies the dual of ker T with the cokernel of xe(b) − 1. Duality with A preserves length. For finite length, dualize a composition series and use that the dual of ℤ/ℓ is again ℤ/ℓ. For infinite length, annihilators reverse strict inclusions of submodules since A separates points of their quotients. Arbitrarily long chains therefore persist in the dual.

length Sha¹(Lm, A(−e)) = length [X / ((χ(γ)ex0(γ))ℓm − 1)X].

Here x0 denotes the untwisted dual action. The equality holds for each nonzero integer e and takes values in the extended natural numbers. The window uses e ≥ 1.

As an algebraic check of the signs, take ℓ = 3, D = ℚ3/ℤ3, χ(γ) = 4, and let the untwisted action on D be multiplication by 4 at γ. The untwisted dual action on X = ℤ3 is multiplication by 1/4. For e = 1 the two twisted actions at γ are the identity. At layer zero the whole character group is fixed and the dual cokernel is all of ℤ3, both of infinite length. Using a negative scalar exponent on the dual would instead give 1/16 − 1 = −15/16, which has 3-adic valuation 1. This example tests the algebra underlying the formula. The arithmetic window supplies its own finiteness estimates.

At the reference layer the proof also needs a comparison with degree two. The Tate dual of A(−e) has integral coefficient twist e + 1. Under finite-level Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness and local Tate duality, the two locally trivial groups have equal length. Take a decreasing filtration on the locally trivial degree-two group and an increasing torsion-level filtration on degree one. The former is separated and the latter exhaustive. At all sufficiently high levels the finite quotients of the first and the finite pieces of the second have equal cardinality by finite-level duality and control of localization. Their lengths therefore agree, including the case of unbounded lengths. The degree-two group embeds into full H², giving the upper bound used for the exceptional twists. The numerical bound on full H² remains a separate input.

8.11The cost of one more cyclotomic layer

Fix a rational prime ℓ and a totally complex number field L0 containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root when ℓ = 2. A layer of index m is an extension of L0 obtained by adjoining roots of unity of ℓ-power order and having degree ℓm. Suppose the tower module X admits a surjection ℤℓR → X, where R ≥ 1. Choosing a cyclotomic generator gives an endomorphism γ of X unipotent modulo ℓ and a scalar u with exact valuation vℓ(u − 1) = c ≥ 1, with c ≥ 2 for ℓ = 2. Normalize vℓ(ℓ) = 1 and set vℓ(0) = ∞. The cited descent theorem identifies the locally trivial degree-one length at twist index e ≥ 1 on every layer m with the following cokernel length.

g = ueγ,   hm(e) = lengthℤℓ X / (gℓm − 1)X,
j0 = ⌊logℓ R⌋ + 3,   hm(e) ≤ hj₀(e) + R max(0, m − j0).

To prove the inequality, reduce X modulo ℓ. The quotient is a vector space of dimension at most R over the field with ℓ elements. On it, g − 1 equals γ − 1 and is nilpotent. Its successive images must strictly decrease in dimension until they vanish, so its Rth power vanishes. Put k = ⌊logℓ R⌋ + 1. Since ℓk ≥ R, the characteristic-ℓ binomial identity gives gℓk ≡ 1 modulo ℓ. For any w ≡ 1 modulo ℓ, the sum S = 1 + w + ⋯ + wℓ−1 maps X into ℓX. As wℓ − 1 = S(w − 1), one more power gives congruence to 1 modulo ℓ². It persists at every higher layer.

Now take w ≡ 1 modulo ℓ². For each x, Sx ≡ ℓx modulo ℓ²X. Thus SX ⊆ ℓX and ℓX = SX + ℓ(ℓX). The quotient ℓX/SX is finitely generated and equals its own multiple by the maximal ideal (ℓ). Nakayama’s lemma makes it zero. Hence the cokernel of S has length at most R. For endomorphisms A,B, the sequence coker B → coker(AB) → coker A → 0 is exact, with first map induced by A. Length subadditivity applied to S(w − 1) gives an increase of at most R per layer. Sum from j0. For m below j0, the larger power minus one factors through the smaller, so the smaller-layer quotient has no greater length. This argument also holds for lengths taking the value ∞.

Write j = j0. Lift γℓj to a matrix M on the free module ℤℓR by choosing a preimage for the image of each generator. Put ae = (uℓj)e. The cokernel of aeM − 1 surjects onto the one defining hj(e). For |z|ℓ ≥ 1, subtract the two defects and apply the ultrametric inequality. For |z|ℓ < 1, both defects have norm 1. Consider the closed balls in ℤℓ centered at e of radius ℓj+c|aez − 1|ℓ. The center of a smallest-radius ball in any finite subfamily lies in every ball of that subfamily. Compactness of ℤℓ gives a common point s for all e. Thus vℓ(aez − 1) ≤ j + c + vℓ(s − e). Sum over the eigenvalues, then apply the layer increment. The resulting centers s1, …, sR work for every twist and layer.

hm(e) ≤ ∑i=1R [max(m, j0) + c + vℓ(si − e)].

Two integers in the same such ball differ by a multiple of ℓB+1, while their ordinary distance is less than Z < ℓB+1. They coincide. At most R twists are marked. On the others each valuation vℓ(si − e) is at most B, giving a finite bound at once.

For every unmarked e in [1, Z],   hm(e) ≤ R(max(m, j0) + c + ⌊logℓ Z⌋).

For a marked twist use the other estimate. Poitou–Tate duality and the local finiteness and duality hypotheses identify the degree-one length at j0 with that of a locally trivial degree-two group. The latter embeds into the full degree-two cohomology with coefficients ℤℓ(e + 1). The full group’s length therefore bounds hj₀(e). The growth inequality carries this bound to every m. The degree-two estimate gives finiteness of that full group and bounds the logarithm of its order by exp((2en)CK log(2D)), where n is the field degree over ℚ and D its absolute discriminant. A finite ℤℓ-module of length d has order ℓd, since each composition factor has order ℓ. Thus keeping the exceptional e small controls this second estimate. The odd-prime window proof takes Z = ⌊XCt⌋ and chooses a window where every marked twist in the active range e ≤ xCt satisfies e ≤ xε/(2CK). Here X is the outer real scale, Ct the cutoff exponent and CK ≥ 1 the chosen constant in that estimate. The exceptional twists thus remain in the cohomological sum.

8.13Why finitely many marked twists leave a whole interval

Fix the outer scale X and combine the dyadic marks with the marks for the fixed collection of odd primes. The union has size at most R, fixed before choosing X. Put α = ε/(2CK) and β = Ct, so 0 < α ≤ β. A marked integer e is troublesome only when xα < e ≤ xβ. Above this range it is absent from the sum. Below it we can use the degree-two estimate, since eCK ≤ xε/2. The field degree and discriminant in that estimate still have to be bounded.

Write u = log x, a = (log e)/β and B = β/α. This mark forbids exactly a ≤ u < Ba. A window [Y, Y²] becomes [y, 2y] in this coordinate. Begin with an upper limit U = log X. If each mark satisfies a ≤ U/(2B) or a > U, the entire top interval [U/2, U] is safe. Otherwise choose a mark with U/(2B) < a ≤ U. Lower the upper limit to U/(2B). This mark now lies strictly beyond it, so remove that mark and repeat. In at most R reductions the process stops. Thus one may use the uniform constant J = 2R+2BR, with X1/J ≤ Y and Y² ≤ X. Every marked twist still in the sum is small enough throughout the same interval.

8.14The degree-two bound for an exceptional twist

This integer is symmetric in its arguments. Compute the sum of the carries for a product of three elements by putting the parentheses on either side. The intermediate logarithm cancels, giving u(a,b) + u(ab,c) = u(b,c) + u(a,bc). Reduce modulo q. On a word of length 2e + 1 take the product of u over its first e consecutive pairs, times v of the last entry. This is a cocycle, a functional vanishing on boundaries. For a weight x let χ(j) = ζxj. Sum one carry u(χ(j),χ(1)) over j modulo q. The sums of L(χ(j)) and L(χ(j + 1)) agree by a cyclic shift. The result is L(χ(1))/r ≡ x modulo q. Insertion immediately before or after the first entry of any pair gives opposite terms since u is symmetric. Only the last insertion survives. Each pair now sums independently, so the scalar prism reads xev(g).

How the determinant reaches an integral matrix group

The interpolation step prescribes a determinant on every block. To use it in group homology, we must construct a map that realizes those numbers and find an integral matrix group carrying the resulting cycle. Start with the number field F in the cyclotomic layer over L′. For a divisor a supported on finitely many prime ideals of 𝒪F, let I(a) be the fractional ideal with ord𝔓(x) ≥ a(𝔓) at every prime, including zero in the ideal. A tuple of divisors defines the lattice Λ(a) = ⊕jI(aj) in FJ. Positive orders require divisibility and negative orders permit denominators.

Take β ∈ F×. A matrix taking Λ(a) onto Λ(b) with determinant β must carry the product of the input ideals to the product of the output ideals by multiplication by β. The proof constructs such a matrix whenever the resulting order equations hold. For a block with no coordinates its determinant must be one.

ord𝔓(β) = ∑j(bj(𝔓) − aj(𝔓))   for every finite prime 𝔓 of F.

In a nonempty block multiply a single coordinate by β. This sets the determinant correctly and leaves the right total divisor for the target lattice. Now move a divisor d from coordinate j to coordinate i with a determinant-one matrix. Repeating this operation fixes one coordinate at a time while a chosen coordinate absorbs the differences. Once all the others agree, equality of the totals fixes the last one.

How can one two-coordinate move work at every prime?

For current divisors ai, aj, write C = I(d) and D = I(ai+d−aj). The proof chooses u ∈ C nonzero and v ∈ D so that uC−1 + vD−1 = 𝒪F. Express 1 in that sum as us − vr with s ∈ C−1, r ∈ D−1. The matrix with rows (u, v) and (r, s) has determinant one. The ideal memberships put the first output in I(ai+d) and the second in I(aj−d). The inverse has rows (s, −v) and (−r, u), giving the reverse inclusions. One pair of fractional ideals thus enforces all the valuation inequalities simultaneously.

Every pair (2a, 3b/2) in the target has preimage (b, a−b) in ℤ². The matrix and its inverse preserve ℤ[1/6]². The target of the integral lattice map is the specified fractional lattice.

Apply this construction to the indices J = (ℤ/q)². At each unwanted slope the fiber sums of η vanish, so the specified determinants are all one. At the selected slope a coordinate with weight κh is conjugated by γ−h to have weight one, where γ(ζ) = ζκ. Equal powers of κ modulo q give equal powers of γ, so this choice is consistent. In the regrouped coordinates the divisors at 𝔓 sum to ord𝔓(β) on the weight-one block and zero on every other block. The weight-one block contains the coordinate (1,0). We have therefore realized β and the unit determinants by F-linear block maps. Undoing the conjugations produces an L′-linear map gt on FJ at each slope. On each regrouped block the cyclic action is scalar, so its block map commutes with that action. The prescribed determinants refer to those blocks.

Choose a common nonzero denominator B ∈ 𝒪L′ covering the divisor support and the excluded splitting primes. All the gt preserve the lattice away from B, and each carries the full integral lattice M = (𝒪F)J to the same target. Thus gt−1gt₀ preserves M itself. Together with the diagonal actions and their required conjugates, these relations allow the prism construction to produce a cycle in the subgroup H stabilizing M inside the group integral away from B.

The module M is finite projective over R = 𝒪L′. A finite free module RN therefore admits a surjection s onto M and a section i with si = 1. For h ∈ H let α(h) act on M. The following matrix acts by α(h) on iM and by the identity on ker s. Its inverse is obtained by replacing h by h−1.

λ(h) = iα(h)s + (1−is) ∈ GLN(𝒪L′).

Pushing the cycle along λ gives the ordinary integral matrix cycle. At each tested residue map 𝒪F → k away from B whose restriction to R is onto, its representation on kN is conjugate to the residue action on kGal(F/L′)×J plus an identity action. The additive cycle test gives the same value after this extension. The rank N is chosen before the residue tests and can depend on the integral construction. The later stable-rank comparison handles varying ranks in the homology count.

How one denominator works for every residue test

The stabilized cycle is chosen before its reductions. Each test must identify the reduction of the coefficient module with one copy of the residue field for each Galois automorphism and each coordinate. Here is the field calculation for one coordinate. Let F/L′ be the finite Galois extension in the construction and write G for its Galois group. Given a ring map r from 𝒪F to a finite field k, denote its restriction to 𝒪L′ by r0. Assume r0 is onto. We want to prescribe all entries of the tuple (r(σa))σ∈G and identify its kernel. Which single element may we exclude from every later test?

Start with a basis ui of F over L′ and its dual ui∨ for the pairing (x,y) ↦ Tr(xy). The pairing is nondegenerate because the extension is separable. Clear the denominators in both finite lists with one nonzero integer m. Put ei = m ui∨, fi = m ui and b0 = m². Multiplying trace-dual expansion by m² gives the first identity below. For the second, apply σ and expand the trace as a sum over τ ∈ G. Linear independence of distinct field automorphisms as functions of x identifies the coefficient of τ(x) on both sides.

b0x = ∑i Tr(xfi)ei,   ∑i τ(fi)σ(ei) = b0 δστ.

Suppose r0(b0) ≠ 0. For a prescribed tuple (vτ), lift each scalar ∑τvτr(τfi)/r0(b0) to a coefficient ci in 𝒪L′ using surjectivity of r0. Then a = ∑iciei has exactly the specified tuple by the second identity. Conversely, if every entry for a vanishes, each integral trace Tr(afi) belongs to ker r0. The first identity shows that b0a belongs to (ker r0)𝒪F. In the quotient b0 has an inverse lifted from k, so a belongs to the same ideal. Its elements all have zero tuple since every σ fixes the base. We have obtained the ring isomorphism

𝒪F / (ker r0)𝒪F ≃ ∏σ∈G k.

The trace formula constructs the required coefficients without choosing an integral basis over the base ring. A linear basis over the field and a common denominator suffice.

Prescribe the two conjugate residues in the Gaussian integers

For ℚ(i)/ℚ take the basis (1,i), trace dual (1/2,−i/2), m = 2 and b0 = 4. Reduce at 5 by sending i to 2. The two rows send a + ci to a + 2c and a − 2c. To obtain (0,1), add the equations to get 2a = 1 and subtract them to get 4c = −1 in 𝔽5. Thus a = 3 and c = 1 work. The kernel consists exactly of multiples of 5. At 2 the two readings coincide, and b0 reduces to zero. This shows why the invertibility assumption matters.

The lattice also has a divisor 𝔡 prescribing lower bounds for the orders of its coordinates. Enlarge b0 to B = b0∏𝔓∈supp 𝔡 Norm(𝔓). Each norm lies in its prime ideal and is nonzero. Every prime in the finite support now contains B. Away from B, the prescribed order and the ordinary integrality condition agree. At a prime dividing B, multiplying by B raises the order by at least one. For any vector integral away from B, one large enough power Bn therefore brings all its finitely many coordinates into the prescribed lattice. This works for either lattice transported by a gluing map. After inverting B, the map and its inverse preserve the same module. The fixed B works across the maps and future residue tests, while n can depend on the vector. For any allowed reduction, r0(B) ≠ 0 implies r0(b0) ≠ 0, so the split tuple above is available for the cycle test.

The coefficient De may have positive ℓ-adic valuation. Its residue modulo q divides ℓm(c+m). For each factor, remove the unit power of κ. The binomial expansion κd − 1 = ℓc(d + ℓct) shows that a factor with 0 < d < m has valuation less than c + m, using m < ℓc. Multiplying the resulting divisibilities gives the stated bound. For q = 9 the elements 2⁸ and 2¹⁷ both have index 8 modulo 9, and their ratio is 2⁹ = −1, a ninth power.

From local powers to a bound for the image

Why do reductions decide whether the ratio β is a qth power in F? Choose x in an algebraic closure with xq = β. At a tested prime choose an integral t whose residue is a nonzero qth root of the reduced β. The product ∏0≤i<q(x − ζit) = xq − tq vanishes upon reduction at a place above that prime. Some factor vanishes. Thus x has the same nonzero residue as an element ζit of F. A Frobenius σ fixes this residue, and σ(x)/x is a qth root of unity reducing to 1. Away from ℓ such a root equals 1. Indeed a nontrivial root would have geometric sum zero, reducing to q = 0 in the residue field. Now a degree-one Chebotarev theorem supplies, outside the finite excluded set, a Frobenius inducing any specified Galois action on x. Its residue field has prime order, so the required surjectivity from 𝒪L′ holds. Every Galois automorphism fixes x. Hence x lies in F, which proves global power detection. By the defining separation of S, the tuple of scaled evaluations at all tested primes is injective on S.

What limits the number of tuples? Lift a degree-m cycle modulo q to an integral chain z. Its boundary is q w, so w gives a class killed by q in integral homology of degree m − 1. This is the Bockstein map. A different lift changes w by a boundary. In one fiber of the map, differences therefore lift to integral cycles. On their scaled evaluations take the stabilized combinations of diagonal copies and ordinary inclusions. Their integral span has rank at most r₂ by the odd-degree rank theorem. In a target killed by q, a rank-r group with finite torsion contributes at most qr times its torsion order. The Bockstein fibers account for the second torsion factor. Writing Tj for the order of integral homology torsion in degree j at GL4e+6(𝒪L′), stability gives

|S| ≤ qr₂ T2e+1 T2e.

The cycles and both torsion groups belong to group homology. The rank estimate below applies to the combinations of cycles selected by block repetition. In the character count a matching qr₂ on the left cancels, leaving the torsion product and the separate kernel loss. The finite relation supplies the filling, and the sum over lines supplies the determinant test. The divisor interpolation explains which determinants must be realized. The lattice construction realizes those determinants. The degree-one Chebotarev theorem supplies the detecting primes.

Why only one real test per complex place survives

In a single Bockstein fiber, the counting proof lifts differences to integral homology in odd degree m = 2e + 1. For a totally complex field L′ with r₂ pairs of complex embeddings, it needs a bound on the number of independent filtered classes. The odd-degree rank theorem gives rank at most r₂ when m < r₂ and the initial matrix size n is at least 2m + 4. The proof uses the homological stability theorem. Over the Dedekind ring 𝒪L′ its stable-range parameter is 2, so enlarging the matrices by identity blocks induces an isomorphism on degree-m integral homology in this range.

Start with a class z0. At step t, take its image under the homomorphism that repeats a matrix in ℓ diagonal blocks, then subtract ℓt+2 times its image under ordinary stabilization to the same size. Call the resulting class zt+1. A linear test of weight j multiplies by ℓj under block repetition and is unchanged by stabilization. After m − 1 steps its value has therefore been multiplied by

∏i=2m(ℓj − ℓi).

Every weight from 2 through m has a zero factor. To see what is left, suppose a real linear combination of the resulting cycles represents a nonzero real homology class. Stability preserves it at a larger matrix size, where a closed cochain detects it. The invariant-form comparison represents that cochain on cycles by integration. In odd degree its evaluation is a sum of the higher-weight tests and one weight-one test τw for each infinite place w. The latter comes from an alternating cyclic trace at that place. Reversing the cycle conjugates the trace. After alternation one of its real and imaginary parts vanishes. If every τw vanished on our combination, the cochain could not detect it. Thus any two cycles with the same test values give the same real homology class. The real homology image is a quotient of the image of the r₂ tests, so its dimension is at most r₂. Independent integral classes stay independent after extension of scalars to ℝ, yielding the rank bound.

Why averaging a differential form preserves its periods here

How can a group cocycle that detects a cycle be replaced by a form invariant under every archimedean matrix? Let m < r₂ be the positive homological degree over the totally complex field L′. Given any starting size, the comparison chooses a size N at least that large. At this one size it applies to every real homogeneous m-cocycle c of Γ = GLN(𝒪L′). The space of integration consists of one positive definite Hermitian matrix per complex place. A bar chain [g₁|…|gm] gives the affine simplex with vertices I, g₁·I, …, (g₁⋯gm)·I, where g·h = (g⁻¹)*hg⁻¹ at each place. Integrating a form ω over these simplices and adding the chain coefficients gives its period ⟨ω,z⟩ on a cycle z.

The partition of unity and Stokes calculation first give a Γ-invariant form with the periods of c. Averaging over central scalars preserves these periods and gives a form ω′ invariant also under those scalars. To compare its values at different points, pull its value at g·I back to the tangent space at I by g. These coefficients are square-integrable on a finite-volume fundamental domain for SLN(𝒪L′) in ∏wSLN(ℂ). Indeed the partition gives a bound by a constant times heightam, and N was chosen to make the moment of order 2am finite. Their normalized Haar mean in the moving frame gives a form ω̄ invariant under all of ∏wGLN(ℂ). To prove that ω̄ represents c, it remains to show that every period of the mean-zero remainder ω₀ = ω′ − ω̄ vanishes.

How does a group cocycle become a differential form?

Let Γ = GLN(𝒪L′) act on the cone of positive Hermitian matrices at the archimedean places. An m-cocycle c assigns a real number to m + 1 group elements. It is invariant when all are left-multiplied by the same element, and its alternating sum over the faces of any tuple of length m + 2 is zero. We want a smooth m-form whose integral on an arithmetic cycle recovers the value of c on that cycle. A partition of unity lets us trade one group argument at a time for a differential.

Write Aγ for the linear action of γ on Hermitian matrices. From a smooth function φ on the cone form the weights ψγ(h) = φ(Aγ⁻¹h). Only finitely many terms occur near any point, and they sum to 1. For a cochain β whose values are forms, let K insert a new first argument and average with these weights. Write δ for the alternating deletion of group arguments and d for exterior differentiation. The construction is

(Kβ)(g₀,…) = ∑γ ψγ β(γ,g₀,…),   η₀ = c,   ηj+1 = d(Kηj).

In Kδβ, deleting the newly inserted γ gives β times ∑ψγ = β. Every other deletion cancels the corresponding term of δKβ. Thus δK + Kδ = 1 in the degrees used here. Starting with δη₀ = 0, induction gives δηj+1 = dδKηj = dηj = 0. Indeed η₀ is constant in the cone variable, and every later ηj is an exterior derivative. After m steps only one group argument remains. The equation δηm = 0 now says its values at any two group elements coincide. This leaves a smooth closed form on the cone. Equivariance of the weights gives arithmetic invariance.

To compare periods, fix the identity matrix I. On a homogeneous tuple (g₀,…,gm), let Wj integrate ηj(g₀,…,gm−j) over the simplex with the last j + 1 vertices Agₘ₋ⱼI, …, AgₘI. Thus W₀ = c. A comparison cochain Bj integrates Kηj in the same way on an input with one fewer group element. In δBj, deleting an early argument invokes δKηj = ηj. The other deletions give the oriented faces of the next simplex. Stokes replaces their sum with the integral of d(Kηj) = ηj+1. Including the orientation sign gives

δBj = Wj + (−1)m−1−jWj+1,   0 ≤ j < m.

Substitute this identity successively for j = 0,…,m−1. The result is c = δb + sWm for an invariant cochain b. The sign starts at 1 and is multiplied at step j by (−1)m−j. Choose ω = sηm. Evaluating δb on a bar chain z gives b evaluated on ∂z. Consequently the periods of ω and c agree on every cycle.

Check the sign in degree one. Let ℤ act on the positive real line by h ↦ 2nh and take c(a,b) = b − a. In the coordinate t = log₂ h, choose a smooth bump θ supported on [−1,1] and positive on (−1,1). Normalize its integer translates to weights ψn(t) = θ(t − n)/∑p θ(t − p). Their weighted mean A(t) = ∑n nψn(t) satisfies A(t + 1) = A(t) + 1. Hence (Kc)(b) = b − A and η₁ = −dA. The sign in the comparison is −1, giving ω = dA. The group element 2 sends h = 1 to h = 4. Their images in the quotient coincide, so the interval from 1 to 4 represents the cycle [2]. Its integral is A(2) − A(0) = 2. This verifies the cocycle construction and its orientation in one dimension.

The arithmetic partition has additional properties. Its generator is unchanged under common positive dilation, so ω already has scalar invariance whenever the scalar moduli agree at all places. Its translated supports have finite overlap, and each weight derivative in the moving frame has norm at most a constant times heighta. At step j + 1 the product rule leaves dψγ wedged with ηj, since dηj = 0. At a point of overlap, translate all active labels on the left by the inverse of one of them. Each resulting label belongs to a fixed finite set. This bounds both the number of terms and the values of c on the relevant tuples, using its invariance. The form therefore grows at most like heightam, with a constant allowed to depend on the cocycle. The construction from the region of bounded lattice minima gives a = 1 for every matrix size N ≥ 1 over the fixed totally complex field. The comparison uses the weaker statement that one a works in every size. For its Stokes input, one obtains the formula on affine simplices by integrating in one coordinate and summing the endpoint faces with alternating signs.

Dividing by the orbit sum. On a compact neighborhood K′ of K inside the cone, choose a nonnegative smooth bump b supported in K′ and scaled to be at least 1 on K. Form S(k) = ∑γ∈Γ b(γ⁻¹k). Only finitely many terms occur near any positive k. In fact, if a matrix and its translate both lie in a fixed compact set, the columns of γ⁻¹ belong to a fixed finite set of lattice points. Reindexing makes S invariant. Choose a smooth function g with g(s) ≥ ½ everywhere and g(s) = s for s ≥ 1. Then ψ = b/g(S) is smooth, even where S = 0. Whenever an orbit meets K, one bump is at least 1, so its orbit sum is large enough for the exact normalization

∑γ∈Γ ψ(γ⁻¹k) = S(k)/g(S(k)) = 1.

To reach these orbits from any h, first remove its common scale by multiplying it by [∏w(det hw)mult(w)]−1/(N[L:ℚ]). Call the result h₀. Next take a smooth arithmetic-invariant approximate dual minimum μ with λ∨/4 ≤ μ ≤ 4λ∨. The source adds positive semidefinite corrections to μ(h₀)h₀. At each scale s = 4j the correction averages outer products of h0,wvw over short lattice vectors, with smooth cutoff and a factor s−2. The corrected form F(h) has both minima bounded below uniformly in h. Thus the translated weights ψ(γ⁻¹F(h)) sum to one on the whole cone. The pulled-back support can extend towards the cusp. Equivariance and the compact support of ψ still bound the possible relative labels of overlapping translates by a finite set.

How many translates of a smooth weight can meet?

The compact set of representatives K meets the orbits of forms with both squared minima bounded below. A smooth weight around K must give the right total even if several group elements carry a form to the same point. Write Γ = GLN(𝒪L) and let γ act on a form by qγ·h(v) = qh(γ⁻¹v). The weight indexed by γ at h is evaluated at τγh = γ⁻¹·h. The properness and bump statements below hold for every number field L and rank N ≥ 0. The final use of the thick set assumes L totally complex and N ≥ 1.

Count matrices by their columns. For a compact subset Q of the positive cone, let Γ(Q) consist of the γ for which both h and γ·h lie in Q for some h. Fix h₀ ∈ Q. On Q times the unit sphere of archimedean columns, qh₀(v)/qh(v) has a finite upper bound A. Homogeneity gives the same comparison on all columns. Put Bⱼ = maxk∈Q qk(eⱼ). For γ ∈ Γ(Q), its inverse has jth column γ⁻¹eⱼ satisfying

qh₀(γ⁻¹eⱼ) ≤ A qγ·h(eⱼ) ≤ A Bⱼ,   |Γ(Q)| ≤ ∏j #{v ∈ 𝒪LN ∶ qh₀(v) ≤ A Bⱼ}.

Each factor is finite by discreteness of the lattice inside a bounded ellipsoid. All columns together determine γ⁻¹, giving the displayed counting bound. For an empty Q there are no incidences. At rank zero the group is trivial.

Normalize on every orbit meeting the compact set. Choose ε > 0 so the closed ε-neighborhood K′ of K is compact and still in the open positive cone. The smooth support lemma on the ambient real vector space gives 0 ≤ f ≤ 1 with nonzero set exactly the open ε-neighborhood. On nonempty K its minimum m is positive. Put b = f/m, so b ≥ 1 on K. For empty K one may take b = 0 and m = 1. Given another compact B inside the cone, use Q = B ∪ K′. Every label γ with τγh ∈ K′ for some h ∈ B satisfies γ⁻¹ ∈ Γ(Q). Taking B to be a small closed ball about a point of the cone therefore gives the same finite list throughout that ball. The orbit sum S(h) = ∑γ b(τγh) is smooth there. Since τδτγ = τγδ, left multiplication by γ reindexes the sum and makes S invariant.

Let Θ be the smooth transition from zero on (−∞,0] to one on [1,∞). The denominator g(s) = ½ + (s−½)Θ(2s−1) is at least ½ everywhere and equals s for s ≥ 1. Define ψ = b/g(S) on the cone and extend by zero outside it. Every point outside the cone has a neighborhood disjoint from K′, so the extension is smooth. If γ₀·h lies in K, the term labelled γ₀⁻¹ is at least one in the raw sum. Consequently

∑γ∈Γ ψ(τγh) = S(h)/g(S(h)) = 1   whenever Γ·h meets K.

All elements giving the same orbit point contribute separately to S. Their multiplicity is the order of the stabilizer.

Two points of one orbit receive different weights

Take 𝒪 = ℤ[ω] with ω² + ω + 1 = 0. Put h₀ = Id₂, s = [[1,1],[0,1]] and h₁ = s∗s = [[1,1],[1,2]]. Every τγh₀ = γ∗γ has entries in 𝒪. Distinct such matrices differ by at least one in the maximum absolute entry norm, because every nonzero Eisenstein integer has absolute value at least one. Choose two disjoint bumps around h₀ and h₁ inside the cone whose supports meet this orbit only at their respective centers. Give their sum b values 1 and 2 at the centers.

The squared length of a column is the sum of two nonnegative integer norms. A unit column therefore has a single nonzero coordinate, one of the six units. Orthogonality puts the second column on the other axis. The stabilizer U of h₀ has 2·6² = 72 elements. Also γ∗γ = s∗s exactly when γs⁻¹ ∈ U, so the labels giving h₁ form U s. At h₀ there are 144 nonzero terms and S = 72·1 + 72·2 = 216. Each label in U receives 1/216 and each label in U s receives 1/108. The two centers receive total weights ⅓ and ⅔.

Pull back the compactly supported weight. Let F be the smooth equivariant map obtained by normalizing the scale and correcting the two minima. Set φ(h) = ψ(F(h)). Every F(h) meets K up to a translate. Hence ∑γ φ(τγh) = 1 for every positive h. For a compact neighborhood V in the input cone, apply properness to F(V) ∪ K′ to get a finite list on its interior. There is also one finite set of relative labels for the whole cone. Let D be the closure in that cone of {φ ≠ 0}. Continuity gives F(D) ⊆ K′. If the supports with labels γ and η meet, some h has γ⁻¹·h and η⁻¹·h in D. Their images under F are in K′ and differ by the action of η⁻¹γ. This puts η⁻¹γ in the single finite set Γ(K′).

Why this bump also works for the derivative estimate

Say k is δ-close to positive h if |qk(z)−qh(z)| ≤ δqh(z) for all archimedean columns. Polarization on coordinate vectors gives ‖k−h‖ ≤ 2δ‖h‖ in the matrix-entry norm. The smooth compactly supported ψ has an ordinary Lipschitz constant Lψ. Choose R ≥ 0 bounding the norm on K′. If the two values differ, at least one point belongs to K′. For 0 ≤ δ < ¼ the norm estimate then gives ‖h‖ ≤ 2R, so |ψ(k)−ψ(h)| ≤ 4LψRδ. For δ ≥ ¼ the bound 0 ≤ ψ ≤ 2/m supplies the upper bound 16δ/m. Thus Cψ = 16/m + 4LψR works for every δ ≥ 0, including cases where k lies outside the cone. Composing with the relative bounds for the normalization and correction, then differentiating in a moving frame, gives the one-power height bound. The companion finite-overlap assertion controls the labels present in sums of derivatives.

Why the exponent is one. Write H(h) = 1/(λ(h)λ∨(h)). Common rescaling preserves H. A perturbation of relative size δ changes every quadratic value by at most δ times that value. The normalization h ↦ h₀ increases this relative error by at most a factor 3 for δ ≤ ¼. For the averaged outer product at scale s, the change is bounded by a constant times δqh₀(z)/s in each test direction z. The active scales for two nearby inputs lie above 3λ(h₀)/64. Summing their reciprocals as a geometric progression costs at most 256/[9λ(h₀)]. To measure this error relative to the output, use qF(h) ≥ μ(h₀)qh₀ and μ ≥ λ∨/4. The reciprocal product of the two minima is exactly H. Including the variations of μ and of the cutoffs gives a total relative error ≤ C(1+H)δ for sufficiently small δ. The bump is Lipschitz for this relative error. Passing to derivatives in the moving frame costs a further factor N, and the positive lower bound H ≥ c₀ gives 1+H ≤ (1+1/c₀)H. The multiplicative constants may depend on L and N. The exponent a = 1 works in every rank N ≥ 1.

For L = ℚ(i) and N = 1, write h = [t], t > 0. Then qh(z) = t|z|² on ℤ[i], λ = t, λ∨ = 1/t, and H = 1. The determinant product is t², so normalization sends every t to 1. All four units ±1, ±i fix every Hermitian scalar. Their four translated partition values are therefore equal, and the orbit sum forces each value to be ¼. Counting only distinct points of this orbit would lose the stabilizer factor.

How the correction keeps both lattice minima positive

The compactness argument needs a constant c > 0 that works for both minima at every input h. Adding positive forms helps its primal minimum but can make its inverse smaller. Why does the dual minimum survive? The proof tests the correction in a direction chosen by an integral covector. Along this direction a whole range of scales vanishes exactly.

Fix the field L and rank N ≥ 1. Write qh for squared length summed over the infinite places, and λ and λ∨ for the minima on nonzero integral vectors of h and its dual h∨, whose matrix at each place is the inverse transpose. Let R be the corrected form. Its base term is μh, where μ is a smooth approximation to λ∨(h). At scale d = 4j, a lattice vector v contributes a rank-one form with local matrix (hwvw)(hwvw)*. Give it weight θ(qh(v)/d), where 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, θ = 1 on arguments ≤ 1 and θ = 0 on arguments ≥ 4. Divide the weighted sum by d²Zd, where Zd is the sum of the weights, to obtain Td. The zero vector has weight 1, so this denominator is positive. Then R = μh + ∑d θ(dμ)Td.

The primal minimum. Let u attain λ(R) and set a = qh(u). If μa ≥ 1/16, the base term suffices. Otherwise choose a power of four with 4a ≤ d ≤ 16a. Its outer weight is 1. For every v with qh(v) ≤ d/4, both v and v+u have inner weight 1, by the parallelogram identity. Put B = Re ∑w uw*hwvw. Translation by u changes B to B+a, and B²+(B+a)² ≥ a²/2. By Cauchy–Schwarz, each square is at most the number r of infinite places times the corresponding rank-one value at u.

Let M count the vectors in the inner ball of squared radius d/4. The positive weighted numerator at u is at least Ma²/(4r). Indeed, each of the two lists v and v+u has no repetitions, so together they can charge the numerator at most twice. The counting estimate with dilation 16 gives Zd ≤ #{v ∣ qh(v) ≤ 4d} ≤ C₁₆M. Since d ≤ 16a, this one scale proves

λ(R) ≥ min{1/16, 1/(1024rC₁₆)}.

This bound depends on the field and rank through the lattice count.

Finding a dual test direction. Now assume L is totally complex. Choose an integral covector f realizing Q = λ∨(R). Among vectors with f(v) ≠ 0, choose v₀ minimizing m = qh(v₀). Such a vector exists because f is nonzero on at least one coordinate vector, and only finitely many lattice vectors have squared length at most that of this first candidate. At some place w we have |f(v₀)w| ≥ 1, because the absolute field norm of this nonzero algebraic integer is at least 1. At that place take the unique y satisfying y*hwx = fw(x) for all x. Set b = y*hwy > 0. The source’s local pairing inequality gives 1 ≤ 4bm.

The transference bound supplies a lattice point within squared distance ρ = CT/λ∨(h) of any real vector. Apply it at the vector z supported only at w, with component ty where t²b = 5ρ. If the nearby v belonged to the kernel of f, testing z−v against y would give (tb)² ≤ 4bρ. Its left side equals 5bρ. Hence f(v) ≠ 0. The parallelogram identity gives qh(v) ≤ 2(5ρ)+2ρ, so

1 ≤ 4bm,   m ≤ 12CT/λ∨(h).

What the correction does to this direction. When 4d ≤ m, a vector with positive inner weight has qh(v) < m. It lies in the kernel of f by minimality. Thus its rank-one form at w evaluates to |y*hwvw|² = 0. Choose d₀ = 4j₀ ≤ m < 4d₀. Only scales d ≥ d₀ need be counted. For the surviving terms use Cauchy–Schwarz in the original metric. A vector of positive weight has qh(v) < 4d, hence |y*hwvw|² ≤ 4bd. The weighted average divided by d² is at most 4b/d. Their sum is ≤ 4b · (2/d₀) ≤ 32b/m by a geometric series. If μ ≤ Cμλ∨(h), the base term contributes at most 12CT|Cμ|b/m. Put A = 12CT|Cμ|+32. Testing the same covector and vector in the corrected metric now gives

b² = |fw(y)|² ≤ 4Q (y*Rwy) ≤ 4QA b/m,   λ∨(R) = Q ≥ bm/(4A) ≥ 1/(16A).

The selected smoothing permits Cμ = 4. For each fixed field and rank the smaller of the primal and dual bounds works for all positive forms, including the normalized inputs to the partition.

One scale can raise one direction and leave another untouched. Take ℤ[i]², h = diag(1,64), u = e₁, and use f(v) = v₂ as a test covector. Then m = 64, y = e₂/64 and b = 1/64. At d = 4 the outer weight is 1 since μ ≤ 4λ∨(h) = 1/16. Every vector with positive inner weight is (z,0) with |z|² < 16. There are 45 such Gaussian integer candidates, so Z₄ ≤ 45. The four points at each squared norm 1, 2 and 4 carry full weight. They contribute 4(1+2+4) = 28 to the numerator at e₁. Hence T₄[e₁] ≥ 28/(16·45) = 7/180, while T₄[y] = 0 exactly. This checks the two estimates on one scale without needing the value of the smooth cutoff between its plateaus.

How does a dual minimum put a lattice point near every target?

The dual test needs a lattice point near a prescribed vector that can have arbitrary real coordinates. A lower bound on the length of every nonzero integral covector supplies a covering radius for the original lattice. We derive the bound first in integer coordinates, then identify which dual lattice appears in the arithmetic statement. All costs below are squared distances.

Find one short direction. For a positive definite real symmetric matrix G of size d ≥ 1 write QG(x) = xᵀGx. Suppose QG⁻¹(c) ≥ δ > 0 for all nonzero integer columns c. To control QG, factor G = BᵀB. The inverse image under B of the box with |yⱼ| ≤ 2|det B|1/d has volume 4d. It is symmetric and convex and its volume exceeds 2d, the Minkowski threshold for ℤd. It therefore contains a nonzero integer v. Summing the coordinate squares of Bv gives QG(v) ≤ 4d(det G)1/d. In particular a positive lower bound ℓ on every nonzero integer vector forces ℓd ≤ (4d)d det G.

Apply that determinant inequality to G⁻¹ with ℓ = δ and to G under the supposition that all its nonzero integer vectors have squared length greater than 2(4d)²/δ. Multiplication cancels the two determinants and gives 2d ≤ 1. Consequently there is a nonzero integer vector with QG(v) ≤ 2(4d)²/δ. Write this vector as an integer multiple of a primitive one, whose coordinates have greatest common divisor one. The primitive vector is at least as short and can be completed to an integral basis by Smith normal form. In that basis the first diagonal entry of the Gram matrix is its squared length, say a. An integral basis change permutes the lattice vectors and its inverse transpose permutes integral covectors, so both the dual lower bound and the covering problem survive.

Round one coordinate after the others. Write the new matrix in blocks [[a,bᵀ],[b,D]] and put S = D − bbᵀ/a. For an error vector (u,y), completing the square gives

QG(u,y) = a(u + bᵀy/a)² + QS(y).

Minimizing in u shows that S is positive definite. For an integral covector c′ on the remaining coordinates, solving Gx = (0,c′) gives x′ = S⁻¹c′. Hence QS⁻¹(c′) = QG⁻¹(0,c′), and the same δ works in dimension d−1. For a target (p₀,p′), use induction to choose an integer c′ with small remaining error y = p′−c′. Round p₀ + bᵀy/a to its nearest integer for the first coordinate. The square on the right now costs at most a/4. Starting with C₀ = 1, the resulting constant satisfies

Cd = Cd−1 + 8d² = 1 + 8 ∑j=1d j²,   QG(p−c) ≤ Cd/δ.

The added cost is at most 2(4d)²/(4δ) by the short-direction bound. In dimension zero the only error is zero, so the initial constant 1 works.

Transfer from integral coordinates to Hermitian forms. Let L be totally complex with discriminant Δ, and take a positive definite Hermitian form h at each complex place in rank N ≥ 1. Choose an integral basis b₁,…,be of 𝒪L, where e = [L:ℚ]. The archimedean quadratic form qh acquires a real Gram matrix G in d = Ne coordinates. Every target tuple has real coordinates in this basis, and integer coordinates give the original arithmetic lattice. The integer theorem requires a lower bound for the inverse real Gram matrix. The input λ∨(h) measures integral covectors using (hw⁻¹)ᵀ at each place w.

For a nonzero integer covector c, let T have entries Tr(bᵢbⱼ), hence det T = Δ. In each block multiply the row of coefficients of c by the adjugate of T, then use those integers as basis coefficients of f ∈ 𝒪LN. Since adj(T)T = ΔI, this gives Tr(fₖbⱼ) = Δckj and f ≠ 0. If z is the tuple represented by real coordinates x, linearity and conjugate pairing of the embeddings give Δcᵀx = 2 Re ∑w fwᵀzw. The factor 2 counts the two embeddings at each complex place.

Now choose x representing zw = hw⁻¹ fw. Set s = qh∨(f). Then QG(x) = s and Δcᵀx = 2s. Expanding the nonnegative square QG(tx−G⁻¹c) gives QG⁻¹(c) ≥ 2t cᵀx−t²s. Substitute t = 2/Δ. Every integral c ≠ 0 now satisfies QG⁻¹(c) ≥ 4s/Δ² ≥ 4λ∨(h)/Δ². Applying the integer result with this δ gives, for each target z, a lattice point v satisfying

qh(z−v) ≤ CdΔ²/(4λ∨(h)).

Thus the constant CT in the dual probe bound depends on the field and rank, and the dependence on the input form is carried by its dual minimum. The short spanning argument uses the same covering estimate.

Check the rounding shift and the discriminant on a Gaussian lattice

Take L = ℚ(i), N = 1, h = 1 and the integral basis (1,1+i). Its Gram matrix is [[1,1],[1,2]]. Coordinates (2/5,2/5) give the complex target 4/5 + 2i/5. Rounding both coordinates separately gives the lattice point 0 and squared error 4/5. The Schur complement equals 1. After rounding the second coordinate to 0, the shifted first coordinate is 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5. Rounding it to 1 gives squared error (−1/5)² + (2/5)² = 1/5.

In this basis the trace matrix is [[2,2],[2,0]], with determinant −4. The integer covector (0,1) times its adjugate is (−2,2), giving f = −2 + 2(1+i) = 2i. Since |f|² = 4, the converted lower bound for this covector is 4·4/(−4)² = 1. Direct multiplication by G⁻¹ = [[2,−1],[−1,1]] gives the same value. This example uses the squared length convention in both calculations.

Which central directions still need averaging?

The form ω realizing the cocycle already has two symmetries. It is invariant under Γ = GLN(𝒪L′) and under a common positive scaling at all infinite places. The next estimate uses independent scalar changes at every place. Write c(t) for the central matrix whose component at w is exp(tw)I. A complex scalar zw acts on a positive Hermitian matrix by Hw ↦ |zw|−2Hw, since the action uses the inverse matrix on the right and its adjoint on the left. Thus only the real logarithms tw = log |zw| matter.

Let r be the number of complex places of the totally complex field L′. The line of constant vectors in ℝr acts trivially on ω by pullback. A unit u gives another symmetry because uI ∈ Γ. Its logarithm vector ℓ(u) = (log |w(u)|)w lies in V = {t ∈ ℝr ∣ ∑w tw = 0} by the product formula. Dirichlet’s unit theorem gives a lattice Λ of rank r − 1 in V, generated by the logarithms of fundamental units. Subtracting the coordinate mean from any t leaves a vector in V. Consequently the central parameters still to be averaged form the compact torus V/Λ. For r = 1 the initial symmetries already suffice.

The proof integrates one unit direction v = ℓ(u) at a time. For the pullback of the form, including its tangent arguments, it takes

Avω = ∫₀¹ c(τv)∗ω dτ.

Unit invariance makes the integrand 1-periodic in τ. Translating the interval of integration therefore preserves the average, so every real multiple of v fixes Avω. Central scalars commute, which preserves the directions already treated. Iterating uses ordinary Lebesgue measure of mass one on each unit interval. In the coordinates of the fundamental units their product induces Haar probability on V/Λ. The output ω′ is invariant under every scalar tuple.

Why does the average have exactly the original periods? Fix a finite bar cycle z based at the identity matrix I. For fixed τ, centrality moves the basepoint of every simplex from I to c(τv)·I, keeping the same group labels. Join the old and new vertices by the simplices of a prism. Its side faces cancel on the cycle because ∂z = 0. The remaining two evaluations agree because ω integrates to a cocycle on simplices. Thus for every τ the sum over the cycle already equals its original value. Interchanging the finite sum, simplex integrals and the unit-interval integral preserves that value. The averaged form still integrates to a cocycle by the same interchange on a boundary. Its moving-frame bound retains the exponent am for a form of degree m, since the path τ ↦ c(τv) is compact and right translation there changes the height by a bounded factor.

Check the factor of two and a period

In L′ = ℚ(i,√2), label the two complex places by the sign of √2. For u = 1 + √2 and a = log(1 + √2), the absolute values of u at these places are exp(a) and exp(−a). Take N = 1 and work with the cyclic subgroup generated by u. On the pair of positive numbers (H₁,H₂) set s = (log H₂ − log H₁)/(4a). Under c(τℓ(u)) log H₁ decreases by 2aτ and log H₂ increases by 2aτ, so s goes to s + τ. Averaging (2 + cos(2πs)) ds gives 2 ds. The cycle [u] moves s from 0 to 1 at the identity basepoint. The two primitives 2s + sin(2πs)/(2π) and 2s both increase by 2 along that cycle. On an open arc from 0 to 1/4 their increments differ by 1/(2π).

How large must the matrix be to integrate the coefficients?

Even a finite-volume quotient can have an unbounded function whose square has infinite integral. Here the possible growth occurs at the cusps, where a lattice or its dual has a short vector. For the tuple of Hermitian forms h = x·I, let λ(h) be the infimum of the sum of its values over the complex places on a nonzero integral vector. The height is 1/[λ(h)λ(h∨)], where h∨ = (h⁻¹)T at each place. For every totally complex number field L′ and every integer A ≥ 0, the proof chooses a finite-volume Haar fundamental domain for SLN(𝒪L′) in ∏wSLN(ℂ) on which heightA is integrable whenever N ≥ A + 2.

For a form of degree m, the bound on the norm of its coefficients in the moving frame is K heightam. The partition of unity supplies a for the field before the matrix size is chosen. Squaring calls for A = 2am. The comparison therefore chooses N large enough for this moment, for the separate Hecke stability threshold, for the requested starting size, and for N ≥ 3. This one size works for every cocycle of the specified degree m < r₂(L′). The zeroth moment gives finite volume, so the inequality u ≤ u² + 1 for the coefficient norm also gives integrability of the coefficients themselves. Their mean is now defined.

Why do finitely many regions suffice for the cusp integral?

Let L be totally complex and set Γ = SLN(𝒪L). In the product of SLN(ℂ) over the complex places, a single matrix can travel arbitrarily far out a cusp. What becomes finite is the choice of arithmetic coordinate system. For fixed L and N ≥ 1, there are finitely many matrices cj and one region S such that for every x, some γ ∈ Γ and some j satisfy cj−1γx ∈ S. Inside S the diagonal parameters can still grow. This is the cover used in the height moment.

How does a shortest row control the cusp diagonal?

Take a number field L of degree d over ℚ and an adelic invertible matrix g of size N ≥ 1. For a nonzero row x over L, form xg at every place. Its height Hg(x) is the product of the Euclidean lengths at the infinite places, squared at complex places, and the maximum entry norms at the finite places. The product formula makes this height invariant under scaling x by L×. Below any fixed height there are only finitely many rational lines. Place a minimizing row last in a rational basis and factor the resulting matrix as an upper triangular matrix times a maximal compact element. The right compact factor preserves all the row lengths. Reduce the upper left block by induction, keeping the last row in place.

For N ≥ 2 the only new adjacent pair is the bottom block [[α, u], [0, β]]. Write A = |α|𝔸, B = |β|𝔸 for the products of their normalized local absolute values. The last row has height B. Two-dimensional approximation produces a nonzero rational row whose image under this block has height at most C√(AB), with C depending only on L. Putting the two coordinates in the last two slots gives a competitor for the minimum, since the triangular matrix has zeros to their left. Hence

B ≤ C√(AB)  ⟹  B ≤ C²A.

Induction gives this inequality for every pair of consecutive diagonal entries, with the same constant.

Where the square root comes from

If A ≥ B, the row (0, 1) already works. Otherwise put s = (A/B)1/(2d). Divide the block by β. After multiplying its first row by a scalar in L×, the upper left entry is a positive idèle of archimedean size s² times an element of a fixed compact set. Call the adjusted upper right entry a. In an integral basis, (H + 1)d candidate multiples of a fall into Hd boxes after rational translation to clear finite denominators and reduction modulo the integer lattice at infinity. Two lie in one box. Their difference gives a nonzero integer ℓ of L of archimedean size O(H + 1) and c ∈ L such that ℓa + c is integral at all finite places and O(1/H) at infinity. For H = ⌈1/s⌉ both coordinates of the resulting row have size O(s) at infinity. Its finite norm product is bounded by compactness. Restoring β bounds the height by a field constant times B sd = √(AB).

To obtain the real cusp parameters, take rᵢ = |bᵢᵢ|𝔸1/d. The idèle with value rᵢ at every infinite place and 1 at every finite place has norm rᵢd. Dividing it out leaves a norm-one idèle. Rational diagonal scalings bring these remainders into compact representatives of the norm-one idèle classes. Rational upper triangular row additions bring the entries of the upper unitriangular factor into compact additive representatives. The resulting factorization has the fixed compact triangular set, positive diagonal and maximal compact subgroup used in the cusp cover, with t ri+1 ≤ rᵢ for t = C−2/d. At finite places the positive diagonal is the identity, so for g = (x, 1) the rational change of basis has finite component in a fixed compact set.

Check the complex-place exponent over ℚ(i)

Take g∞ = [[1, 2], [0, 3]] and identity at every finite place. Every rational line has a primitive Gaussian integer representative (u, v), whose finite height factors are 1. Its height is |u|² + |2u + 3v|². Height 1 would require a unit u with 3 dividing 2u, since u = 0 gives height 9 for a primitive row. The row (1, −1) attains height 2. Use it as the last row of γ = [[0, −1], [1, −1]]. Multiplying γg∞ on the right by the unitary matrix [[1, 1], [1, −1]]/√2 gives [[−3/√2, 3/√2], [0, √2]]. At finite places γ is integral and invertible, so the triangular factor there can be the identity. The last diagonal idèle has norm 2, and its real parameter is √2. The first has norm 9/2 and real parameter 3/√2.

First choose finitely many rational matrices. Append the identity at the finite places to an archimedean point x. The shortest-row construction supplies a rational matrix η such that ηx has a bounded upper triangular factor, a positive diagonal and a compact factor. The positive diagonal equals the identity at the finite places. Thus the finite part of η belongs to one compact set C, the finite projection of the product of the compact triangular set and the maximal compact subgroup. The subgroup U of matrices integral and invertible at every finite place is open. Its left cosets cover C, and finitely many suffice. In each of these cosets that occurs for a rational η, choose one rational representative a. Then a−1η and its inverse are integral at every finite place. Each entry therefore lies in 𝒪L. Writing δ = a−1η, we have δ ∈ GLN(𝒪L) and δx equals a−1 times the reduced factors. The finite list for this GL cover consists of the inverses g = a−1.

Correct the determinant. The unit det δ can be written vNu₀. Here v is a unit and u₀ comes from a finite list. Indeed, express a unit as a root of unity times powers of the fundamental units and reduce each exponent modulo N. The list has at most |μ(L)|Nrank 𝒪L× entries. Put D(u) = diag(u,1,…,1). This gives an integral change of coordinates of determinant one.

γ = v−1D(u₀−1)δ,   det γ = v−Nu₀−1 det δ = 1.

The chart now depends only on (g, u₀). Set G = D(u₀−1)g. At each complex place w choose a scalar zw with zwN det w(G) = 1 and take cj,w = zww(G). This is the precise rationality used for the height bound. The underlying matrix G is defined over L, while the scalar can depend on the place.

A determinant correction over the Gaussian integers

Test the correction with N = 2, L = ℚ(i), x = g = I and δ = [[i,1],[0,1]]. Here v = 1 and u₀ = i work. Then γ = [[1,−i],[0,1]]. Choose z = exp(πi/4), so z² = i and c = z diag(−i,1) has determinant one. In this chart c−1γ = z−1δ = [[1,1],[0,1]] diag(i/z,1/z). The last factor is unitary of determinant one. This tests the correction on one admissible triangular factorization. The full list of charts may contain other representatives.

How are the chart bounds shared across places?

Before the determinant correction, write the positive diagonal entries as rᵢ, with t ri+1 ≤ rᵢ for fixed t > 0. Compactness bounds the entries of each triangular factor Bw by M and bounds its diagonal moduli below by M−1. After the correction the local scalar is αw = w(v−1)/zw. Use the same diagonal coordinates at every place by setting

sᵢ = log rᵢ + meanw(log |αw| + log |Bw,ii|).

The local determinant-one equations give ∑isᵢ = 0. Subtracting two places’ determinant equations also gives |log |αw| − log |αw′|| ≤ 2 log M. After removing exp(sᵢ) and moving the diagonal phases into the unitary factor, every triangular entry has modulus at most M⁴ and each diagonal modulus is at least M−4. In each diagonal position their product over the places is one, by the definition of the mean. The common region uses si+1 ≤ sᵢ + 4 log M − log t. These bounds hold across all charts for this field and matrix size.

Integrate over the cover. Write F for a Haar fundamental domain, and let f be a nonnegative Γ-invariant integrand. Moving pieces of F by Γ gives an upper bound by the integral over the union of the charts. Subadditivity and left invariance of Haar measure then give

∫F f dμ ≤ ∑j ∫S f(cjy) dμ(y).

Overlaps are allowed. Each chart has its own finite height constant, and there are only finitely many summands. For f = heightA the remaining integral on each chart is finite when N ≥ A + 2. This last convergence comes from the decay in the unbounded diagonal variables.

Why the cusp integral converges

Reduction theory covers the quotient by finitely many charts. After a fixed translate, each point has a bounded triangular factor, a diagonal factor with entries exp(sᵢ) shared across the complex places, and a unitary factor. The determinant gives ∑sᵢ = 0, and the adjacent entries satisfy si+1 ≤ sᵢ + T for a fixed T. Clearing denominators in a chart gives lower bounds proportional to exp(−2 max sᵢ) and exp(2 min sᵢ) for the primal and dual minima. Set W = ∑i<N|sᵢ − si+1|, using indices 1,…,N. Then max sᵢ − min sᵢ ≤ W, so heightA ≤ C exp(2AW).

Write Φ = ∑i<j(sᵢ − sⱼ). A unit box in the logarithms has Haar measure at most C′ exp(−2Φ) for every admissible s in it. Indeed, the packing argument fits at least exp(2Φ) translates of the box in a translate of a fixed compact set, with uniformly bounded overlap. When the coordinates decrease, the gap sⱼ − sj+1 occurs j(N − j) times in Φ, at least N − 1 times. For the allowed upward errors of size T, the cone estimate gives the following quantitative version.

2AW − 2Φ ≤ C″ − δ ∑i|sᵢ|,   δ = 2(N − 1 − A)/N > 0.

Index the boxes by the integer parts of their coordinates. The integral over a box with index u is bounded by a constant times exp(−δ ∑|uᵢ|). Summing over all boxes gives a product of convergent geometric series. For instance, along (3t, −t, −t, −t) with t ≥ 0, W = 4t and Φ = 12t. At A = 2 the combined exponential is exp(−8t). At A = 3 it equals 1 along the ray. This explains the strict inequality A < N − 1 in the estimate and leaves the endpoint moment undecided.

How a finite incidence count bounds an angle

Let π be the prime element used in the Hecke average, 𝒪 the ring of integers of the field, and k = 𝒪/(π), of order q ≥ 25. Take N ≥ 3. In SLN(L′) consider three conjugates of SLN(𝒪). The group Kᵣ is Dᵣ−1SLN(𝒪)Dᵣ, where the diagonal matrix Dᵣ has π in its first r positions and 1 elsewhere, for r = 0,1,2. Put Eᵢⱼ = Kᵢ ∩ Kⱼ and B = K₀ ∩ K₁ ∩ K₂. At each vertex Kᵣ, the two incident subgroups stabilize a pair of nested subspaces after reduction modulo π. Such a pair is a flag.

Use coordinates 0,…,N − 1 after conjugating by Dᵣ. The following pairs are in the order used by the angle bound. The first subgroup in each pair is called E and the second E′.

  • In K₀, E₀₁ fixes the line spanned by e₀ and E₀₂ fixes the plane spanned by e₀,e₁.
  • In K₁, E₁₂ fixes the line spanned by e₁ and E₀₁ fixes the hyperplane x₀ = 0.
  • In K₂, E₁₂ fixes the hyperplane x₁ = 0 and E₀₂ fixes its subspace x₀ = x₁ = 0.

Here “fixes” means preserves the subspace as a set. The bipartite graph has a vertex for each subspace of the first or second type, and one edge for each incident pair. Equivalently, take the translates of the two coordinate subspaces under Kᵣ. The stabilizer of their common edge is B. In the first two cases a matrix outside E moves the distinguished line to a different line. Row additions preserving the first line can take that new line to a fixed second coordinate line. Thus all such matrices form one double coset of E. Transposing gives the same result for the distinguished hyperplane in the third case.

Count the flag choices in a finite group

At any one vertex, the proof passes to the finite group G = Kᵣ/core(B), where core(B) is the intersection of all Kᵣ-conjugates of B. Use the same letters for subgroup images. A real function f constant on the cosets Ek has a value at each vertex of the first type. Suppose its mean is zero. Use the uniform measure on G and form its correlation c(s) = meank f(sk)f(k). It equals ‖f‖² on E. Elsewhere it is constant because it depends only on the double coset. Its mean over s is zero, so its value outside E is nonpositive.

Average f over left multiplication by E′, writing P′f for the result. Expanding its squared norm and reindexing gives the mean of c(s) over s ∈ E′. Only the elements of E′ ∩ E = B can give a positive contribution. Their proportion is 1/[E′:B]. For a function g constant on the cosets E′k, averaging preserves the pairing with g. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|⟨f,g⟩| = |⟨P′f,g⟩| ≤ ‖f‖‖g‖ / √[E′:B].

At vertex 0, the matrices I + t e₁₀ in E₀₂ move the line to span(e₀ + t e₁) inside the same plane. Distinct t modulo π give distinct flags, so [E₀₂:B] ≥ q. Likewise I + t e₂₁ in E₀₁ sends e₁ to e₁ + t e₂ while fixing e₀. This supplies [E₀₁:B] ≥ q, the other needed index. Thus every pairing has coefficient at most 1/√q ≤ 1/5. On the arithmetic quotient the first vector is orthogonal to all Kᵣ-invariant functions. Subtracting its local Kᵣ-average gives a representative with zero mean on each finite fiber. Integrating the finite estimate gives the three angles used in the Hecke norm calculation.

A calculation at the threshold. In size N = 3 over 𝔽₂₅, the graph at vertex 0 joins points to lines in the projective plane. There are (25³ − 1)/(25 − 1) = 651 points and as many lines. Each line contains 26 points. Give one point value +1, a second point value −1, and all other points zero. Averaging on each line gives +1/26 on the 25 lines through just the first point, −1/26 on the 25 through just the second, and zero elsewhere. The common line cancels. The ratio of output norm to input norm is √(50/26²)/√2 = 5/26. In fact this is the norm on the entire mean-zero subspace. If A is the line-by-point incidence matrix, ATA has diagonal entries 26 and off-diagonal entries 1, since two points determine one line. It acts by 25 on vectors with zero sum. The averaging matrix is A/26. Here the general bound 1/√26 and its uniform relaxation 1/5 both exceed the exact value 5/26.

Why are the common invariant functions constant?

The Hecke angle estimate applies after the common invariant component has been removed. Work on the common finite cover for the three groups in the flag calculation. Put Eᵢⱼ = Kᵢ ∩ Kⱼ and B = K₀ ∩ K₁ ∩ K₂. A real L² class fixed by all three edge groups Eᵢⱼ is represented almost everywhere by a constant. Since the cover has positive finite volume, a constant with integral zero is zero. In the proof the Hecke average v has integral zero. Its inner product with every such constant vanishes, which places v in the orthogonal complement needed for the angle estimate.

Which arithmetic group is dense? Write Γ = SLN(𝒪L), where L is totally complex and N ≥ 3. For a prime element π let Dᵣ have its first r diagonal entries equal to π and the rest equal to 1. Then Kᵣ = Dᵣ−1ΓDᵣ inside SLN(L). It is the group generated by K₀ and K₁ whose simultaneous archimedean image is dense in ∏w SLN(ℂ). The norm threshold |𝒪L/(π)| ≥ 25 enters the flag estimate; the density theorem requires only that π be prime.

For distinct indices let Tᵢⱼ(a) = I + a eᵢⱼ, with eᵢⱼ the matrix unit. K₀ supplies these transvections for every integral a. Conjugating supplies T0j(1/π) in K₁. With three distinct indices, ordinary matrix multiplication gives

[Tᵢₖ(a), Tₖⱼ(b)] = Tᵢⱼ(ab),   [A,B] = ABA−1B−1.

This multiplies denominators. In the induction from πm to πm+1, use coordinate 0 as the intermediate index for two nonzero endpoints. For a starting index 0, use a third index and the new 1/π on the first factor. For an ending index 0, append an integral transvection to a pair of nonzero endpoints already obtained at the new level. This produces all Tᵢⱼ(a/πm) with integral a.

These parameters are dense simultaneously in ∏wℂ. The integer lattice has a finite covering radius R in this product. Given ε > 0, put ε′ = ε/(1 + R). Minkowski’s theorem supplies a nonzero q = y/πm with all |w(q)| < ε/(1 + R). Indeed the volume of the body |w(y)| < ε′|w(π)|m grows in proportion to |Norm π|m, and |Norm π| ≥ 2. Round the tuple (zw/w(q)) to the embeddings of a single algebraic integer a ∈ 𝒪L within distance R. Then aq approximates the whole tuple within ε. By continuity the group closure contains a complex transvection at any one place with identity at the others. Transvections generate SLN(ℂ), giving every factor of the finite product.

Two commutators that give a denominator of 49

Take L = ℚ(i), N = 3 and π = 7. The residue field has 49 elements. The first commutator [T₁₀(a), T₀₂(1/7)] gives T₁₂(a/7). The second, [T₀₁(1/7), T₁₂(a/7)], gives T₀₂(a/49). Choose a = 69 + 85i by rounding the coordinates of 49(√2 + i√3). The resulting parameter is within √2/98 of √2 + i√3. This is the one-place version of the simultaneous approximation.

How does density act on an L² class? Choose a measurable, B-invariant representative F of a common class. For each edge group E the finite coset average of F is pointwise E-invariant. Its difference from F has squared norm zero on the cover, so the two agree almost everywhere there. Both are B-invariant, hence the exceptional set is Haar-null in the whole group by the fundamental-domain formula. Left translation preserves null sets. It follows for each γ ∈ E that F(γx) = F(x) for almost every x. The set of γ satisfying this condition is a subgroup, since a translated null set is null.

Why does this subgroup contain both full vertex groups? In K₀ the stabilizer E₀₁ has only one double coset outside itself, by two-transitivity. The index [E₀₂ : B] ≥ 25 supplies an element of E₀₂ outside E₀₁. The subgroup therefore contains that whole double coset and all of K₀. In K₁ use E₁₂ and an element of E₀₁ outside B in the same way. Thus F is invariant almost everywhere under each element of the dense subgroup above.

Why does invariance extend to every translation?

Fix a Borel set U of real values and let T = F−1(U). The translations preserving T up to a null set form a closed set. To see this, take gₙ → g. On a compact test region C, the images gₙC and gC eventually lie in one compact set L₀. The set T ∩ L₀ has finite measure. The measure of the symmetric difference between its two translation preimages tends to zero. If each gₙ preserves T almost everywhere, then g does so on C. A countable compact cover gives the assertion everywhere up to Haar measure zero. Density now gives invariance for every fixed g.

Such a set has measure zero or has null complement. Indeed, if T has positive measure, Fubini gives a point a ∈ T such that ba ∈ T for almost every b. Right multiplication by a preserves the Haar null sets, so the complement of T is null. Applying this argument to inverse images of a countable family separating real values shows that F is constant almost everywhere. The argument allows the exceptional set to depend on the translation throughout.

How the three local bounds of 1/5 give a gap of 3/5

Work in the real Hilbert space of square-integrable coefficients on the common cover. Let P₁, P₂ and P₃ be the orthogonal projections onto the spaces of functions invariant under E₀₁, E₀₂ and E₁₂, respectively. Write Qᵢ = I − Pᵢ for the part lost in this projection. Start with a pair of spaces, and remove from x its projection onto their common subspace. Call the result z. This removal leaves both Qᵢx and Qⱼx unchanged. Write a = Pᵢz, b = Pⱼz and S = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖². The flag estimate gives 2⟨a,b⟩ ≤ S/5. Since S = ⟨z,a + b⟩, Cauchy–Schwarz gives S² ≤ ‖z‖² · (6/5)S. Thus the sum of the two squared losses, T = 2‖z‖² − S, is at least (4/5)‖z‖².

Set rᵢ = Qᵢx. For the pair, ⟨rᵢ + rⱼ,z⟩ = T. A second application of Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖rᵢ + rⱼ‖² ≥ (4/5)T, including the zero case. Sum over all three pairs. Every individual ‖rᵢ‖² occurs twice on the right. On the left the sum of pair squares is ‖∑rᵢ‖² + ∑‖rᵢ‖². Subtraction leaves the factor 2 · (4/5) − 1 = 3/5. In operator notation, for D = ∑Qᵢ, we have ‖Dx‖² ≥ (3/5)⟨Dx,x⟩.

To put the bound on the original coefficient, write E(x) = ⟨Dx,x⟩ = ∑‖Qᵢx‖². Cauchy–Schwarz for the positive form ⟨D·,·⟩ gives ‖Dx‖⁴ ≤ E(x)E(Dx). The preceding estimate now implies E(y) ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every y in the range of D. The kernel of D consists of the vectors fixed by all three projections. The common-invariance argument identifies these vectors with the constants. Since D is self-adjoint, its range is dense in their orthogonal complement. Continuity gives the same inequality for every mean-zero coefficient on the cover.

Where the Hecke factor 3/5 enters

For a prime element whose ideal has norm at least 25 and N ≥ 3, take a continuous, arithmetic- and scalar-invariant real coefficient of mean zero in L². To estimate its Hecke average, lift its translate w and the coset average v of that translate to a common finite cover. Averaging there gives ⟨v,w⟩ = ‖v‖². The angle bound for the invariant subspaces gives |⟨v,w⟩| ≤ (2/5)‖v‖‖w‖. Cancelling ‖v‖ when positive gives a norm bound of 2/5. Both squared norms acquire the same positive covering index, so it cancels on returning to the quotient. The proof weakens 2/5 to 3/5 and preserves mean zero at each step, giving the norm factor (3/5)j after j averages. This is the upper estimate compared with (4/5)j for the stabilized periods.

The average v is orthogonal to the constants. Subtracting the mean of w therefore preserves ⟨v,w⟩, preserves the edge-group invariance of w, and can only decrease its norm. We can now estimate the angle using mean-zero vectors on both sides. The preceding Hilbert-space estimate gives ∑‖(I − Pᵢ)y‖² ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every mean-zero y. Take mean-zero unit vectors u fixed by P₁ and P₂, and z fixed by P₁ and P₃, choosing the sign so t = ⟨u,z⟩ ≥ 0. For y = u + z the first error is zero. Since ⟨u,P₂z⟩ = t, the second error has square 1 − ‖P₂z‖² ≤ 1 − t². The third has the same bound. Thus (3/5)·2(1 + t) ≤ 2(1 − t²). Cancelling 2(1 + t) gives t ≤ 2/5.
