How can the mean of the coefficients define a form at every point?

The previous average over central scalars produced a form ω′ with the original periods. Now we want a form invariant under every archimedean matrix. Let G = ∏w GLN(ℂ), let S = ∏w SLN(ℂ), and write Agh = (g−1)*h g−1 for their action on Hermitian matrices. The tangent spaces of the positive cone are copies of the same real vector space. At y ∈ S pull the form at AyI back to the identity. This gives an alternating multilinear form F(y) = ω′(AyI) ∘ Ay, with Ay applied to each tangent argument. It is left invariant under the arithmetic subgroup Λ = SLN(𝒪L′) in its archimedean embedding. Let D be a fundamental domain for Λ in S of positive finite Haar volume. The height moment makes F square-integrable there, hence integrable. We can now take an ordinary vector-valued mean in a fixed space.

M = (vol D)−1 ∫D F(y) dy,   ω̄(AgI) = M ∘ Ag−1.
Why do two matrices taking the identity to the same point give the same answer?

The ambiguity at the identity is a tuple of unitary matrices u. At each place choose a unit-modulus Nth root of det u and divide by it. The resulting k belongs to S and acts exactly like u on Hermitian matrices. Hence F(y) ∘ Au = F(yk). Right translation by k preserves Haar measure on S. It also carries a fundamental domain to another one, since it commutes with left multiplication by Λ. Integrating a Λ-invariant integrable function over either domain gives the same integral. This proves M ∘ Au = M. Every positive Hermitian tuple can be written AgI by factoring each matrix in the tuple as B*B and choosing g = B−1. Two choices differ on the right by a stabilizer of I. The displayed transport rule therefore gives a single value at every point. The group law then makes ω̄ invariant under all of G, with constant moving-frame coefficients M.

At h = AgI the transported value on V is tr(g*Vg) = tr(h−1V). For h = diag(4,9) and V = diag(4,0) it equals 1. Taking the upper-left entry instead would already fail at h = I. How does a bound in L² control the period of one cycle?

A low-dimensional simplex can have zero volume in the surrounding space. An L² estimate on the ambient quotient therefore gives no direct estimate for restriction to that simplex. What makes the argument work here is that a closed cycle has the same period after its vertices are averaged. The resulting integral can be estimated using ambient volume.

Fix a finite bar cycle z of degree m ≥ 1 in GLN(𝒪L′). Write F(y₀,…,ym) for the integral of the form ω on the affine simplex with those vertices in the cone of positive Hermitian matrices. The proof assumes that F is invariant under the arithmetic group and that its alternating sum over the faces of every (m + 1)-simplex vanishes. For a bar symbol [g₁|…|gm], set h₀ = 1 and hj = g₁⋯gj. Choose independent points Y₀,…,Ym with normalized volume on a closed ball about the identity matrix I, small enough to lie inside the cone. Then

⟨ω,z⟩ = ∑g z(g) · 𝔼[F(h₀·Y₀,…,hm·Ym)].

To see why, allow each vertex to carry one of two marks, “fixed at I” or “averaged.” Removing a vertex leaves the same product probability law on the others. The alternating face sum of the marked cochain is therefore the expectation of a face sum of F, hence zero. The prism between the two choices of basepoint has coboundary equal to the difference between all-averaged and all-fixed evaluations. On z this difference is zero because ∂z = 0.

A one-dimensional check. Let ℤ act on ℝ by translations, put P(x) = x + sin(2πx), and take F(x,y) = P(y) − P(x). Integer translation leaves F unchanged and its three face terms telescope. The bar cycle [2] has period F(0,2) = 2. Take independent Y₀,Y₁ uniform on {0,1/4}. The four values of F(Y₀,2 + Y₁) are 2, 13/4, 3/4 and 2. Their mean is 2. This discrete example checks the averaging identity. The volume estimate uses the ball with its continuous distribution.

For that estimate, fix a bar symbol. Let Aj be the invertible real linear action of hj on the ambient Hermitian space of real dimension d. A point of the random simplex is ∑j τjAjYj, with nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one. Some τi ≥ 1/(m + 1). Hold all the other vertices fixed. Changing variables in Yi gives a density bounded by (m + 1)d/(vol(B) |det Ai|), where B is the ball. The edge lengths are uniformly bounded and the possible simplex points fill a compact set K inside the cone. Integrating in the simplex parameters now bounds the expected absolute simplex integral by a constant times ∫K ‖ω‖.

Central-scalar invariance lets the proof unfold this last integral into a bound by the integral of the moving-frame norm ‖fr ω‖ on a compact set K′ inside ∏w SLN(ℂ). Write Λ for the image of SLN(𝒪L′) and D for its fundamental domain. If λ₀x and λx both belong to K′, then λλ₀⁻¹ lies in the finite set Λ ∩ K′(K′)⁻¹. Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the last factor vol(D)1/2 ‖fr ω‖2. Summing over the finite support of z with weights |z(g)| gives a constant Cz independent of the form.

Apply this bound to ωj = Hjω₀. The Hecke contraction acts on each scalar coefficient in a fixed basis at the identity. Finite-dimensional norm comparison bounds the squared norm of the whole form by Kbasis times the sum of its squared coefficients. |⟨Hjω₀,z⟩| ≤ Cz √(KbasisS₀) (3/5)j.

The local estimate holds for each fixed cycle and every admissible square-integrable form. Mean zero, N ≥ 3 and a prime element of norm at least 25 enter when applying the contraction. The second estimate on the stabilized cycles recovers the period before iteration.

Choose a prime element π whose ideal has norm at least 25. The normalized Hecke operator H averages over the finite cosets in Γ diag(π,1,…,1) Γ. On each mean-zero coefficient its L² norm contracts by a factor at most 3/5. The estimate for an averaged cycle then gives |⟨Hjω₀,z⟩| ≤ Cz(3/5)j for each fixed cycle. (4/5)j‖x₀‖ ≤ ‖xj‖ ≤ C(3/5)j,   ‖x₀‖ ≤ C(3/4)j.

Letting j tend to infinity forces x₀ = 0. Homological stability makes the chosen cycles span also in size N, so ⟨ω̄,z⟩ = ⟨c,z⟩ for every cycle. This equality lets one test a nonzero filtered homology class by an invariant form. On the filtered cycles every such test is a linear combination of the r₂ one-place traces. This gives the upper bound on the rank of their homology image.

Where the lower factor 4/5 comes from

Let In and IN be the numbers of cosets in the respective Hecke averages and put α = In/IN. The cosets inherited from size n contribute α times a smaller-size Hecke period vector yj. For the other cosets, transfer from their stabilizers gives the original periods after summing. Thus xj+1 = (1 − α)xj + αyj. The smaller-size operator acts linearly on a finite-dimensional space of period vectors, so ‖yj‖ ≤ K‖xj‖ with K independent of N and j. Since IN ≥ N, we can arrange α(1 + K) ≤ 1/5. The reverse triangle inequality now gives ‖xj+1‖ ≥ (1 − α(1 + K))‖xj‖ ≥ (4/5)‖xj‖. For example, if ‖x₀‖ were 1 and the upper constant were 2, three iterations would require 64/125 ≤ ‖x₃‖ ≤ 54/125. The limit argument works for every finite constant.

Which cosets carry the original period into the next Hecke average?

Fix the smaller size n while enlarging to N = n + r. To obtain the lower bound on a period, we need the share of the Hecke sum that acts as the original period on a stabilized cycle. That share has a concrete description in the residue field.

Write ΓN = GLN(𝒪L′), q = diag(π,1,…,1) and k = 𝒪L′/(π). A matrix γ lies in the subgroup SN that labels the Hecke cosets precisely when qγq−1 is integral and invertible over the integers. Conjugation divides the first column below its top entry by π and multiplies the rest of the first row by π. The determinant stays a unit. Thus membership is equivalent to preserving the line ke₁ modulo π. For a right coset SNc, take the residue line of c−1e₁. Two representatives determine the same line exactly when they determine the same coset. There are finitely many such lines, and swapping the first coordinate with each coordinate realizes N distinct lines. In particular the index IN is at least N.

A coset inherited from Γn has all its last r coordinates zero on this line. Conversely, if those coordinates vanish, some coordinate in the first block is nonzero. Swap it into first position. Over k, subtract multiples of the first row to clear the other entries. These row additions lift to invertible integral operations in size n. The resulting line is ke₁, so the original coset came from the smaller group. Stabilization identifies its cosets bijectively with this part of the larger sum. Their normalized total is the smaller Hecke average times In/IN.

Why summing the other cosets recovers an unshifted period

The smaller group permutes the complementary set X of cosets by right multiplication. For each x take the difference Φx between the cocycle translated by its Hecke representative and the original stabilized cocycle. On cycles of the stabilizer of x, this difference has zero period. Here the nonzero coordinate in the last block matters. It permits a change of basis in which the translated stabilizer acts by integral matrices with diagonal blocks h and 1 and only one possible off-diagonal block above them. The arithmetic affine-block homology comparison identifies the image of a stabilizer cycle under this action with its block-diagonal image. Basepoint independence on cycles then gives the claimed zero.

To pass from a stabilizer to the whole group, choose one representative x₀ per orbit. The cochain criterion for a zero class supplies a primitive Ψ on tuples from the whole smaller group, invariant under the stabilizer, with δΨ = Φx₀. Transport it to each x in that orbit by an element carrying x₀ to x. Two such choices differ on the left by a stabilizer element, so give the same translate. The sum of these translates is invariant under the smaller group, which permutes the terms. Its coboundary is ∑x∈X Φx. Evaluated on a cycle z, this is the primitive evaluated on ∂z = 0. The sum over X therefore contributes |X| copies of the original period before normalization.

Why can the upper-right block be erased on a stabilizer cycle?

f∗z − (D ∘ f₀)∗z = ∂y.

Both chains live in that same matrix size over the same field. The separate stable-range condition n ≥ 2m + 4 is used when comparing homology across sizes. Here one can take any block sizes. Find a unit that detects every translation degree. Put A = Matn×r(𝒪L′) with addition. The block group P consists of pairs (B,g) with product (B + gB′,gg′). Here aw are nonnegative integers and |·|w is the usual complex modulus at a place. For any one choice of exponents, some aw is zero because m < r₂. Dirichlet’s unit theorem supplies a unit with negative logarithm at every other place. The corresponding sum of logarithms weighted by the aw is strictly negative. Its kernel thus has infinite index in the unit group. To see why one unit works for all the exponents, pass to the free abelian group of units modulo roots of unity. Each kernel there has smaller rank, so its rational span is a proper subspace. Finitely many proper subspaces cannot cover a vector space over ℚ. Clear the denominators of a point outside their union to obtain an integer exponent vector, hence a unit outside every kernel. At total degree r₂, the all-ones choice would instead give one for every unit by the product formula.

Its real cohomology in degree j is spanned by cup products of j additive coordinate functionals. After extending the coefficients to ℂ, the embeddings of each matrix entry give coordinates in which multiplication by v scales such a product by Λ = σ₁(v)⋯σj(v). For 1 ≤ j ≤ m its modulus differs from one by the choice of unit. To return to real coefficients, pair each eigenvalue with its conjugate. The real polynomial (X−Λ)(X−Λ) kills this component and takes the value |1−Λ|² at 1. Multiplying these factors gives a polynomial Fj that kills degree j in the translation cohomology and satisfies Fj(1) ≠ 0.

Which cochains detect the translations in the upper-right block?

A translation in the affine block is a matrix in the additive group A = Matn×r(𝒪L′). Its entries lie in a free abelian group of finite rank. We first work with any such A and trivial real coefficients. A homogeneous cochain of degree j is a function on Aj+1 unchanged when the same element is added to all its vertices. The coboundary δ sums the values obtained by omitting vertex i, with sign (−1)i starting at i = 0. Tuples can have repeated vertices. For an additive character α ∶ A → ℝ, the edge value α(y₁ − y₀) is closed because the two edge increments along a triangle add to the third.

Choose j characters α₁, …, αj. Read the ordered edges of a simplex in succession. Their product is the following closed j-cochain.

Cα(y₀, …, yj) = ∏i=1j αi(yi − yi−1).

In every degree j ≥ 1, any invariant closed c has an equality of cochains c = ∑ν aνCαν + δe, with finitely many real coefficients and an invariant (j − 1)-cochain e. The proof writes j = q + 1, so c takes q + 2 vertices and e takes q + 1. The formula uses coefficient one on each ordered cup before the linear combination. It asserts generation and allows different choices of characters and primitive.

Proof by splitting off one integer coordinate

Choose an integral basis. At rank zero every cochain is constant. In odd positive degree, closedness forces the constant to be zero. In even positive degree the constant of the same value one degree lower is its primitive. This follows by counting the alternating face signs. For the induction write P = ℤ × G, let ι(g) = (0,g), let ρ discard the first coordinate, and let ℓ read it as a real number. The known result on G supplies words for the part U = ρ∗ι∗c seen on the slice of height zero.

The missing information is a cocycle one degree lower. Put ψ(h,g) = (−1,g). The prism Kψ on an ordered tuple sums over i the evaluations on (y₀, …, yi, ψyi, …, ψyj−1) with sign (−1)i. Its identity δKψ + Kψδ = ψ∗ − 1 makes b = ι∗Kψ(U − c) closed. Indeed, on the slice, ψ translates every vertex by (−1,0), which preserves both cochains. In ℓ ∪ ρ∗b, the first edge supplies the height difference, and the remaining vertices supply b. On the slice the prism of this cup evaluates to −b. Only the first prism simplex has a first edge of height −1. All the later first edges have height zero.

[c] = [U] + [ℓ ∪ ρ∗b].

To see exactness in the invariant complex, set R = c − U − ℓ ∪ ρ∗b. Both its restriction and its restricted ψ-prism are zero. Put x = KιρR. Then δx = −R, and x is invariant under G. Let Δ be pullback by translation by (1,0) minus the identity. For j ≥ 2 the two vanishings give (Δx)|G = 0, so w = −KιρΔx satisfies δw = Δx. A finite signed sum of translates of w, from height zero to the height of the first vertex, gives a G-invariant W with ΔW = w. Thus −x + δW is invariant under the new generator as well, and its coboundary is R. In degree one Δx is already a constant of value zero.

Apply induction to ι∗c and to b. Prepending ℓ to an ordered cup gives the next word, and δ(ℓ ∪ e) = −ℓ ∪ δe absorbs the coboundary with its sign. When j = 1, b is an invariant function of one vertex, hence a scalar. Transporting the resulting decomposition along the chosen basis proves it for A.

A unit square distinguishes the two orders

Every coboundary evaluates to zero on this cycle, so the first cup represents a nonzero class.

In the affine argument a separate eigenvalue calculation supplies a polynomial Fj that kills each cup word under pullback by multiplication by a chosen unit v. In the first column the horizontal translation fixes the cochain and the vertical coboundary alone suffices. Repeating through the positive vertical degrees expresses any degree-m cocycle c of P as p∗b + δe for a quotient cocycle b.

Write S = s ∘ p. Subtracting the pullback by S gives c − S∗c = δ(e − S∗e), since pS = p. Thus every real cocycle evaluates to zero on w − S∗w for a cycle w of P. Why does one trace per complex place suffice on the filtered cycles?

The transported mean gives a form ω invariant under every archimedean change of basis. To integrate it on a homology class, we first need its integral to vanish on boundaries. Write M = ω(I) for its value at the identity tuple and Y₁,…,Ym for Hermitian tangent vectors. All matrix operations below are taken place by place. For a positive Hermitian tuple x, the matrix g = x−1 takes I to x², and sends Y to xYx. Invariance therefore gives ω(x²)(xY₁x,…,xYmx) = M(Y₁,…,Ym). Near I the squaring map has a smooth inverse because its derivative is twice the identity. Solving this formula for ω by undoing each tangent map gives smoothness near I.

DωI[X](Y₁,…,Ym) = −½ ∑j=1m M(Y₁,…,XYj + YjX,…,Ym).

To obtain the derivative, put x = I + tX in the preceding identity. The base point moves with velocity 2X and the jth argument with velocity XYj + YjX. The right side is constant. To obtain the exterior derivative, alternate the left side of the displayed formula in its m + 1 inputs. Swapping X and the selected Yj preserves their sum of products and reverses the sign. Every term cancels. Invariance carries dω = 0 from I to every positive tuple. Stokes’ theorem now makes the integral of ω over the boundary of every affine simplex zero. Its periods therefore descend to homology. The two Hecke estimates then show that the transported mean has the periods of the original detecting cocycle.

Count the independent block labels. At I, M is invariant under unitary conjugation at each place. The tensor invariant theorem expresses it as a real linear combination of alternating real or imaginary parts of products of traces. Each product is indexed by a permutation of the m inputs. A cycle (i₁ … iℓ) contributes tr(Yi₁,w ⋯ Yiℓ,w) at a single place w. This trace sums over matrix indices around a closed loop. Replace each matrix by d identical diagonal blocks. A nonzero matrix entry must stay within one block, so the entire loop chooses a single block in d ways. With j permutation cycles there are dj choices. This is the weight j of the period under block repetition.

In odd degree m, a single cycle orders all the matrices at one place. Relabeling the inputs of its alternating trace changes only the sign. Reversing their order conjugates the trace because each matrix is Hermitian. Reversal has sign (−1)m(m−1)/2, so the alternating trace is real for m ≡ 1 modulo 4 and purely imaginary for m ≡ 3 modulo 4. This leaves at most one real functional per place. The filter on the selected cycles kills every weight from 2 to m. Any surviving invariant period is thus a linear combination of these r₂ one-place evaluations. A nonzero filtered homology class has a detecting period, which gives the rank bound.

Why do these trace products span all invariant tensors?

After allowing complex scalars, the tensor at the identity is represented by a matrix T acting on a tensor power. Unitary invariance says that T commutes with every tensor power of a placewise unitary matrix. Consider the operators that permute the tensor slots and select a place in each slot. The first finite-dimensional matrix result says that every operator commuting with all of them is a linear combination of those unitary tensor powers. Thus T commutes with all such operators. The second matrix result says that this puts T itself in the span of the slot permutations with place selections. In one such term, a matrix entry links index ai to aπ(i). Summing around each cycle gives its trace. If the place changes across a link, the entry vanishes. Taking real parts and alternating recovers the real tensor M.

Why do permutations account for every invariant tensor?

Let W be a finite set of places and V = ⊕w∈W ℂN. A separate unitary matrix uw acts on each summand. On V⊗q the resulting operator is D⊗q, where D = diag(uw). To recover the invariant forms, we need the matrices T that commute with every such operator. The proof works for all finite block sizes N and tensor degrees q, including N < q. It gives a spanning family whose members can coincide in small dimension.

A basis index I is a word of q pairs (place, coordinate). For a place pattern w = (w₁,…,wq) and a permutation σ, define Pσ,w by its rows and columns.

(Pσ,w)I,J = 1 if place(Ii) = wi for every i and J = I ∘ σ, and 0 otherwise.

These matrices commute with every D⊗q. Indeed, a block unitary preserves the place pattern and the same D acts in every slot. Let 𝒜 be their complex span and 𝒰 the span of the unitary tensor powers. Write 𝒮′ for the matrices commuting with all of 𝒮. The archive proves 𝒜′ ⊆ 𝒰 by interpolation and 𝒜″ ⊆ 𝒜 by orthogonal projection. Thus 𝒰′ = 𝒜.

If Z commutes with the projections Pid,w, its entry ZI,J can be nonzero only if the places of I and J agree slot by slot. Commuting with all the other Pσ,w gives ZI∘σ,J∘σ = ZI,J. If EI,J denotes a matrix unit, expand Z in these units and sum over slot permutations. The resulting identity counts each permutation, including those fixing an index pair.

q! Z = ∑I,J ZI,J ∑σ EI∘σ,J∘σ.

Suppose a complex linear functional φ vanishes on 𝒰. For any block diagonal D, we claim φ(D⊗q) = 0. Start with Hermitian blocks and fix their unitary eigenbases. As the diagonal eigenvalues vary, the expression is polynomial of degree at most q in each variable. It vanishes on the grid where every diagonal entry is a (q + 1)st root of unity, because every resulting block is unitary. Interpolating in one variable at a time gives vanishing at the actual eigenvalues. Now write arbitrary blocks as H + iK with H, K Hermitian. The same argument on the grid {0,…,q}² for aH + bK gives vanishing at (a,b) = (1,i).

For a pair I,J of matching places, put D(t) = ∑i tiEIᵢ,Jᵢ on V. Each matrix unit stays in one block. The coefficient of t₁⋯tq in D(t)⊗q is exactly the inner permutation sum above, because each variable must be chosen once. The polynomial vanishes after applying φ, hence so does this coefficient. It follows that q! φ(Z) = 0. In finite dimension, if Z lay outside 𝒰 some functional vanishing on 𝒰 would be nonzero at Z. This proves 𝒜′ ⊆ 𝒰.

The product Pσ,wPτ,v vanishes unless v = w ∘ σ, in which case it is Pσ∘τ,w. The adjoint is Pσ⁻¹,w∘σ, and the sum of all Pid,w is the identity. Thus 𝒜 is a unital algebra closed under adjoints. Orthogonally project the space of all matrices onto 𝒜 using ⟨X,Y⟩ = tr(X∗Y), where ∗ denotes the adjoint. Denote the projection by Π. For a ∈ 𝒜, both 𝒜 and its orthogonal complement are stable under left multiplication by a, the latter because a∗ ∈ 𝒜. Hence Π(aY) = aΠ(Y).

View a matrix Y as a list of columns. Each block of Π taking one input column to one output column now commutes with a for every a ∈ 𝒜. Any T ∈ 𝒜″ commutes with every such block, so Π(TY) = TΠ(Y). Substituting the identity for Y gives Π(T) = T. Thus T belongs to 𝒜.

Write Γn(R) = GLn(R) and use integral group homology with trivial coefficients. Stabilization sends g to diag(g,1). The proof establishes two one-step bounds in homological degree m. The stable-range parameter s belongs to the ring. A unimodular row of length n + 1 can be shortened whenever n ≥ s, by adding multiples of the last entry to its first n entries while keeping them generators of the unit ideal. For a Dedekind domain the proof takes s = 2.

Hm(Γn(R)) → Hm(Γn+1(R))   is surjective for n ≥ 2m + s + 1, and bijective for n ≥ 2m + s + 2.
Compute the stabilization map from an alternating face map

Fix an ambient size b and put G = Γb(R). An ordered split sequence of length p is a list of vectors and covectors (v₁,λ₁), …, (vp,λp) with λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on these sequences. The group acts on the vectors by g and on the covectors by precomposition with g−1. The differential dp from Cp+1 to Cp deletes one pair with alternating signs. The empty sequence gives C₀ = ℤ.

When p + s ≤ b, the action is transitive. The stabilizer of the last p standard vector–covector pairs is diag(Γb−p,Ip). Fixing both the vectors and the covectors forces the two off-diagonal blocks to vanish. Shapiro’s lemma for this permutation module therefore identifies Hq(G,Cp) with Hq(Γb−p,ℤ). When p + 1 + s ≤ b, both consecutive identifications are isomorphisms. In these coordinates each deletion gives the same stabilization map. A permutation of the final coordinates arranges the remaining pairs in standard order and commutes with Γb−p−1. The sum of p + 1 alternating signs is one for even p and zero for odd p.

Hq(Γb−2)   ⟶0   Hq(Γb−1)   ⟶stab   Hq(Γb).

Set b = n + 1. The integral filling argument shows that cycles on split sequences of length p bound when 2p + s + 1 ≤ b. It gives the exactness of the required part of the sequence of coefficient modules. Group homology need not preserve exactness in each row. For this reason the proof uses induction on the target degree m. In degrees q < m each relevant pair of adjacent maps is a stabilization next to a zero map. Exactness there asks for injectivity of the outgoing stabilization or surjectivity of the incoming one, already known in the corresponding smaller degree and matrix size.

To reach degree m, factor each dp+1 through the kernel of dp. The long exact group homology sequences for these kernels transfer the lower-degree row exactness to surjectivity of Hm(d₀). With one further step of module exactness they give ker Hm(d₀) = im Hm(d₁). The displayed row shows that the latter image is zero. For m ≥ 1, the lower-degree map at p = 2 and q = m − 1 starts at rank n − 2. Surjectivity there requires n − 2 ≥ 2(m − 1) + s + 1, while injectivity requires the right side plus one. The two induction steps check the remaining positions in their respective ranges. Composing the resulting one-step isomorphisms over 𝒪L carries degree-m integral homology unchanged from size n to every size N ≥ n once n ≥ 2m + 4.

When does every cycle of ordered split pairs bound?

A split pair in Rn is a vector v with a specified linear functional λ satisfying λ(v) = 1. An ordered list of pairs is split if λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on such lists of length p. Its boundary deletes one pair at a time, starting with sign +. Thus a vertex has boundary the empty list, and an edge has boundary its last vertex minus its first. The stability argument needs to know when these signed lists can fill a cycle.

2p + s + 1 ≤ n   ⟹   for every c ∈ Cp with ∂c = 0, some B ∈ Cp+1 satisfies ∂B = c.

This holds for every commutative ring with identity and all nonnegative integers n, p, s satisfying the ring’s stable-range hypothesis at s. That hypothesis says that whenever d ≥ s and the entries of (r₁,…,rd,t) generate the unit ideal, one can find a₁,…,ad so that the entries ri + ait still generate it. Length zero gives surjectivity onto the augmentation group ℤ. For p ≥ 1 the conclusion is vanishing of reduced integral homology in degree p − 1. In particular, length one controls differences of vertices.

Separate the chosen covectors from the auxiliary vectors

A plain unimodular list admits covectors making it split, but leaves the choice open. Introduce chains Da,b on a split list of length a and a plain list of length b. Each covector in the first list must kill every vector in the second. Deleting from the first list defines h and deleting from the second defines v. The deletions commute because their signs count positions in separate lists. Each operator squares to zero.

Fix the split list on the diagonal a + b = p. When a + s ≤ n, a matrix g carries it to the last a standard pairs. Acting by g on vectors and by precomposition with g−1 on covectors preserves all pairings. The proof straightens one pair, then straightens the remaining pairs in its coordinate complement. The auxiliary vectors must now have their last a entries zero. Restricting their witnessing covectors, or extending such covectors by zero, identifies this column with ordinary unimodular lists in Rn−a.

The ordinary-list theorem fills every cycle of length b when b + s ≤ n − a, as required on this diagonal. For s ≥ 1 its proof uses exactness of links in coordinate subspaces and their unions with affine translates. At s = 0, shortening the row (1) forces the zero ring, where prepending zero fills every cycle.

Why does the final auxiliary vector cost one fewer dimension?

To place the split vectors in the opposite kernels as well, inspect a prefix of length t and the tails one may append to it. Replacing each prefix vector x by the vector below preserves its pairings with all split covectors and puts it in every ker μj.

x′ = x − ∑j=1b μj(x)wj,   μi(x′) = 0.

The auxiliary pairs together with the corrected prefix form a split list of length b + t. The admissible tails whose vectors also lie in all the opposite kernels are exactly the tails one can append to this combined list. Straightening it reduces their complex to rank n − b − t. To fill in length a − t, induction on rank requires 2(a − t) + s + 1 ≤ n − b − t. For every 0 ≤ t ≤ a this follows from 2a + b + s + 1 ≤ n. Filling these links moves a cycle into the opposite kernels by successive boundaries. The empty-prefix case then fills it there. On the diagonal a + b = p + 1, the required bound becomes 2p + s + 3 − b ≤ n, which holds for b ≥ 2.

For b = 1 the cycle need only bound in the full split complex. Write its auxiliary vector as u and choose μ(u) = 1. Moving the cycle into ker μ uses only prefixes whose last vector lies outside that kernel, so t ≥ 1. This time 2(p − t) + s + 1 ≤ n − 1 − t already follows at the stated rank. For the resulting cycle c′ = c − ∂B₁ both cross-pairings vanish. Prepending (u,μ) gives a chain with boundary c′ by alternating deletion. Adding B₁ fills the original cycle.

Assemble the individual fillings

Place the original cycle c in Dp,0 with an empty auxiliary list. Both boundaries vanish. The column fillings give vertical lifts. A lift y with vy = c may have a horizontal boundary. Induct on the first index. At index zero the horizontal boundary vanishes. At a positive index, hy has lower first index and is killed by both operators. Induction supplies z′ with vz′ = hy and hz′ = 0. Its second index is now at least two, so the row filling supplies u with hu = z′. The corrected lift satisfies

z = y − vu,   hz = hy − vhu = 0,   vz = c.

In bidegree (p,1), group the finitely many terms of z by their sole auxiliary vector. Each group is a horizontal cycle because h preserves that vector. Their sum after deleting the auxiliary vectors is c, since a singleton has deletion sign +. The preceding cone construction fills each group in the full complex. Summing gives the required integral filling, which supplies the exact sequence used in the stability argument.

What the detecting cycles can miss

The cycle bound controls the image of a twisted norm. Here is how much of the arithmetic count that image can miss. Keep the enlarged field L′ fixed, with r₂ complex places. At depth ν the cyclic layer F/L′ has generator γ and degree n = ℓν−c. Write q = ℓν, a = (1 + ℓc)e and f = vℓ(e) for the positive twist e. Each element assigns a value φ(P) in ℤ/q to each prime ideal, vanishes on principal divisors when extended additively, and satisfies φ(γ−1P) = aφ(P). Define C by quotienting the ideal class group of F by the image of γ−1 − a. Each φ descends to C and is recovered from its values on primes. Its target is an ℓ-group, so there are at most |C|ℓ such characters, where |·|ℓ means the ℓ-part of a finite group order.

Where the matching power of q comes from. Write E for the integral units 𝒪F× modulo roots of unity and the image of γ−1 − a, using additive notation. The finite group W in the norm construction satisfies |W| = |E| |C|. Indeed, its map to the class group has unit kernel E and image the kernel of γ−1 − a on that group. A finite group endomorphism has kernel and cokernel of equal order. To compute |E|, take logarithms of units at the infinite places and add one constant coordinate direction to complete the unit lattice. Above each complex place of L′ the action permutes n places in a cycle. On this block the absolute determinant of the permutation minus a times the identity is an − 1. The extra constant direction contributes a − 1. Thus |E|(a − 1) = (an − 1)r₂.

The valuation formula vℓ((1 + ℓc)h − 1) = c + vℓ(h) holds for positive h, with c ≥ 1 and c ≥ 2 when ℓ = 2. Apply it with h = e and h = en. The unit identity gives |E|ℓ ℓc+f = ℓ(ν+f)r₂ ≥ qr₂. The second valuation also shows that the exact valuation of (an − 1)/q is f. For example, at ℓ = 3, c = 2, e = 3 and ν = 3 we have a = 1000 and n = 3. The number 1000³ − 1 has 3-adic valuation 4. Dividing by 27 leaves valuation 1. Increasing ν by one also increases the numerator’s valuation by one.

Why the kernel cost stays bounded. Write N for the twisted norm, additively, and δ = γ−1 − a. Expanding the geometric sum gives δN = Nδ = (1 − an)γ−1. Those elements inject into invariant classes represented by α with all valuations divisible by ℓ. If ρ generates the roots of unity in F, their invariance gives γα/α = vℓρt, 0 ≤ t < ℓ. Hilbert’s Theorem 90 then lets the ratio of the two α’s descend to the base field modulo ℓth powers. Its valuations away from ℓ remain divisible by ℓ because the layer is unramified there. The base-field classes with this property have at most ℓ2D+⌊log₂ h⌋ elements, where D = [L′:ℚ] and h is its class number. The three contributions come from units modulo ℓth powers, ℓ-torsion ideal classes, and the valuations modulo ℓ at primes over ℓ. The ≤ ℓ² choices of the pair thus give |W[ℓ]| ≤ ℓg for g = 2D + ⌊log₂ h⌋ + 2.

|𝓧| qr₂ ≤ B ℓX,   X = (b + f)g + c + f.

How an integral boundary matrix bounds torsion

The character count above uses the orders of the torsion subgroups of two integral homology groups. A torsion class is killed by a nonzero integer. An infinite free summand in homology can therefore coexist with the finite quantity we need to bound. Start with a free lattice E = ℤr, with r ≤ A, and any set of integral relation vectors. Write Λ for their integer span. Suppose each relation has sum of absolute coordinates at most b, where b ≥ 1. The bound used in the proof is

|tors(E/Λ)| ≤ bA.

If we have r independent relation vectors, put them in a square matrix V. The sublattice they generate has index |det V|. Expanding the determinant as a signed sum over permutations and taking absolute values gives a sum of products. Allowing every choice of one column for each row only increases this sum, and the enlarged sum factors as ∏i ∑j |Vij|. This proves the bound br. Additional relations give a quotient of this finite group.

Suppose instead that the relation vectors span only a proper rational subspace. Choose a maximal independent subset and complete it to a rational basis using standard unit vectors. Let K be the integer span of that completed list. Its determinant still has absolute value at most br, since every added vector has length one. To compare torsion, choose a lift in E for each torsion class in E/Λ and reduce its lift modulo K. If two images coincide, the difference x of their lifts lies in K. Their difference class is torsion, so some nonzero multiple of x belongs to Λ. Consequently x lies in the rational span of the original relations. In the completed basis every coefficient of an added vector must then vanish. Because x belongs to K, the remaining coefficients are integers. Thus x is an integer combination of selected relations and the two classes were equal. This injects the set of torsion classes into the finite set E/K.

For example, impose the three relations (2,0,0), (0,2,0), (1,1,0) in ℤ³. The third coordinate stays free. In the first two coordinates a vector is a relation exactly when the coordinates have the same parity. Hence the torsion subgroup has order two. Choosing the first two relations and the third unit vector gives det V = 4. The general bound gives 2³ = 8. The three numbers measure respectively the actual torsion, the index for this completed list, and the estimate using the common row bound.

Let a group G permute the simplex basis in each degree and commute with each face map. Suppose the augmented complex is exact through degree m. An orbit identifies simplices related by the action. For positive degree, take the short exact sequence given by the first permutation module, its augmentation and its kernel. The long exact homology sequence compares the desired torsion with the torsion one degree lower for that kernel and the finite homology of the permutation module. For a single orbit the latter is the homology of the stabilizer by Shapiro’s lemma. A group of order h has hj bar generators in degree j > 0, and multiplication by h kills its homology. The cycles form a subgroup of a free abelian group with that many generators, hence the homology has order at most hhʲ. Combining the orbits costs at most sA sʲ. Repeating the exact-sequence comparison for j = m, …, 1 gives

|tors Hm(G,ℤ)| ≤ (m + 2)A sm A sᵐ.

The last exponent uses ∑j=1m sj ≤ m sm. This part needs the orbit and stabilizer estimates, exactness of the complex, the long exact sequence, Shapiro’s lemma and annihilation of finite-group homology. Each supplies a distinct input.

For G = GLN(𝒪L) with L totally complex of degree n, there is an exact complex, an orbit bound A and the stabilizer bound s = 3nN². How many faces can an arithmetic group have up to symmetry?

In the homology inequality, A bounds the number of face orbits and s bounds the order of the subgroup fixing any one face. A face in this chain model is an ordered tuple of vertices, with repetitions allowed. Two such tuples represent one orbit if the same group element moves every entry of the first tuple to the corresponding entry of the second. Here the group is G = GLN(𝒪F), with F a totally complex number field, n = [F : ℚ], D = |disc F|, N ≥ 1 and d = nN. Thus d is the integer rank of the vector lattice 𝒪FN. We will count orbits in each face degree p ≥ 0.

Find a frame shared by the whole face

For each infinite place of F take a Hermitian form on ℂN. Their values on the images of a lattice vector y add to a real number qh(y). Impose qh(y) ≥ 1 for every nonzero y. A vector is minimal for h when equality holds. A vertex is a feasible family h uniquely determined by its equalities. A degree-p face in the complex is an ordered list of p + 1 such vertices at which one supporting linear functional attains its minimum. That functional is strictly positive on nonzero positive semidefinite families. The definition allows repeated vertices.

The common minimal vectors of a face span FN. To see why, average the vertices. At the average a lattice inequality is tight exactly when it is tight at every vertex. If the common minimal vectors missed a direction, a nonzero F-linear functional λ would vanish on their span. The family of rank-one forms obtained from |λ|² at all embeddings is positive semidefinite and nonzero. A sufficiently small subtraction of this family from the average preserves the tight constraints. Local finiteness of the inequalities keeps the others feasible. The supporting functional would strictly decrease below its minimum. Thus we can choose N independent common minimal columns and place them in a matrix A. They form a basis over F. Its integral determinant can be a nonunit. The determinant estimate gives

r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| ≤ J,   J = DNdd.

For this last inequality pull back each local form by A. The pulled-back determinants have product at most one by the diagonal bounds and Hadamard’s inequality. Their product is r times the product of the original determinants, for which the geometric lower bound is 1/J.

One congruence count for the frame

Fix its positive integer r. Over F put B = rA−1. Why does this have integral entries? The principal ideal (det A) has norm r and contains the integer r. Hence r/det A lies in 𝒪F, and multiplying the integral adjugate of A by that element gives B. Reduce its entries modulo r𝒪F. Suppose a second frame A′ has the same norm and its matrix B′ has the same residue list. Write B − B′ = rX with X integral. Over the field this gives

A′A−1 = 1 + A′X,   AA′−1 = 1 − AX.

Both matrices are integral and they are inverses. The first therefore belongs to G and takes A to A′ by left multiplication. An integral basis identifies 𝒪F/r𝒪F as an additive group with (ℤ/rℤ)n. The list of N² entries has at most rnN² = rdN values. Choosing one frame for each attained list covers every orbit. Summing the bound for r = 1,…,J costs at most J1+dN.

Example. In ℤ[i] take the one-column matrices A = 1 + i and A′ = 1 − i. Both norms are 2. The scaled inverses are B = 1 − i and B′ = 1 + i, so X = −i. The formula gives g = −i, and multiplication by this Gaussian unit sends 1 + i to 1 − i. This tests the congruence argument for frames of bounded determinant norm.

How many vertices can share a chosen frame?

Fix a representative A. A nearby vector is one that can be minimal for some feasible form making every column of A minimal. The coordinate estimate gives |σ((By)j)| ≤ R = NNJ² at every embedding. Since AB = r·1, the vector By determines y. Each of its coordinates has at most (2R + 1)n possibilities. Indeed, if two such algebraic integers differ by (2R + 1)x, every conjugate of x has absolute value at most 2R/(2R + 1) < 1. A nonzero algebraic integer has nonzero integer norm, ruling this out. The residue count thus bounds the number of nearby vectors by M = (2R + 1)d.

The equations qh(y) = 1 are linear in the unknown coefficients of h. At a vertex, at most dN independent equations suffice to determine it. Their vectors lie in the nearby set. A set of at most dN vectors drawn from M choices can be recorded as a list of length dN by sorting it and padding with a blank. Hence this frame admits at most (M + 1)dN vertices. Each entry of an ordered tuple can use any of these in an upper bound. Together with the frame count this gives the orbit bound

Ap = J1+dN(M + 1)dN(p+1) ≤ (2Dd)12(p+1)d³N.

This count allows lists that fail the common-support condition, which only enlarges the bound. Formally choose a frame and a translated tuple for each orbit. Equal choices of frame and entries give the same tuple, hence the same orbit.

Why reduction modulo three counts stabilizers

An element fixing an ordered tuple fixes its first vertex. The first vertex has finitely many minimal vectors, and these include N independent ones. The images of those basis vectors under an element fixing the vertex are again minimal and determine the element. Thus the stabilizer is finite. Now view it as a subgroup of the units of the matrix ring T = MN(𝒪F). Distinct elements have distinct residues in T/3T. Otherwise their quotient would be a finite-order unit congruent to 1 modulo 3.

Here is the divisibility argument behind this separation. If such a unit were nontrivial, one of its powers would have prime order l and still be congruent to 1. Write that power as 1 + 3kY with k ≥ 1 maximal and Y nonzero modulo 3. Maximality follows by looking at any nonzero integer coordinate in the free abelian group T. For l ≠ 3 its lth power differs from 1 by l3kY modulo 3k+1, which is nonzero. For l = 3 the leading term is 3k+1Y modulo 3k+2. The other two terms in the cube are divisible by 32k+1 and 33k, both at least the required power. This contradicts prime order in both cases. Induction on the order gives the same separation.

The additive rank of T is nN² = dN, so the stabilizer bound is s = 3dN, uniform in the face degree. In rank one over ℤ[i] the units 1, −1, i, −i already have four distinct residues among the nine available. In homology degree m, Am bounds every face degree p ≤ m. Substituting it and s into the homological torsion inequality gives the estimate used in degree two. The discriminant lower bound for the form determinants, the Cramer estimate for nearby coordinates and exactness of the face complex are inputs to this calculation.

From the locally trivial group to full cohomology

What survives when a localization map is reduced modulo ℓ?

Let L be a number field, ℓ a prime and S the finite places over ℓ. Choose a prolongation of each place and write Dv for its decomposition group. On the global Galois group GS unramified outside S, take T = ℤℓ(e + 1) and A = (ℚℓ/ℤℓ)(−e). The shift comes from the cyclotomic factor in the Tate dual. The dual of T/ℓrT with this factor identifies with A[ℓr]. The arithmetic application has e ≥ 1 and L totally complex. The finite-level global duality used here requires ℓ odd or no real places of L.

Write X = H²(GS, T) and Y = ∏v∈S H²(Dv, T). Localization λ sends a class to its restrictions. Its kernel K is the locally trivial integral degree-two group. Its cokernel C measures which tuples of local classes come from global ones. At depth r ≥ 1, reduction identifies the degree-two groups for the finite coefficients T/ℓrT with X/ℓrX and Y/ℓrY. This uses vanishing of degree three modulo ℓ to lift cocycles. A class reducing to zero is an ℓr multiple. Restriction commutes with reduction on cocycles, so the finite localization is the resulting map λr.

Which reduced classes lift? Put t = ℓr and B = λ(X). Both C/tC and coker λr are quotients of Y by B + tY. For a kernel class, choose a representative x in X. Its reduction belongs to ker λr precisely when λ(x) belongs to tY. To obtain an integral kernel representative, subtract tx′ from x. This works precisely when λ(x) = tλ(x′). The following criterion spells out the distinction.

K/(K ∩ tX) ↪ ker λr   is onto exactly when   B ∩ tY = tB.

For e ≠ 0, every Dv contains an element g with χ(g)−e ≠ 1. The nonzero ℓ-adic integer χ(g)−e − 1 annihilates the invariants ADᵥ. The finite set S gives a common exponent c such that ℓc kills all these invariants. Finite local Tate duality, local finiteness and passage through the torsion levels give each local H² the length of its finite invariant group. Thus Y has finite length and ℓmY = 0 for some m. At every depth r ≥ m the criterion holds.

How the finite dualities give a length. The last arrow of the finite Poitou–Tate sequence identifies the order of coker λr with the order of the global invariants in A[ℓr]. These invariants increase to H⁰(GS, A). The quotients C/ℓrC separate points because C is finitely generated over ℤℓ. Comparing their orders gives length(C) = length H⁰(GS, A).

The finite kernel ker λr is paired with the locally trivial H¹ for A[ℓr]. To pass to A, filter its locally trivial H¹ by the classes represented by a cocycle whose values and local coboundary witnesses are all killed by ℓr. Every class occurs because a continuous cocycle from a compact group to discrete A has finite image and only finitely many local witnesses are needed. There is one more lifting issue. If a finite-level cocycle becomes the global coboundary of a in A, choose a local witness b killed by ℓr at any place over ℓ. Then a − b is locally invariant, so ℓc(a − b) = 0. For r ≥ c, a itself is an allowed witness. At sufficiently large depths the filtration terms therefore have the orders of K/(K ∩ ℓrX). This decreasing filtration on K has zero intersection. If the common orders stay bounded, they attain a maximum. Beyond that level the inclusions and quotient maps are bijections. Exhaustion then gives the whole degree-one group, and separation makes the remaining integral kernel of reduction zero. If the orders grow without bound, both groups have infinite length. Hence length(K) = length Ш¹(GS, A), where Ш¹ denotes the kernel of all restrictions at S. The source treats e = 0 separately using the trivial action.

Finally, X/K ≃ B and Y/B = C. Additivity of length in the two short exact sequences gives length(X) + length(C) = length(K) + length(Y). Substituting the three duality comparisons gives the balance below. Lengths take values in ℕ ∪ {∞}, so this additive form also applies before finiteness is known.

length H²(GS, T) + length H⁰(GS, A) = length Ш¹(GS, A) + ∑v∈S length H⁰(Dv, A).

The nonnegative global H⁰ term gives the upper bound used in the degree-two estimate. At that point the proof inserts the previously bounded degree-one length and the local invariant estimates to deduce finite length of the full integral H². The arithmetic inputs here are finite-coefficient Poitou–Tate duality, finite-coefficient local Tate duality and local finiteness. The reduction and filtration arguments explain their passage to integral length.

A kernel class that disappears when lifted

For a finite-module model take ℓ = 3, X = ℤ/27, Y = ℤ/9 and λ(x) = 3x. Its kernel is 3ℤ/27 of order nine. Its image in Y is 3ℤ/9 and its cokernel has order three. Modulo 3 the reduced map is zero. The class of 1 is in its kernel, but every integral lift has the form 1 + 3k and maps to 3 in ℤ/9. At depths r = 1, 2, 3 the reduced kernels have orders 3, 3, 9. The images of the integral kernel have orders 1, 3, 9. The agreement begins at depth two, when 3²Y vanishes. The reduced cokernel has order three at every listed depth. In the integral balance the lengths give 3 + 1 = 2 + 2.

At a place over ℓ the decomposition group has cyclotomic image U of index 1 ≤ h ≤ n in ℤℓ×. An invariant of order ℓk requires ve ≡ 1 modulo ℓk for every v ∈ U. In particular (1 + ℓ²)h belongs to U, and the valuation of (1 + ℓ²)he − 1 is exactly 2 + vℓ(h) + vℓ(e). This controls the local length also at ℓ = 2. For example, with ℓ = 3, h = 2 and e = 3, the tested integer is 10⁶ − 1 = 27 · 37037 and its 3-adic valuation is 3. Summing over at most n places gives

length H² ≤ s(L) + n(2 + ⌊logℓ n⌋ + e).

This proves finite length. Each simple ℤℓ-quotient has ℓ elements, so log order equals length times log ℓ. Since ℓ ≤ n + 1 and ⌊logℓ n⌋ log ℓ ≤ log(n + 1), the local addition to log order is at most n(3 + e) log(n + 1). The detecting cycles bound the finite image, and the orbit and stabilizer counts control the two integral torsion orders. 8.15Which characters contribute to the plus bound?

Fix the primitive character χ of conductor Q. Write n for the height index of the field, q,d for the auxiliary primes and e for a cohomological twist. Here n ≥ 2, q ≡ 3 modulo 8, d ≡ 7 modulo 16, and qd is coprime to Q. At a fixed host the integer level is N = lcm(2n+2, Q)qd. A unit lies in H if it reduces to a sign modulo 2n+2, is killed by χ modulo Q, and is a square modulo each of q and d. Over an ℓ-adic coefficient ring O containing the roots of unity of order φ(N), the set Xe consists of the characters ψ trivial on H with ψ(−1) = (−1)e. This parity selects the required eigenspace of conjugation.

The proof first bounds a degree-one cohomology length over ℚ for each ψ. Its coefficient module is O ⊗ℤℓ (ℚℓ/ℤℓ), with action ψ−1χcyc−e, where χcyc is the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character. The classes restrict to zero on inertia everywhere and on decomposition groups over the primes dividing ℓN. Write ve(ψ) for their O-module length divided by the ramification index lengthO(O/ℓO). Each individual estimate establishes finiteness before using the numerical length. When ℓ is odd and does not divide the index of H, the sum over Xe bounds the field’s plus length. For a general odd ℓ the integral character decomposition incurs an additive loss for each character. The source bounds this loss and carries it through the final finite sum.

Let Bχ contain 3 and the odd prime divisors of ord(χ) · Q · pK · h* · p1. Here pK is the first prime at least 7 congruent to 3 modulo 4 and coprime to Q, h* is the class number of ℚ(√−pK), and p1 is the first prime coprime to 2QpK and congruent to 1 modulo the odd part of ord(χ). The host requires both auxiliary primes to exceed 2t+1 and the fixed arithmetic parameters of χ.

Why does ψ survive both steps defining ψ′ in the second row? On the two auxiliary prime factors the characters have order dividing two, and the group of units modulo the power of two also has power-of-two order. Thus taking the prime-to-ℓ part and removing the component at ℓ both preserve ψ.

8.16Why the exterior sum is uniform in the number of primes

Take any finite set of odd primes outside Bχ. Bounding every prime by a constant and then counting the whole set would lose uniformity. In case I the source instead groups pairs (ℓ,ψ) by the kernel K of ψ on G = (ℤ/Nℤ)×. The image of a character is cyclic. A cyclic quotient of order m has φ(m) faithful complex characters, one for every primitive mth root. Their pullbacks have precisely kernel K. Distinct kernels give disjoint lists, and G has |G| complex characters. Therefore the sum of φ([G : K]) over kernels that occur is at most |G| ≤ N. For example, in a cyclic group of order six, the quotients of orders 1, 2, 3, 6 contribute 1+1+2+2=6.

The rank-three unitary estimate supplies the sum over primes for each kernel, with its totient weight. Its two test primes r1, r2 and its constants are chosen for χ before the host and the twist. Both host primes q and d must exceed each of r₁ and r₂. If A is its power exponent, the preceding count leaves a bound of the form C₀N[N(e+1)]A. Choose k with C₀ ≤ 16k. Since 16 ≤ N and e+1 ≤ t, this is at most Mk+1+A. Write CI for this exponent.

Outside case I, ℓ−1 divides 2e, so ℓ ≤ 2e+1 ≤ 2t. There are at most 2t such primes and at most N characters per prime. Let K0 be the maximum exponent from Z, II and III. Their individual bounds already include log ℓ. The inequality ℓNe ≤ M³ gives at most 2M·M3K₀ at each twist. The Z branch is especially simple. The parity of the trivial character forces e even, hence e ≥ 2. The excluded set contains 3, so ℓ ≥ 5. The vanishing theorem at such divisible even twists bounds the restricted length by zero. Cases II and III receive their estimates from the joint rank-four symplectic construction.

t (MCI + 2M1+3K₀) ≤ MCI+3K₀+4.

Here t ≤ M and M ≥ 2. This bound holds for every finite exterior prime set, however many case-I primes it contains.

Fix ℓ ∈ Bχ and a layer index j. Characters in branch IV have conductor dividing Q. All of them become trivial on the absolute Galois group of the same field L1. 8.18How a trace congruence bounds one character

Fix the primitive character χ. The level N may vary among the hosts built from χ. Given a cutoff t satisfying the host condition, an odd prime ℓ, a coefficient ring O and an integer e with 0 < e < t, take a character ψ trivial on the host subgroup and satisfying ψ(−1) = (−1)e. The exponent is chosen before the host, ℓ, O, t, e and ψ. How can a finite list of Galois representations measure this length?

In cases II and III the matrices have size four and preserve a symplectic form up to a scalar. At a prime p of good reduction, choose a Frobenius element σ. For each representation r let a(r) = tr r(σ) − tr r0(σ), where r0 is the reference representation. Two integral traces whose difference has valuation d agree to ℓ-adic precision d. With |ℓ|ℓ = ℓ−1, that difference contributes −log |a(r)|ℓ = d log ℓ.

The deformation algebra records the allowed lifts of the reference data. A first-order variation of a point r has matrices r(g) + εB(g), where ε² = 0. Multiplication makes B(g)r(g)−1 a cocycle for conjugation. The rigidity proof places its projection, after a twist over a CM field, in an adjoint Selmer group with prescribed local conditions. The supplied vanishing makes the class a coboundary. Projecting back gives B(g) = Y r(g) − r(g)Y for one symplectic Lie algebra element Y. This is exactly the variation obtained by conjugating with 1 + εY.

Coordinates in the deformation algebra have integer weights for a rescaling action. With rigidity, finiteness of the degree-zero part and exclusion of the specified endoscopic points, the algebraic lemma M produces a finite set meeting the rescaling orbits of points having nonzero coordinates of both signs. It bounds the length of the weight −1 cotangent quotient at the reference point by twice the sum of the valuations of the trace differences. This quotient keeps the linear terms in the defining equations. Lemma M′ bounds the obstruction length through its injection into the solutions of those linear equations modulo a coefficient ideal. Choosing a minimal orbit cover gives a finite family Ξ with one representative for each orbit in the cover. Conjugate matrices give the same orbit, so no conjugate representation is counted twice. Transferring the cotangent bound to the original obstruction gives

(L/eO) log ℓ ≤ 2 ∑r∈Ξ −log |a(r)|ℓ.

Indeed rescaling that coordinate by (1 + εb)j gives precisely this derivative. For each nonzero d ∈ O the finite-coefficient obstruction embeds into vectors over O/(d) supported in weight −1 and killed by the linearized relations. The resulting bound is uniform in d. Taking d = ℓn bounds the length of the full torsion obstruction because every element is killed by some power of ℓ.

Choose an inert prime p ≡ 3 modulo 4 with 7 ≤ p ≤ 12ℓN and p ∤ ℓN. The Frobenius over this prime has residue norm p². The trace test uses its inverse. Representatives are distinguished up to isomorphism after restriction to the Gaussian subgroup. Group them by the two embeddings of ℚ(i) into the chosen algebraic closure. The unitary counting theorem includes all φ(N)th roots of unity in its integral product. Applying it in each embedding group gives

∑r vℓ(a(r)) log ℓ ≤ 2a φ(N)[N(e+1)]b log p ≤ X2a+1+b+3.

The constants a,b here come from the counting theorem for the fixed field. The inequalities φ(N) ≤ X, N(e + 1) ≤ X and log p ≤ p ≤ X³ explain the exponent. The cotangent estimate introduces a final factor two, absorbed into one more power of X. The final comparison uses the integral automorphic counting statement, a unitary lifting theorem, adjoint rigidity, local and global cohomology theorems, and the commutative algebra length lemma. The linked proofs identify where each enters.

8.21One field for all three estimates

The exterior exponent Cout and auxiliary test primes depend on χ. The interior exponents also depend on the layer choices j(ℓ). Bound each by their sum D over Bχ, and put k = |Bχ|. Splitting any finite set of odd primes into its two parts now gives at most k(MD+DB)+MCout. With M ≥ 2, one can take C=Cout+D+k+kD. In particular, 1+k ≤ Mk absorbs the number of polynomial terms and kD ≤ C absorbs the multiple of B. The window chooses j(ℓ)=⌊logℓ Rℓ⌋+3 and B=exp(x4ε/5) before applying this result to any field at x.

Why is M equal to t times the field conductor, as the next theorem requires? Let E be any realization of the four fixing conditions. It embeds into the cyclotomic field of modulus N. If it also embeds at modulus M′ with a smaller exponent at a prime p dividing N, there is a unit c modulo N congruent to 1 modulo N/p outside the fixing subgroup. At the auxiliary primes one can use −1 in the corresponding component, since these primes are 3 modulo 4. At a prime whose exponent comes from χ, primitivity supplies a unit detected at the last power of that prime. In the remaining 2-primary case, 1+2n+1 is 1 at the preceding level and is neither sign at modulus 2n+2. The Chinese remainder theorem puts the chosen component together with the required trivial components.

Pass to lcm(M′,N). The witness lifts to a unit reducing to c modulo N and to 1 modulo M′. Its automorphism would both move and fix the same field. Hence N divides every admissible modulus and the conductor is exactly N. The field is also CM. In the ambient cyclotomic field a quadratic Gauss sum has square −q and transforms by the quadratic character at q. The defining subgroup fixes it, so E contains a square root of −q. An abelian extension of ℚ containing this element is totally imaginary and hence CM. Thus conjugation, the plus estimate, and the minus estimate all refer to this same field. The large-prime hypotheses make q,d coprime to Q and allow the same pair throughout the chosen window.

Which representation results supply these inequalities?

The final call obtains I from the unitary rank-three orbit estimate, II and III jointly from symplectic rank four, and V from a reduced unitary lift with cohomological finiteness, local duality and Euler characteristics. IV is the restriction argument on the bounded-degree layer above. The Z branch uses a trivial-character vanishing theorem. The separate estimate for large R₁ at twist one uses degree two. These distinct calls make clear which proof inputs one would have to strengthen to improve the plus bound.

8.22What bounds the odd-prime minus summand?

Fix a CM field E in the theorem’s family. Write n = [E : ℚ], N for its least positive cyclotomic conductor, and o for the degree of the fixed abelian datum M. For an odd prime ℓ and a twist 1 ≤ j < t, take the first cohomology group of the Galois group unramified away from the primes above ℓ, with coefficients ℚℓ/ℤℓ on which the cyclotomic character acts to the power −j. Inside its kernel of localization, let mℓ,j be the ℤℓ-length of the complex-conjugation eigenspace of sign (−1)j+1. Thus the “minus” summand has positive conjugation sign when j is odd. Since 2 is invertible in ℤℓ, the two sign lengths add to the whole kernel length.

For every choice of algebraic closure, every compatible family of local data, and every finite set S of odd primes, the selected argument proves finiteness of each length and gives

∑ℓ∈S log ℓ ∑1≤j<t mℓ,j ≤ 3nt² log(tN) + C ∑ℓ∣o, ℓ odd prime ℓn²t² log²(tℓN).

A single C works for every base datum M, layer e ≥ 2, height t ≥ 2, allowed prime pair q,d, and associated field E. The proof supplies 240 as an admissible value. Its division into cases depends on the prime divisors of n. The larger fixed set in the displayed bound becomes important when E varies in the window.

8.23A single integer controls the primes away from the field degree

Fix j and put k = j + 1. The cyclotomic action gives a surjection ρ from (ℤ/Nℤ)× onto Gal(E/ℚ). Select the characters factoring through ρ with χ(−1) = (−1)k. For each one, let χ* denote its primitive character and f its conductor. The algebraic number in the estimate is

αk(χ) = N · (∏p≤k+1, p prime p) · Bk,χ*,   Bk,χ* = fk−1 ∑a=1f χ*(a) Bk(a/f).

The front factor clears denominators. The special-value identity reads L(1−k,χ*) = −Bk,χ*/k. In the selected parity the functional equation relates its absolute value to a positive factor times |L(k,(χ*)−1)|. Here k ≥ 2, so this value is nonzero. The polynomial estimate and the primorial bound give |αk(χ)| ≤ 16Nk+1k! in the complex realization.

Check the normalization at conductor four

Take the odd character modulo 4, put N = 4 and k = 3, and use B₃(x) = x³ − 3x²/2 + x/2. The polynomial takes values 3/64 and −3/64 at 1/4 and 3/4. The character takes values 1 and −1 there, so B3,χ = 4²(6/64) = 3/2. Clearing denominators as above gives α₃(χ) = 4·(2·3)·(3/2) = 36. This checks the parity and scaling in the character formula. The estimates for a tower will require the additional field hypotheses below.

Let ℓ be odd and ℓ ∤ n. In the selected proof, Poitou–Tate duality and unramified orthogonality yield the reciprocity input for the character bound. A character pulled back along ρ has order dividing n, so its order is prime to ℓ. The primitive-character calculation bounds the length by the discrete valuation of αk(χ). At the change of level from f to N, the primitive character is the same and the smaller denominator-clearing factor divides the larger one. Prime-to-ℓ restriction identifies the character component with the required eigenspace. Within the primitive calculation, the reciprocity count and its evaluated divisibility give the valuation inequality in the case admitting a unit difference of characters. In the complementary case the relevant module has length zero.

Over a finite coefficient DVR containing the required roots of unity, let eℓ be the ramification index. The sum of the selected character lengths is at least eℓmℓ,j. In the norm normalized by |ℓ|ℓ = ℓ−1, each character length times log ℓ is at most eℓ(−log |αk(χ)|ℓ). Cancelling the positive finite index gives the required estimate for this prime.

The product Ak of the αk(χ) over the full selected character set is rational because the set is defined by character kernels and the factors commute with change of coefficient field. Each factor is integral and nonzero, so Ak is a nonzero integer. Every omitted ℓ-adic factor has nonnegative valuation. The sum needed at ℓ is therefore at most vℓ(Ak) log ℓ. Summing these valuations over any finite set costs at most log |Ak|. For example, if a product has absolute value 45, the prime contributions at 3, 5 and 7 are 2 log 3, log 5 and 0. Their sum is log 45. Any subset costs at most this amount. The integer in the proof is formed once per twist from all the selected characters. There are at most n selected characters because they inject into the dual of the quotient by ker ρ, of order n. Thus the sum over odd primes ℓ ∤ n for this j is at most n log(16Nk+1k!). Bounding the logarithm by (2t+5) log(tN) and using (t−1)(2t+5) ≤ 3t² gives the first term.

How one Bernoulli value bounds a module length

Fix a primitive character ψ of conductor f, an odd prime ℓ prime to its order, and a twist e ≥ 1 with ψ(−1) = (−1)e+1. Write O for the coefficient ring, a discrete valuation ring finite as a module over ℤℓ, v for its additive valuation with v(π) = 1 at a uniformizer π, and A for the cleared Bernoulli value at the conductor. The goal is lengthO ≤ v(A) for this character component. An integer can kill a whole module without controlling its length. For example, 3 kills (ℤ/3)d for every d. The proof needs local tests that measure how much length remains after each one.

Let χ be the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character and ψG the Galois character attached to ψ. The scalar action on the cocycles in the count is α = (χeψG)−1. First consider the case where α(g) − χ(g) is a unit for some g. Choose a nonzero cutoff a₀ ∈ O. Work with cocycles c in the torsion coefficient module O ⊗ℤℓ (ℚℓ/ℤℓ) whose values are killed by a₀. At one auxiliary cyclotomic level, choose δ inducing −1 on the exponents of its roots of unity. Parity gives α(δ) ≡ −1 modulo the maximal ideal. Since ℓ is odd, α(δ) − 1 is a unit. The same δ works for every cutoff. Normalize the cocycles to have c(δ) = 0. Subtracting the coboundary of c(δ)/(α(δ) − 1) achieves this.

Outside the level the scalar action is trivial on inertia, so the local coboundary condition forces the normalized cocycle to vanish there. At a conductor prime p ≠ ℓ the initial condition supplies a witness w on inertia I. Primitivity in this prime-to-ℓ character case supplies t ∈ I with α(t) − 1 a unit. For any d in the decomposition group, d−1td lies in I. Evaluate the cocycle identity on td = d(d−1td). It gives (α(t) − 1)[c(d) − (α(d) − 1)w] = 0. Cancellation extends the same witness to the entire decomposition group. At ℓ a decomposition-group witness is already part of the original condition. Choose a single cutoff killing that witness and the finite image of the continuous cocycle on its compact source. It then kills the witnesses at conductor primes by the same unit cancellation, and conjugation covers the other places over ℓ.

As a₀ runs through powers of π, the images of these spaces cover the locally trivial classes. A bound uniform in the cutoff will therefore bound the entire length.

Choose m after a₀ and put F = fℓ′ℓm, where fℓ′ is the prime-to-ℓ part of the conductor. Outside the primes dividing fℓ this introduces no new ramification. Here F denotes an integer level. Write [t] for the least nonnegative representative of t modulo F. For a suitable b < F and lifts σt acting on Fth roots of unity by the power t, the scalar used in the count is

z = ∑t∈(ℤ/Fℤ)× (⌊[t]b/F⌋ − ⌊[−t]b/F⌋) α(σt)−1.

The evaluation theorem arranges a₀z ∣ ℓm and z ∣ A. Here is the valuation principle behind the second divisibility. The unit-difference hypothesis gives a residue b for which ψ(b)be+1 − 1 is an ℓ-adic unit. The congruence for the floor sum compares it, after explicit scaling, with the nonzero Bernoulli value divided by e + 1. The source takes m large enough that the approximation error is strictly smaller than the norm of the comparison term after scaling. In a nonarchimedean norm, |x−y| < |y| forces |x| = |y|. The resulting norm of z is |Be+1,ψ/(e+1)|. Multiplying by integral factors to get the cleared value A can only increase its valuation.

How multiplication modulo the level produces a Bernoulli value

The length argument needs an integer-like scalar whose ℓ-adic valuation is exactly that of a special value. The floor in its definition records the carry when an integer product is reduced modulo the level. This permits a direct comparison of the two quantities, one residue at a time. Keep the level F = fℓ′ℓm chosen above, put k = e + 1 ≥ 2, and let χ denote the Dirichlet character induced by ψ at level F throughout this calculation. The cyclotomic character will enter again when the sum is compared with the Galois lifts.

For a unit residue, write u for its representative in 1,…,F−1. Choose b prime to F and divide bu by F, obtaining a quotient j and a remainder y between 1 and F−1. The opposite residue is represented by F−u. Its product with b is (b−j−1)F + (F−y). Subtracting the two quotients gives the signed carry θ(u) = 2j − (b−1). Define S = ∑u θ(u)ueχ(u), summed over the unit representatives. The use of ue in place of a lifted cyclotomic character changes the scalar by a multiple of ℓm.

Write C(u) = Fk−1Bk(u/F)/k, where Bk(x) is the Bernoulli polynomial. Let P be the product of the primes at most k + 1 and set D = 2kP. The first two coefficients of the polynomial give

C(u) = uk/(kF) − uk−1/2 + (2F/D)nu,   nu ∈ ℤ.

Indeed the term of Bernoulli index h ≥ 2 has a factor Fh−1. The denominator bound for the Bernoulli number Bh says that PBh is an integer for h ≤ k. Thus the terms after the first two are all multiples of F/(kP).

Compare C(y) and bkC(u) with y = bu − Fj. In the leading power, the first-order change divided by kF is −j(bu)e. In the second power, the surviving term is (b−1)(bu)e/2. Their sum is −θ(u)(bu)e/2. To keep track of the remainder, expand yk modulo F² and ye modulo F. Multiplication by D clears every denominator in the remainder, with one factor F left. In particular the following quantity is an integer multiple of F.

D[beθ(u)ue + 2(C(y) − bkC(u))] ∈ Fℤ.

Multiply by χ(bu) and sum over u. Multiplication by b permutes the units, so ∑χ(bu)C(y) = ∑χ(u)C(u) = TF, the generalized Bernoulli value at level F divided by k. The other terms use χ(bu) = χ(b)χ(u). Every summand on the remainder side is divisible by ℓm in the coefficient ring. This gives the congruence used by the count.

D[χ(b)beS − 2(χ(b)bk − 1)TF] ≡ 0   (mod ℓm).

For example, take the primitive trivial character, ℓ = 5, e = 1, F = 5 and b = 2. The four signed carries are −1, −1, 1, 1, giving S = −1 − 2 + 3 + 4 = 4. Raising the level from 1 to 5 multiplies B₂ = 1/6 by 1 − 5. Hence T5 = −1/3 and D = 24. The left side is 24[2·4 − 2(4−1)(−1/3)] = 240, a multiple of 5. In this example the valuation of S is zero, as is the valuation of the primitive value 1/12.

In general the change of level multiplies the primitive Bernoulli value by factors 1 − ψ(p)pe. At p dividing the conductor the character vanishes, and at a newly added ℓ the subtracted term has norm less than one. Thus |TF|ℓ equals the norm of the primitive value. The unit-difference hypothesis in the character argument gives a b for which χ(b)bk − 1 is a unit. Since ℓ is odd, 2 is a unit too. The depth is chosen so that |ℓm|ℓ is strictly smaller than |D|ℓ|TF|ℓ, also allowing for the original cutoff. The congruence then forces |S|ℓ = |TF|ℓ. Replacing S by the lifted scalar z preserves that norm. This is the valuation that the successive Frobenius tests spend.

What a Frobenius test measures

Choose a base prime r ≡ 1 modulo F. Let L be a list of distinct auxiliary primes q ≡ 1 modulo F, different from r, at which the multiplicative order of r is prime to ℓ. Call the space at this cutoff, before imposing the base-prime condition, Sbefore. Write SL for its cocycles vanishing on the entire decomposition groups over r and the primes in L. Even S∅ imposes vanishing over r. With each list comes a second function νL in the dual character χα−1. On the subgroup fixing the Fth roots of unity its values are additive and killed by ℓm. Their annihilator is a principal ideal, with generator aL. Put jL = v(aL) and J = v(ℓm). Thus jL ≤ J. The induction uses lists for which the cutoff a₀ divides aL. The initial list has this property, and each new test preserves it.

If SL contains a nonzero c, the prime selection theorem chooses a new q with two properties at once. Evaluation on a Frobenius element φ at q detects c, meaning c(φ) ≠ 0. Every value of νL on the subgroup fixing the roots of unity is an O-multiple of νL(φ). For the longer list L′ there is then an inertia element τ at q for which νL′(τ) equals νL(φ) times a unit. The two values have identical annihilators. Since the entire next system contains this inertia value, aL divides aL′. Denote their quotient by d.

Reciprocity controls the image of the linear evaluation map c ↦ c(φ). In the finite coefficient quotient the characters of the two cocycles multiply to χ. Their cup product is a global degree-two class. At the other primes in the finite ramification set the local coboundary condition makes its restriction trivial. The global sum of local invariants thus leaves zero at q. Local unramified orthogonality, with c zero on inertia there, makes the product of the inertia coefficient of the dual class and the value c(φ) vanish. This conclusion holds in the finite coefficient quotient. The proof first tests it with linear functionals which separate its elements.

Concretely, choose a generator w of the cyclic coefficient subgroup killed by aL′ and write νL′(τ) = y w. Its annihilator is (aL). If the inertia value is nonzero, its order in a cyclic module over a discrete valuation ring gives v(y) = v(d). Thus the reciprocity relation y c(φ) = 0 implies d c(φ) = 0. If the inertia value is zero, its annihilator is the unit ideal and the cutoff dividing aL forces the cutoff space to vanish. The chosen nonzero evaluation therefore forces v(d) > 0. The image of evaluation, lying in cyclic d-torsion, has length at most v(d). An element in its kernel vanishes at the whole decomposition group over q. On the roots-of-unity subgroup it is additive, and the quotient of the decomposition group by inertia is topologically generated by Frobenius. Conjugation transports vanishing to the other places over q. Thus the kernel lies in SL′.

length SL + jL ≤ length SL′ + jL′,   jL′ = jL + v(d) ≤ J.
Check one length loss over ℤ₃

In ℚ₃/ℤ₃ take w = 1/27 modulo ℤ₃. Its annihilator is (27), and the annihilator of 3w is (9). Their quotient is 3. As an example of the evaluation map, send (ℤ/9) ⊕ (ℤ/3) onto the order-three subgroup generated by 1/3 via the second coordinate. The source has length three, the kernel has length two, and the image has length one. Adding this loss to the old annihilator valuation changes 2 to 3. This finite calculation checks the direction and size of one step. Choosing a Frobenius with these properties is the arithmetic assertion above.

Returning to the character length

Whenever SL is nonzero, the next integer jL′ is strictly larger. It cannot exceed J. Induction on J − jL ends with a zero space and proves length SL + jL ≤ J at every admissible state reached, even before finiteness of the starting length has been established. It remains to remove the condition at the base prime r. Take k = ℓm/z. The initial inertia value is a unit times z w for a coefficient element with annihilator (ℓm), so that value has annihilator (k). Write a∅ = k d₀. The same test at r gives length Sbefore ≤ length S∅ + v(d₀). Since J = v(k) + v(z) and j∅ = v(k) + v(d₀), cancellation leaves at most v(z) ≤ v(A). Every cutoff has now received the same final bound.

In the complementary case α agrees with χ modulo the maximal ideal at every group element. Primitivity and the prime-to-ℓ order imply that α is unramified away from ℓ. At ℓ, an inertia element acting by −1 on ℓth roots of unity gives a unit α(δ) − 1 since ℓ is odd. For a normalized cocycle killed by π, the local coboundary witness over ℓ must be zero. Evaluating its defining equation at δ multiplies the witness by the unit α(δ) − 1 and gives zero. Away from ℓ the cocycle already vanishes on inertia.

To see what these local conditions force globally, apply an additive functional from the π-torsion to the field of ℓ elements. The resulting scalar cocycle s has cyclotomic action. Kummer theory realizes it by a radical β with βℓ = a ∈ ℚ× and gβ/β = ζs(g) for a primitive ℓth root ζ. Vanishing on inertia makes every prime exponent of a divisible by ℓ. Unique factorization in ℚ and oddness of ℓ now give a = uℓ for a rational u, including its sign. For example, −8/125 has exponents 3 and −3 and cube root −2/5. Thus β = uζi, so s(g) = i(χ̄(g) − 1), where χ̄ is the action modulo ℓ. At δ the left side is zero and χ̄(δ) − 1 is nonzero. Hence i = 0. All the scalar tests vanish, and linear functionals separate the π-torsion points. Finally, if πk+1c = 0, apply this first step to πkc and descend on k. The original length here is zero.

The construction of the auxiliary functions gives the unit relating the two local values. The carry congruence gives the valuation against which the length is bounded. Prime selection uses Chebotarev, and the test of each new restriction uses duality and orthogonality.

xd = P(Xd)2N₀d,   S = q s(d,q),   Nq(xqd) = (xd/φ−1xd)S.

Which character takes values in the cyclotomic integers?

The Jacobi identity multiplies two algebraic integers. A sum computed only modulo p would lose the ideal it is supposed to measure. Let K = ℚ(ζ), where ζ has order M ≥ 1, and choose a prime ideal of norm p with p ∤ M. Its quotient has p elements. Identify it with 𝔽p and call the resulting reduction π. The algebraic integer ζ satisfies the cyclotomic polynomial ΦM. Its reduction satisfies the same polynomial modulo p. As p ∤ M, the roots of XM − 1 are simple, and the cyclotomic factors for the divisors of M have disjoint roots. A root of ΦM therefore has exact order M. In particular πζ has that order and M divides p − 1.

Put h = (p − 1)/M. For each nonzero x in 𝔽p, the element xh is an Mth root of unity. The M powers of πζ are distinct and list every such root. Find the exponent 0 ≤ a < M with xh = (πζ)a and set χ(x) = ζa. Set χ(0) = 0. Multiplying two residues adds their exponents modulo M, so χ is multiplicative. Its order is exactly M. Indeed, if χk = 1, a generator g of 𝔽p× satisfies ghk = 1 after reduction. Hence Mh divides hk, so M divides k. Conversely all nonzero values have Mth power one. This explains why the nontriviality checks on the Jacobi characters reduce to exponent checks.

Lift the residue 2 at level five

Take M = 5 and p = 11, with πζ = 3. The powers of 3 starting at exponent zero are 1, 3, 9, 5, 4 and then 1. Since h = 2, square the input 2 to obtain 4. The required lift is χ(2) = ζ⁴. Squaring this value gives χ(4) = ζ³. Checking the other way, 4² ≡ 5 ≡ 3³ modulo 11. For the other reduction π′ζ = 9, the input 2 still gives 2² = 4. Since 9² ≡ 4 modulo 11, its lift is now χ′(2) = ζ². The prime ideal is part of the construction.
