Why every prime above p occurs only once

For each invertible residue t modulo M let σt(ζ) = ζt and put Pt = ker(π ∘ σt). This inverse-image convention is what sets the indices in the signed divisor. Every reduction is onto, since ordinary integers already give all of 𝔽p. Its kernel is therefore a maximal ideal of norm p. If two kernels agreed, subtract from any algebraic integer the ordinary integer representing its first reduction. The difference would also belong to the second kernel, forcing both reductions to agree on that element. Applying this to ζ gives (πζ)s = (πζ)t, hence s = t.

These φ(M) distinct maximal ideals are pairwise coprime, and each divides (p). Their product divides (p) and already has norm pφ(M). This equals the norm of (p), because [K : ℚ] = φ(M). The leftover integral ideal has norm one and is the unit ideal. Thus (p) = ∏tPt. For a Jacobi sum J dividing p, this gives ordPₜ(J) ∈ {0,1}. Testing π(σtJ) = 0 tells exactly which exponent is one. In the example at 11 the four reductions send ζ to 3, 9, 5 and 4. A repeated prime would exhaust too much of the norm.

To tell which primes occur, reduce σt(Jj) modulo P. The result is ∑ xA(1 − x)B with A = h[t]N and B = h[jt]N. Both exponents lie strictly between 0 and p − 1. Expand the binomial. In degree A + k the sum of powers over the field vanishes unless p − 1 divides the degree. Since all degrees are positive and below 2(p − 1), only k = p − 1 − A can contribute. When this index is in the expansion its binomial coefficient is nonzero modulo p, since B < p. Thus the residue is zero exactly when A + B < p − 1, or [t]N + [jt]N < N. Each addition without a carry contributes one factor of Pt to (J).

Let e(t) count these additions. For b ≥ 1 there are b − 1 steps. The number of carries is ⌊b[t]N/N⌋, since each new addition increases the integer quotient by one precisely when a carry occurs. Hence e(t) = b − 1 − ⌊b[t]N/N⌋. Conjugation exchanges Pt and P−t, so the exponent in (c(J)/J) is e(−t) − e(t) = θN(t). The product with its complex conjugate is 1 by cancellation. At b = 0 the Jacobi product is empty and XP = 1, as all the floor weights vanish.

Compute a denominator at level 5

Take N = 5, b = 3 and p = 11, so h = 2. At t = 1 the Jacobi factors for j = 1,2 give exponents (A,B) = (2,2),(2,4). Both sums vanish modulo 11 because their degrees stay below 10. At t = 4 the pairs are (8,8),(8,6). Both reach degree 10. The surviving terms give −28 ≡ 5 and −15 ≡ 7 modulo 11. Thus e(1) = 2 and e(4) = 0. The quotient c(J)/J has exponent −2 at P1, +2 at P4, and 0 at the other two primes. This agrees with θ5(1) = ⌊3/5⌋ − ⌊12/5⌋ = −2.

Why each Jacobi sum divides the split prime

The cyclotomic construction determines a signed ideal by testing a product of Jacobi sums at the primes above p. A zero residue proves that one such prime divides a factor. How can we tell that its square does not? Each factor has an explicit partner whose product with it is p. At a split unramified prime, the order of p is one, so the nonnegative orders of the two partners sum to one. This turns the residue test into an exact exponent.

Let χ and φ be multiplicative characters of 𝔽p× taking values in a characteristic-zero integral domain R, extended by zero at zero. Assume χ, φ and χφ are all nontrivial. Define J(χ,φ) = ∑x∈𝔽pχ(x)φ(1−x). The partner uses the inverse of each character. Its values already lie in R, since every nonzero character value is a unit.

J(χ,φ) J(χ−1,φ−1) = p.

To compute the product, pass to the fraction field of R and then to a cyclotomic extension containing a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽p. Write Gψ(ρ) = ∑xρ(x)ψ(x). In the product Gψ(χ)Gψ(φ), group pairs (x,y) by t = x+y. At t = 0 their total is φ(−1)∑x(χφ)(x) = 0. At t ≠ 0 put x = tu. The two characters contribute (χφ)(t)χ(u)φ(1−u). Summing yields Gψ(χφ)J(χ,φ).

A second orthogonality identity says Gψ(ρ)Gψ−1(ρ−1) = p for nontrivial ρ. To see why, expand the two sums and put x = uy for y ≠ 0. At each y the summand becomes ρ(u)ψ(y(u−1)). We can include y = 0 because its total is ∑uρ(u) = 0. Summing over all y now leaves only u = 1, contributing p. Apply the first identity twice, once with ψ and once with its inverse and the inverse multiplicative characters. Multiplication and the second identity give pJ(χ,φ)J(χ−1,φ−1) = p². Cancelling p and using injectivity of the two field embeddings gives the claimed identity in R.

See the two factors of 7 in the Eisenstein integers

Take the level M = 3, b = 2 and p = 7. In ℤ[ω], with ω²+ω+1 = 0, choose the cubic character determined by χ(3) = ω, since 3 generates 𝔽₇×. At the prime where ω reduces to 2 it satisfies the required reduction χ(x) ≡ x². Here the Jacobi product has one factor, J(χ,χ). The inputs 0 and 1 contribute zero. For x = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 the five contributions are ω², 1, ω², 1, ω². The sum and its inverse-character partner are 2+3ω² and 2+3ω. Their product is 4+6(ω+ω²)+9 = 7. At ω ≡ 2 modulo 7 the first is zero and the second is one. At ω ≡ 4 their roles reverse. Each factor has order exactly one at the prime where it vanishes.

How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class

The Jacobi sum uses a prime ideal P whose residue field has a prime number of elements. To apply that calculation to an arbitrary nonzero integral ideal 𝔞, the same P must make 𝔞P principal. For a prime of a number field K above a rational prime p, its absolute norm NP is the residue field size pf. Thus absolute residue degree one means NP = p. We can require this degree, prescribe the ideal class [P] = c and exclude any finite set of prime ideals of K.

Let H be the Hilbert class field of K. Its Artin isomorphism sends [P] to the arithmetic Frobenius at a prime above P, acting on residues by x ↦ xNP. Apply the degree-one prime theorem to H/K with target automorphism Art(c). The Frobenius supplied by the theorem restricts to this precise automorphism. Two Frobenius lifts at the same place agree modulo inertia, and inertia in H/K is trivial. Applying Art−1 gives [P] = c. In the cyclotomic application take c = [𝔞]−1 and exclude the primes dividing N𝒪K, where N is the cyclotomic level. This set is finite because N ≠ 0. Then p ∤ N, reduction preserves the order of ζN, and N divides p − 1 as the character construction requires. The inverse on [𝔞] comes from [𝔞][P] = 1.

How can the proof still impose absolute degree one?

Write L/K for the finite Galois extension and g for the requested automorphism. The proof chooses an auxiliary prime ℓ with [L : K] dividing ℓ − 1 and Φℓ irreducible over L. In L(ζℓ) choose an automorphism h restricting to g on L and raising ζℓ to a generator τ of (ℤ/ℓℤ)×. Irreducibility permits this choice by adjusting a lift of g with an automorphism fixing L. Take the fixed field Z of ⟨h⟩ inside this compositum. The powers of h realize every exponent on ζℓ, so Φℓ is still irreducible over Z.

Above the finite exclusions and the ramified primes of L/K there are only finitely many primes of Z. Away from these, seek a prime w with Nw ≡ τ modulo ℓ. A prime-distribution result gives divergence of the sum of reciprocal prime-ideal norms in this residue class. Primes of absolute degree at least two contribute at most [Z : ℚ]∑p primep−2, since at most [Z : ℚ] primes of Z lie above each p. The finite exclusions also contribute a finite amount. Hence a remaining w has prime norm p. For P below w, the equality Nw = (NP)f(w/P) forces NP = p.

A Frobenius lift at w fixes Z and acts on the ℓth roots by the pth power, since p ≠ ℓ and those roots remain distinct after reduction. Its action in the compositum is therefore hj with τj = τ. Thus j ≡ 1 modulo ℓ − 1. The order of g divides [L : K], which divides ℓ − 1, so gj = g. The equality of norms lets the same lift serve as an arithmetic Frobenius at P.

Which degree counts the conjugates, and which degree counts the ideal?

Put N = Fd and enlarge the level to qN by a fresh prime q coprime to N. The construction chooses its two cyclotomic fields inside one algebraic closure. Even if the two embeddings were initially chosen separately, every Nth root of unity is a power of a primitive root of order qN. This puts the smaller field inside the larger one in precisely one way compatible with the chosen embeddings. Restricting the same place above the rational prime r then gives primes 𝔭′ above 𝔭.

The field norm counts conjugates. A relative automorphism fixes the roots of order N and can act by any nonzero residue on a primitive qth root. Indeed, for a generator g modulo q, the Chinese remainder theorem gives an exponent equal to 1 modulo N and to g modulo q. The resulting power map on roots gives an automorphism τ of KqN over KN. Its first q − 1 powers are distinct on the primitive qth root. They exhaust the relative Galois group since the degree is φ(qN)/φ(N) = q − 1, where φ counts invertible residues. Hence the product of τi(Xqd) for 0 ≤ i < q − 1 is its field norm.

The ideal norm counts residue-field degree. For r ∤ qN, write ordn(r) for the least positive k with rk ≡ 1 modulo n. At either level the prime is unramified, and Frobenius acts on the roots by the rth power. Its order is the absolute residue degree. Write κ(𝔭) for the residue field at 𝔭. Degrees multiply in the tower of residue fields, giving

s = [κ(𝔭′) : κ(𝔭)] = ordqN(r) / ordN(r),   Norm(𝔭′) = 𝔭s.

Thus Xds satisfies the two generator conditions for Norm(𝔭′). Raising to the power s multiplies each ideal exponent by s and preserves the identity with complex conjugation. This explains its exponent in both the norm formula and the congruence. The denominator in the norm formula uses the inverse of the qth-power action on the lower roots. The admissible auxiliary primes have orders of r prime to ℓ, and r ≡ 1 modulo F. By the Chinese remainder theorem their least common multiple is ordqN(r), so ℓ ∤ s.

Check the two norms at levels 21 and 273

Take F = ℓ = 3, d = 7, q = 13 and r = 307. Both auxiliary primes are 1 modulo 3. Modulo 3, 7 and 13 the residues of 307 are 1, −1 and 8, of orders 1, 2 and 4 respectively (8² ≡ −1 modulo 13). The absolute residue degrees at levels 21 and 273 are therefore 2 and 4. The relative ideal norm is 𝔭². The residue field at 𝔭′ has 307⁴ elements and (307²)² = 307⁴. On elements the relative norm has twelve factors. For a primitive thirteenth root ζ these give Norm(1 − ζ) = ∏j=112(1 − ζj) = 13 by evaluating 1 + T + ⋯ + T12 at 1. Here 3 divides the number of conjugates and is coprime to the exponent 2 needed for the next normalization.

Both comparisons now use the same exponent s, prime to ℓ. The norm identity has a root factor of order dividing 2N. The congruence uses one root at all places over q, of order dividing 2qN. The two roots may differ. Their common order bound 2qN lets the next normalization remove each root, giving a norm identity and congruence with exponent qs.

8.24Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

To combine several primes in the minus estimate, the proof discards some character factors from an ℓ-adic product. This step is safe when each discarded factor has nonnegative valuation. Where does that integrality come from? At twist j put k = j + 1 ≥ 2. If χ has level N, conductor f and primitive character χ*, its denominator-cleared Bernoulli value is α = NPkBk,χ*, where Pk is the product of the primes at most k + 1. The two integer multipliers pay for different denominators.

Expand the Bernoulli polynomial in ordinary Bernoulli numbers Bh. The rational coefficient attached to one residue a is

fk−1Bk(a/f) = ∑h=0k binom(k,h) Bh fh−1ak−h.

At h = 0 the factor f−1 can introduce a conductor denominator. Multiplying the entire sum by f changes every exponent to the nonnegative integer h. For a positive even h, the von Staudt–Clausen formula expresses Bh as an integer minus a sum of 1/p over primes with p−1 dividing h. Each such p is at most h+1 ≤ k+1, so it divides Pk. The remaining indices give B₀ = 1, B₁ = −½ and Bh = 0 for odd h > 1. Thus PkBh is integral throughout, and fPk times the displayed coefficient is an integer, residue by residue.

Multiplying these integers by χ*(a) and summing keeps the result in the ring generated by the character values. A unit value is a root of unity, hence an algebraic integer, and a nonunit contributes zero. Each unit modulo f lifts to a unit modulo N, so the values of χ* belong to the ring generated by the original χ. Finally f divides N. Multiplying by the integer N/f proves the required integrality of α in that ring.

The same scaling also allows a single archimedean bound. For k ≥ 2 the Fourier expansion on [0,1] pairs the positive and negative frequencies. Each pair of unit complex phases has absolute value at most 2. Its reciprocal-power sum is bounded by 2∑m≥11/m² = π²/3 < 4. Consequently |Bk(x)| ≤ 4k!/(2π)k. There are f terms in the primitive sum, each carrying fk−1 and a character value of absolute value at most 1. Using f ≤ N, Pk ≤ 4k+1 and 4/(2π) ≤ 1 gives |α| ≤ 16Nk+1k!. The denominator bound uses von Staudt–Clausen and the primorial estimate. The absolute-value bound uses the Fourier series and the sum of reciprocal squares.

8.25When an odd prime divides the field degree

The proof now works in the integral group algebra at modulus H = Nℓ, using the odd smoothing integer a = 2H+1, coprime to H. A higher Stickelberger element has an ℓ-integral lift z. For a localization-kernel class x, choose a power ℓs killing x. At a sufficiently high cyclotomic level the congruence for z holds modulo ℓs and the restriction of the approximating element vanishes on x. The error acts by zero on x. Descent gives z(φ(H)x) = 0. On the sign component c acts by (−1)k, so the determinant of multiplication by z on the quotient imposing this sign also kills φ(H)x. This last deduction uses the adjugate identity in the quotient.

A denominator-cleared nonzero integer multiple of this determinant has absolute value at most the determinant bound raised to ⌊n/2⌋. Its ℓ-adic valuation bounds an exponent r₀ for the determinant. With r₁ = vℓ(φ(H)), the power ℓr, r = r₀ + r₁, annihilates the minus summand. Bounding the logarithm of the determinant bound together with log(Nℓ) gives

r log ℓ ≤ 30n(j+1) log(jℓN).

For the other factor in the length estimate, pass to the first cyclotomic layer of degree m over ℚ, with m ≤ ℓn. The ℓ-torsion of the ambient cohomology injects into a finite Selmer quotient of size at most ℓ2m times that layer’s class number. The class-number estimate gives a torsion length g ≤ 8ℓn log(ℓN). For the minus submodule M killed by ℓr, multiplication by ℓa−1 embeds each layer M[ℓa]/M[ℓa−1] into M[ℓ]. The bottom layer is finite by the Selmer count. Induction through at most r layers proves that M is finite and its length is at most rg. For ℤ/9 ⊕ ℤ/3, the subgroup killed by 3 has order 9, and the next quotient has order 3. Its length is 2+1=3, within the allowance 2·2. The annihilating determinant bounds the number of layers and the Selmer count bounds the size of each. Combining these inequalities gives mℓ,j log ℓ ≤ 240ℓn²(j+1) log²(jℓN). The constant in the public theorem is existential. The factors 30 and 8 exhibit one witness.

Each automorphism of the ambient cyclotomic field, raised to 2e+1o, fixes E. This follows from the 2-power congruence, the kernel condition defining the base field, and the two quadratic character conditions, which are killed by squaring. The Galois quotient has order n. If an odd prime ℓ divides n, Cauchy’s theorem gives a quotient element of order ℓ, hence ℓ divides o. Summing the preceding estimate over 1 ≤ j < t bounds the contribution of each such prime by 240ℓn²t² log²(tℓN). All terms are nonnegative, so the sum can be enlarged to the fixed odd prime divisors of o. In particular, for o a power of two the first term alone suffices.

Counting the generators before bounding the length

Fix an odd prime ℓ dividing the degree of the field E. The determinant calculation above tells us how many powers of ℓ annihilate the minus group. One also needs to bound how many independent classes can survive a single multiplication by ℓ. Write X for the ambient twisted first cohomology group and X[ℓ] for its subgroup killed by ℓ. The argument counts this subgroup even though it only needs a bound for the minus classes.

Let F = E(μℓ) and put m = [F:ℚ], n = [E:ℚ]. Choose, for each class in X[ℓ], a cocycle taking values in the order-ℓ subgroup of ℚℓ/ℤℓ. Indeed, if ℓ times a representative is the coboundary of a coefficient b, choose b′ with ℓb′ = b in the divisible group ℚℓ/ℤℓ. Subtract the coboundary of b′. The new representative is killed by ℓ pointwise. Over F the cyclotomic character is 1 modulo ℓ. Restricted to this subgroup of values, the twisted cocycle rule becomes ordinary addition. One obtains an additive character of the absolute Galois group of F, unramified outside the primes over ℓ because the original cocycle factors through the Galois group with that ramification condition. If two chosen cocycles give the same character, their difference restricts to zero. The index [F:E] divides ℓ − 1, so averaging over the cosets is allowed in ℤℓ. The coboundary lemma then identifies their classes over E. This gives an injection of sets. If E embeds in the cyclotomic field of level N, then F embeds at level ℓN.

Choose a primitive ℓth root ζ in F. Kummer theory attaches to such a character φ a nonzero radical β with gβ = ζφ(g)β and βℓ = a in F×. Unramifiedness makes the valuation of a divisible by ℓ at each prime outside S, where S is the set over ℓ. Changing a by an ℓth power in F leaves the character determined by the radical unchanged. Indeed the two resulting radicals, after scaling, differ by a root of unity fixed by every g. The characters therefore inject into the multiplicative group of allowed a modulo ℓth powers.

To count this quotient, remove the primes in S from the fractional ideal of a and divide the remaining prime exponents by ℓ. Its class in the ideal class group with these primes inverted belongs to ClS(F)[ℓ]. Every such class occurs because its ℓth power is principal away from S, and a generator gives an admissible a. The kernel consists of S-units modulo powers. These are the elements with valuation zero outside S. For a concrete count, take ℚ, S = {3} and cubes. After removing a rational cube every allowed number is represented by exactly one of 1, 3 and 9. The sign is already a cube. This illustrates the quotient being counted. The earlier injection uses a field containing μℓ.

Over F, the S-unit factor has order ℓr₁+r₂−1+|S| |μℓ(F)|, where r₁ counts real embeddings and r₂ counts conjugate pairs. The root-of-unity factor is at most ℓ, both r₁+r₂ and |S| are at most m, and the order of ClS(F)[ℓ] is at most the ordinary class number hF. If g is the dimension of X[ℓ] over the field with ℓ elements, the count gives the following inequality.

ℓg ≤ ℓ2mhF.

The cyclotomic comparison gives log hF ≤ 3m log(ℓN). Taking logarithms, using m ≤ ℓn and log ℓ ≥ log 2 > 5/8, gives g ≤ 8ℓn log(ℓN). Finally, if ℓr kills the group being bounded, its length is at most rg. For successive kernels of ℓi on X, multiplication by ℓi injects the next quotient into X[ℓ]. There are r quotients. This explains the product of the constant 8 from the dimension estimate and the constant 30 from the determinant estimate. The underlying arithmetic inputs here include Kummer radicals, the S-unit theorem and the class-number estimate used in the discriminant comparison.

8.27Finding two primes that work for every required twist

The host construction applies the following prime-pair theorem to a fixed primitive character’s window. For a fixed primitive ψ, take M equal to its conductor and A equal to the cohomological window exponent J. Fix 0 < ε < 1/52 and A ≥ 1. For every sufficiently large Y one pair of primes q,d has to work at every y between Y and YA, for every required character. A zero-free box of height H means that L(s,χ) never vanishes for Re s > 1 − 1/400 and |Im s| ≤ H.

Put z = Yε/5 and z′ = z(log Y)². Take q ≡ 3 modulo 8 with z/2 < log q ≤ z. For this q, let B be q times the product of the odd primes at most z. The second prime must satisfy d ≡ 7 modulo 16 and d ≡ −1 modulo B, with z′/2 < log d ≤ z′. The Chinese remainder theorem makes these two conditions one reduced residue class modulo 16B. For a small illustration, z = 3 and q = 11 give B = 33. The prime 263 is 7 modulo 16 and 263 + 1 = 8 · 33. This checks the congruences alone. The analytic selection still has to take place inside that progression.

8.28How many primes can a failed twist eliminate?

In either selection step write U for the upper bound on the candidate prime p. The candidates form a set P in one reduced progression with √U < p ≤ U. The modulus m must be positive and divisible by 8, with a residue class coprime to m. The size conditions are (log Y)² log m/4 ≤ log U and Yε/6 ≤ log U ≤ Yε/5(log Y)². For ξ ∈ Ξ, twisting by the quadratic symbol (·/p) gives a primitive character of conductor fp, where f is the conductor of ξ. The inequality p > F ensures coprimality. Set H = FU.

Why the progression still contains enough primes

The selection argument spends a fraction of the primes in one residue class. It needs a positive lower bound for the denominator even when the modulus grows with the first chosen prime. As in both stages, 8 divides m and a is coprime to m. Put L = log U, let π(U;m,a) count all primes up to U congruent to a modulo m, and write li(u) = ∫₂ᵘ dt/log t. The progression theorem supplies a main term B. Without an exceptional zero it is li(U)/φ(m). With an exceptional pair (χ, β) it is

B = [li(U) − Re χ(a) li(Uβ)] / φ(m).

Here χ is a nontrivial quadratic character modulo m with a real zero β between 1 − 1/(8 log m) and 1. Keeping this term matters for a progression on which χ(a) = 1, because it subtracts almost the whole main term if β is close to one. The relative prime-number estimate bounds the error by B times a constant times [exp(−c₃L/log m) + exp(−√(c₃L))]. Uniformly over the admitted data this multiplier is at most ½ for sufficiently large Y. Indeed L/log m ≥ (log Y)²/4 and L ≥ Yε/6. The lower and upper admitted bounds on L also give log m ≤ 4Yε/5, which puts L in the theorem’s range C₀ log m · log(log m + 2) ≤ L.

How small can B become? The separate exceptional-zero estimate, used with exponent one, supplies a fixed 0 < c ≤ 1 such that 1 − β ≥ c/m. For L ≥ 4 we have Uβ ≥ 2 and Uβ/U ≤ exp(−c/m) ≤ 1 − c/(2m). In the worst sign the remaining integral from Uβ to U is at least (U − Uβ)/L. With no exceptional pair the integral runs all the way from 2. Using φ(m) ≤ m gives the same floor in every case.

B ≥ cU/(2Lm²) ≥ 4U9/10,   |P| ≥ ½B − √U ≥ U9/10.

For the middle inequality, the threshold gives 80 log m ≤ L and log(320/c) ≤ L/20. Thus m² ≤ exp(L/40), L ≤ 40 exp(L/40), and 320 ≤ c exp(L/20). Multiplication absorbs the denominator into the spare exponent 1/10. The last subtraction discards every integer up to √U, covering all the primes too small for P. This proves the cardinality floor before any twist is tested. The relative progression theorem and the Siegel lower bound used here are deeper analytic inputs.

How can one count characters whose L-function has a zero?

Write Q for the height H of the box in the preceding prime selection. Consider all primitive characters of conductor at most Q that have at least one zero ρ with Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. The number of these characters is at most CQ1/4 for every real Q ≥ 3 and a single absolute constant C. One zero, chosen separately for each character, suffices. The argument turns it into a large finite sum on one interval, then bounds how many characters can give large sums on the same interval.

Detecting one zero. For large Q take X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋ + 1) and N = 2J. Here Y is the length of an auxiliary sum within this proof. Multiply the first N terms of L(s,χ), denoted P(s), by M(s) = ∑d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−s, summing over positive integers. The Möbius function μ is zero on multiples of squares of primes. On a product of k distinct primes it is (−1)k, including μ(1) = 1. In the product the coefficient multiplying χ(n)n−s is

a(n) = ∑db=n, 1≤d≤Y, 1≤b≤N μ(d).

For 2 ≤ n ≤ Y every divisor occurs, since Y ≤ N. The sum is zero by expanding (1−1)k over the distinct prime divisors. At n = 1 it is one. Thus PM = 1 + D, where D uses only Y < n ≤ YN. For a short calculation set Y = 3 and N = 4. At 6 only (2,3) and (3,2) qualify, so a(6) = −2. At 4 only (1,4) and (2,2) occur, and their contributions cancel. Truncating the product can leave either outcome beyond the initial range.

Why must at least one block be large at a zero?

For a primitive character of conductor q > 1, complete periods of χ sum to zero. The resulting partial-sum bound and partial summation give, at the chosen zero with σ = Re ρ, |P(ρ)| ≤ 2(q+1)(1+|ρ|/σ)N−σ. Every term of the second polynomial has modulus at most one, so |M(ρ)| ≤ Y. When Q ≥ 20 we have q+1 ≤ 2X and 1+|ρ|/σ ≤ 3X. Also N ≥ X⁸ and σ > 15/16, so Nσ ≥ X⁷√X ≥ 4X⁷. Multiplication by Y = X⁴ gives |PM| ≤ 3/X ≤ 1/2. Since PM = 1 + D, the reverse triangle inequality forces |D| ≥ 1/2. Split (Y,YN] into J successive blocks (U,2U] with U = Y2j. At least one block sum has modulus ≥ 1/(2J).

Write σ₀ = 399/400. Suppose T characters selected one block (U, 2U]. Place their values in rows vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀), and put b(n) = a(n)n−σ₀. Partial summation against the complex power gives the bound 2Q²(1+|w|) for the inner product, with w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀). Each of these nonprincipal zeros has real part below 1, and the two imaginary parts have absolute values at most Q. Thus the inner product has modulus at most 8Q³.

With N = ⌊Z⌋ and cn = Λ(n) min(1,y/n), expand the square of Sq = ∑n≤N cnκ(n)(n/q). Each ordered pair (n,n′) contributes a coefficient cncn′κ(n)κ(n′) times a sum of quadratic symbols. We can take the absolute value of each such sum after summing over q. This order retains cancellation among primes.

For a product nn′, let s be the product of primes outside m whose exponent in nn′ is odd. For an admitted progression and sufficiently large Y, its lower cutoff √U is at least N² and hence every q exceeds N², so a square factor has symbol +1. The primes dividing m contribute a fixed sign on the progression. Indeed, 8 divides m, which fixes the symbol of 2 and the sign in quadratic reciprocity. For odd primes dividing m it also fixes the residue of q modulo that prime. Hence for a sign σ depending on the pair and the progression,

(n/q)(n′/q) = σ(q/s),   σ ∈ {−1,+1}.

For example, 53 and 101 are both 5 modulo 24. The pair (4,3) has s = 1 even though 12 is not a square. Its symbol is −1 at both primes. For (3,5) the symbol is −(q/5), giving +1 at 53 and −1 at 101. These two terms cancel exactly. The example illustrates the correlation on two primes.

Why should ∑q∈P(q/s) be small for s > 1? Split the progression into reduced classes b mod ms above a. Their ordinary prime-counting main terms cancel because the nontrivial character (b/s) sums to zero. A real zero β of a quadratic character χ can add a term proportional to ∑b(b/s)χ(b). Multiplying every class by a unit u ≡ 1 mod m permutes the sum. If χ(u) differs from (u/s), this multiplies it by −1, forcing it to vanish. If the characters agree on these units, the logarithmic integral li(Uβ) is small enough unless β > 1 − c₀/log(mY800K). The near-one uniqueness theorem makes any two such near-one characters agree on common units. Distinct squarefree s would give different symbols on one of those units. The Chinese remainder theorem lets us choose a nonresidue at one prime dividing just one of them and 1 at every other prime involved, as well as modulo m. Thus at most one integer s★ escapes the bound |∑(q/s)| ≤ η|P|, η = Y−(K+1). It is chosen for the progression before y and κ.

Why only one quadratic twist can keep a near-one zero

In the fixed-height mean square, the prime number theorem for a residue class modulo M can contribute a term involving li(Uβ). Here β is a real zero of a nonprincipal quadratic Dirichlet character. Two such terms at different moduli might both be large. To compare them, the proof first puts both characters at the same modulus. The analytic reason this works is that two nearby zeros would force a sum of four logarithmic derivatives to be negative, while every coefficient in its Dirichlet series is nonnegative.

Fix a positive modulus Q and two distinct nonprincipal characters χ₁, χ₂ with χ₁² = χ₂² = 1. Their product is nonprincipal because each character is its own inverse. Write Dψ(σ) = Re(−L′(σ,ψ)/L(σ,ψ)). At a real σ > 1, this is an absolutely convergent sum with coefficients Λ(n) Re ψ(n), where Λ is the von Mangoldt function. On units modulo Q, χ₁ and χ₂ take the values ±1. At every nonunit all four characters, including the principal character 1 modulo Q, vanish. Consequently

D₁ + Dχ₁ + Dχ₂ + Dχ₁χ₂ = ∑(n,Q)=1 Λ(n) (1+χ₁(n))(1+χ₂(n))/nσ ≥ 0.

Each unit has a multiplier of 0 or 4. Suppose both characters have real zeros β₁, β₂ near 1. Put ℓ = log(2Q). In the interval 1 < σ ≤ 6/5 the expansion over zeros in the closed disk of radius 1/5 about 11/10 bounds Dχ by Cℓ minus a sum of Re(1/(σ−ρ)), counted with multiplicity. Every summand is positive since Re ρ < 1. A real zero β in [9/10,1) thus subtracts at least 1/(σ−β). The product character contributes at most Cℓ, and the principal character contributes at most 1/(σ−1)+C′, with C′ ≥ 0. Both constants are uniform in Q.

Set H = 3|C| + 2C′ + 1, e = 1/(20Hℓ), and test at σ = 1+2e. Since ℓ ≥ log 2 > 1/2, we have e ≤ 1/10. If β₁, β₂ ≥ 1−e, each contributes at least 1/(3e). The upper bound for the same four-term sum is then

3Cℓ + C′ + 1/(2e) − 2/(3e) ≤ (H−1)ℓ − (10/3)Hℓ < 0.

This contradiction excludes two distinct characters. A single zero is compatible with the calculation: the pole allowance 1/(2e) exceeds the one guaranteed subtraction 1/(3e).

A second estimate handles two zeros of the same real character at small imaginary part. At its test point σ = 1+1/T, the local sum over zeros is strictly less than 8T/5, and each zero in the restricted region contributes at least 4T/5. Two distinct zeros or one zero of multiplicity at least two exceed the available bound. A nonreal zero would occur with its complex conjugate, so a surviving zero is real and simple. Combining these estimates with the exclusions for the principal character, nonreal characters and larger imaginary parts produces an absolute c > 0. For every Q ≥ 1 the closed region Re z ≥ 1−c/log(Q(|Im z|+2)) contains at most one character–zero pair, with the pole of the principal character excluded.

Now take levels M₁, M₂ ≤ D with D ≥ 3 and induce both characters to Q = M₁M₂. The change-of-level formula preserves a zero by multiplying its L-value by Euler factors. Since log(2Q) ≤ 3 log D, any two real zeros above 1−c/(3 log D) lie in the same region. Their induced characters must agree on every common unit. For example, take m = 8 and squarefree denominators 3 and 5. At the levels 24 and 40, the common unit 41 is 1 modulo 8, but (41/3) = −1 and (41/5) = +1. Thus characters agreeing there with the respective quadratic symbols cannot both have such a zero. The example uses no assumption that either zero exists.

Fix 0 < ε ≤ 1 and K ≥ 1. For every sufficiently large Y and every admitted progression with modulus m, take D = mY800K and c₀ = c/3. A denominator s can produce an uncontrolled contribution only if the progression formula at ms supplies a pair with 1−β < c₀/log D and its character agrees with (·/s) on units congruent to 1 modulo m. For a misaligned character the weighted sum of its main terms vanishes. For an aligned character with 1−β ≥ c₀/log D, the ratio li(Uβ)/li(U) is at most 4 log U exp(−c₀ log U/log D), small enough at the common threshold for Y. At most one odd squarefree s > 1 coprime to m, s ≤ Y800K, can survive both tests. The proof chooses it (or 0 if none) before the height y and coefficients κ. Its pairs are included in the quadratic estimate. A separate use of Siegel’s lower bound gives 1−β ≥ c₁/m at the original modulus and supplies the lower bound on the number of primes.

The remaining task is to count the pairs where cancellation can fail. Since Λ vanishes off prime powers, each index has the form pj. It contributes the single prime p to the parity calculation when p ∤ m and j is odd, and contributes nothing otherwise. Let R be the total weight of indices contributing nothing, sp the total weight of all powers of p, B a common upper bound on sp, and T the total weight. All weights in these definitions are cn, for 1 ≤ n ≤ N.

  • For s = 1 the two indices either contribute nothing or contribute the same prime twice. Their weight is at most R² + ∑psp².
  • If s★ is a prime r, the source covers same-base pairs by sr². For distinct bases, one index contributes r and the other contributes nothing, costing at most 2srR in the two orders. ∑q∈P|Sq|² ≤ |P| [∑psp² + R² + 2B² + 2BR + ηT²].

How the finite prime sum controls the centered ramp

The prime-selection argument has found a prime p for which the finite sums are small throughout the required interval. There is still a term to estimate for its twist χ(n) = ξ(n)(n/p). Write an = Λ(n)χ(n) and D(s) = −L′(s,χ)/L(s,χ). For a height y and a cutoff Z ≥ y > 0, set

R(y) = ∑1≤n≤y an(y/n − 1),   SZ(y) = ∑1≤n≤Z an min(1,y/n),   PZ = ∑1≤n≤Z an/n.

For n ≤ y, subtracting 1 from y/n gives the ramp weight. For y < n ≤ Z, the two weights in yPZ − SZ(y) cancel. Hence the centered ramp satisfies an exact identity, with a tail that is a single complex number for the whole interval.

Gχ(y) = R(y) − yD(1) = −SZ(y) − y[D(1) − PZ].

How close is the finite slope PZ to D(1)? Measure the same increment ΔR = R(Z + h) − R(Z) in two ways. First, every term already present at Z advances by exactly han/n. The new terms have Z < n ≤ Z + h. For Z ≥ 1 and h > 0, there are at most h + 1 of them, each with ramp weight ≤ h/Z and |an| ≤ log(Z + h). Thus |ΔR − hPZ| ≤ h(h + 1) log(Z + h)/Z.

A prime power entering the ramp. Take the nontrivial character modulo 3, with values 1, −1, 0 on residues 1, 2, 0. From Z = 7/2 to Z + h = 5, the old slope is PZ = −log(2)/2. The ramp goes from −(3/4)log 2 to −(5/4)log 2, so ΔR − hPZ = (1/4)log 2. The entire correction comes from 4 = 2², since χ(4) = 1 and 5/4 − 1 = 1/4. The new prime 5 has weight zero at the endpoint. This calculation checks the finite difference for arbitrary cutoffs.

The same increment from a contour. Suppose χ is nonprincipal of modulus N ≤ Q, with Q ≥ 2, and L(s,χ) has no zero for Re s > 1 − 1/400 and |Im s| ≤ Q. For u ≥ 1, Perron inversion writes R(u) as the integral of D(s)us/[s(s−1)] on Re s = 2, with measure ds/(2πi). Move the segment of height |Im s| ≤ T = Q/2 to σ = 1 − 1/400 + δ, where 0 < δ ≤ 1/800. The rectangle lies inside the zero-free box and stays to the right of 0. Its only possible pole is at 1. Multiplication by s−1 leaves D(s)us/s, whose value there is uD(1). At u = Z + h and u = Z, subtracting these residues gives hD(1).

Put h = ηZ with 0 < η ≤ 1. On the left edge, differentiate us with respect to the positive variable u. This gives |(Z + h)s − Zs| ≤ |s|ηZσ. The factor |s| cancels one denominator. Integrating 1/|s−1| over the segment costs at most 4 log(1 + 800T). The other logarithm comes from |D(s)| ≤ Cδ log Q on the smaller box Re s ≥ σ, |Im s| ≤ Q − 1. In the local formula for L′/L, the nearby zeros stay at least δ away and their total multiplicity is bounded by a constant times log Q. On the two horizontal sides the denominator has size at least T². On the unshifted right tails the integrand decays as 1/|Im s|². Together these give a constant Aδ independent of χ, Z, η and Q.

|ΔR − hD(1)| ≤ Aδ log Q [(log Q)ηZσ + Z²/Q].

Why use the 400th power? Fix 0 < ε ≤ 1/4, K ≥ 1 and τ > 0. For sufficiently large Y, the selection stage has Yε/6 ≤ log Q ≤ Yε/4. Take τ = ε/2, η = 1/2 and work at base modulus N₀ = 8M. In the first progression take U = exp z, F = N₀ and the primitive characters inducing the characters modulo N₀. Whatever q was chosen, this family has at most twice the number of characters modulo N₀. The second-stage theorem verifies the modulus and conductor bounds uniformly in q. In particular q > (YA)400 for large Y, while the other odd prime factors of B are at most z. At least half of this second nonempty set also survives. The two thresholds were fixed before choosing either prime.

The first selection controls the twist by q alone. The second controls the twist by d and the twist by both primes. For a real base character of conductor dividing 8M, change of level places it in the same family, hence the same rectangle excludes all zeros for the induced primitive character, with height 8M exp(z + jz′) if j records the presence of d. For a base character modulo M these estimates bound the centered sum by y1/2+ε/2. The logarithmic derivative at one satisfies the sharper bound 4 log y. The source first proves 1000 log log H + C from the zero-free box and then uses log H ≤ 3Yε/5(log Y)². The leading coefficient in units of log Y is at most 1000/(5 · 52) = 50/13 < 4, so the log log Y and constant terms fit in the remaining margin for large Y. Write r = 2 + 8ε and b = c1/r. Choose the tower exponent function e using the fact that some power of two lies between z and 2z for z ≥ 1. x400 = b400(x′)400 ≤ (x′)401,   exp((x′)ε/2) ≤ exp(xε/2).

8.31From finite subsets of primes to a series

The arithmetic comparison eventually needs a summable sequence of nonnegative terms. Choose the algebraic closure and local data attached to the arithmetic datum. Finiteness of each module length ensures conversion from extended natural numbers to integers recovers its value. Only after the arithmetic comparisons are added does the proof divide the error by the total weight to bound the centered prime sum.

9The one-sided window theorem

Suppose the arithmetic argument repeatedly finds a stretch of scales on which a centered prime sum stays below a small power of the scale. A zero of an associated L-function would force a pole of its transform. How can a bound on scattered stretches rule out even one pole? High derivatives let us choose where the integral sees the function.

9.1The hypothesis in logarithmic coordinates

Fix 0 < θ < 1 and δ > 0. Write g(u) = GF(exp u) for a real weighted sum from a finite character family F. The abstract theorem below allows any real measurable g with |g(u)| ≤ C0 exp(2u) for u ≥ 0. Its transform Φ(s) agrees with ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−su) du for Re s > 2. Assume it extends holomorphically in the right half-plane outside a set Z of simple poles, every one of which has positive real part. Every point of the half-plane must have a punctured neighborhood free of Z, including points outside Z. At each pole the residue is nonzero, and at each real pole it is real and strictly positive.

Put U = log Y. Then [Y, Y1+δ] becomes I = [U, (1 + δ)U]. For every η > 0 and every lower limit U0, suppose there exist U ≥ U0 and a majorant R on I with R ≥ max(g, 0), such that R(u) exp(−θu) is integrable there and

∫I R(u) exp(−θu) du ≤ exp(ηU).

Theorem. Every ρ ∈ Z satisfies Re ρ ≤ θ. The window and its majorant may depend on η and U0. Between windows the growth estimate still holds. An arithmetic upper bound GF(y) ≤ C yθ on arbitrarily distant windows suffices. Take R(u) = |C| exp(θu). Its weighted integral equals |C|δU, which is at most exp(ηU) once U is large.

Test the hypothesis on a single pole. Take θ = ½, δ = ½ and g(u) = exp(¾u). Its Laplace transform is 1/(s − ¾). On [U,3U/2] even the smallest admissible majorant has weighted integral 4(exp(3U/8) − exp(U/4)). For η = ⅛ this eventually exceeds exp(ηU) on every window. Change the sign of g and R = 0 works on every window, although the transform still has a pole at ¾. Its residue is now −1. This example explains the sign hypothesis at real poles and why the arithmetic only needs an upper bound.

9.2Choosing a derivative that sees the window

For Re z = σ > 2, define Ak(z) = (−1)kΦ(k)(z)/k!. In a small neighborhood with Re z ≥ 2 + α, α > 0, the differentiated integrand is bounded by C0uk exp(−αu), an integrable function. Repeated differentiation under the integral therefore gives

Ak(σ + iγ) = ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−iγu) Kk,σ(u) du,   Kk,a(u) = ukexp(−au)/k!.

This nonnegative kernel has its maximum at u = k/a for k > 0. Its integral is a−k−1, by substitution and integration by parts. The term g itself may change sign. Adding Re Ak(σ) to the triangle inequality for |Ak(σ + iγ)| replaces |g| by |g| + g = 2 max(g, 0). On I, use this majorant and the inequality vk/k! ≤ exp(v) at v = (σ − θ)u. Off I, use the growth bound. The result is

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ 2 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k + 2C0 ∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,σ−2(u) du.

The real derivative acts as a correction for sign. Write g = g+ − g−, both parts nonnegative. The triangle inequality at σ + iγ counts both with a plus sign. At the real center, Ak(σ) = ∫(g+ − g−)K. Adding cancels the entire negative part and leaves at most 2∫g+K. The same derivative order must therefore work at both centers.

The integrand in this tail contains σ − 2 because |g| can grow as exp(2u). Estimating the tails of Kk,σ alone would lose that factor.

Locate one of the kernels numerically

Take δ = 1 and U = 10. These choices give λ = 8, M = 16, σ = 160 and k = 2400. The known interval is [10,20], and K2400,160 peaks at 15. Even the kernel after the growth correction peaks at 2400/158 ≈ 15.19. For fixed δ and growing U, how wide is a kernel compared with the interval? Normalizing Kk,a to have integral one gives mean (k + 1)/a and variance (k + 1)/a². Both follow by taking its first two moments with the integral formula above. Thus its standard deviation grows like √U, while the window’s width grows like U. The exponential tail inequalities give the stronger rate needed for the pole argument.

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ C1 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k.

The order k can change each time the arithmetic supplies a new window.

9.4Isolating the pole seen by the derivatives

Suppose a pole has real part greater than θ. All poles lie to the left of σ because the Laplace integral is holomorphic on Re s > 2. Write E = σ − θ. The closed disk of radius E about σ lies in Re s ≥ θ > 0, so it contains finitely many poles by compactness and the punctured-neighborhood assumption. If it contains no poles, take D = E. The hypothesized pole then has horizontal distance strictly less than D and gives the first case below. Otherwise let D be the distance from σ to a nearest pole in the disk. In both cases the open disk of radius D is pole-free.

If a pole ρ1 has σ − Re ρ1 < D, then a disk of radius D centered at σ + i Im ρ1 contains it. Move that center by a sufficiently small vertical amount. Only finitely many poles in a slightly enlarged disk matter, and two distinct poles equally far from the moving center can tie at at most one height. Indeed their squared distances have a difference affine in the height. For equal imaginary parts the equality would also require equal real parts, since both poles lie to the left of σ. Avoiding the finitely many ties gives a center z = σ + iγ with a unique nearest pole ρ at distance d < D. This nearest pole can differ from the one that led us to shift the center. Its real part is at least σ − d > σ − D ≥ θ, so proving a contradiction for it suffices. Choose a radius r with d < r ≤ D isolating this pole.

In the other case all horizontal distances σ − Re ρ are at least D. There must be a nearest pole in the disk because the hypothesized pole has horizontal distance less than E. For any nearest pole the Euclidean distance D is at least its horizontal distance, now at least D. Equality forces the imaginary part to vanish. This identifies one real pole β = σ − D > θ. Every other pole in the finite disk is strictly farther away. Choose r with D < r ≤ E isolating β.

9.5Two incompatible derivative rates

In the first case subtract c/(s − ρ), where c is the nonzero residue. Its subtraction leaves a holomorphic function on the disk after filling the removable value at ρ. For R = (d + r)/2, Cauchy's estimate on the circle of radius R gives

|Ak(z) − c/(z − ρ)k+1| ≤ M1/Rk.

The real center also has a pole-free disk of radius D > R, so |Ak(σ)| ≤ M2/Rk. Substituting these estimates into the upper bound for the derivatives yields

(|c|/d) d−k ≤ (M1 + M2) R−k + C1 exp(ηU) E−k.

For a numerical reading of the last step, suppose d = 2, R = 3 and E = 4. With η = ½ log(3/2), multiplying by 2k leaves a first error proportional to (2/3)k. Since U ≤ k, the window error is at most a constant times (√(3/2)/2)k. Both tend to zero, however sparsely the integers k occur, while the residue contributes |c|/2 every time. The inequalities below apply the same comparison to the actual radii.

Choose 0 < η < log(R/d). Multiply the inequality by dk. Because U ≤ k and E ≥ R > d, the right side tends to zero along the chosen windows. The left side is a fixed positive number.

In the real-pole case take d = σ − β. At the real center the pole contributes c/dk+1 to Ak(σ) with real c > 0. Cauchy's estimate bounds the remainder by M1/Rk for R = (d + r)/2. The nonnegative absolute-value term in the derivative bound can be dropped. The same rate contradiction follows. A negative real residue would reverse the critical sign, which explains the positive-residue hypothesis.

9.6Choosing the exponent after choosing the alleged zero

Let β > 1/2 be the real part being tested. Pick h = ½ min(β − 1/2, 1/2) and θ = 1/2 + h. This ensures θ < min(β,1). Fix a level containing a retained character with the alleged zero. The associated Dirichlet characters, their weights and the function tested for poles are now fixed. The arithmetic construction supplies eD, eL and ε1 > 0 before ε is chosen. Set C = eD + eL + 7 and take ε = min(ε1/2, h/(|C| + 1)). Then Cε ≤ h. Choose the auxiliary arithmetic data for this ε and their large-scale threshold, then choose windows beyond that threshold and beyond 1. These data supply a bound for the weighted sum at the level already fixed. On those windows, the arithmetic exponent can be increased to θ. The theorem excludes a family pole with real part β. For the concrete analytic family, the proof also invokes known nonvanishing at Re s ≥ 1 and uses its pole construction for the remaining open strip.

9.7A zero at 0.60 and the interval that excludes it

Fix the character family that sees the zero, as in the opening example. With θ = 0.55, choose ε ≤ 0.005 within the arithmetic threshold. The specialized estimate gives ½ + 9ε ≤ 0.545. For any prescribed lower cutoff, the arithmetic construction supplies an interval [Z, Z3/2] beyond it. At every point there, the fixed family sum is at most x0.55. Put U = log Z. The function R(u) = exp(0.55u) bounds the positive part on [U, 3U/2]. Multiplication by exp(−0.55u) leaves the constant one. Its integral is U/2, at most exp(ηU) once U is large, for every prescribed η > 0. The window theorem now bounds every pole of this family by 0.55 in real part. A pole at 0.60 contradicts that conclusion.

10Reflection and the final statement

Once every Dirichlet character has a zero-free right half-plane, the passage to classical RH is short. Two small points do most of the work. A change of modulus introduces finite Euler factors, and reflection changes the character.

10.1Removing an imprimitive level

The conductor f of χ modulo N is the least divisor through which its character on units factors. Write ψ for the primitive character at that conductor. Changing to modulus N suppresses Euler factors at primes dividing N. On the common domain of the change-of-level identity, this gives

L(s,χ) = L(s,ψ) ∏p∣N (1 − ψ(p) p−s).

For a prime dividing f, ψ(p) = 0 and the displayed factor equals one. For every other prime its absolute value before subtraction satisfies |ψ(p) p−s| ≤ p−Re s < 1 whenever Re s > 0. Each factor is therefore nonzero. The formula initially follows from Euler products and extends where the continued identity applies. The formal change-of-level lemma asks that ψ be nonprincipal or s ≠ 1. If χ is nonprincipal then ψ must be nonprincipal too, since inducing a principal character would give χ principal. Thus the exception χ = 1 and s = 1 is accounted for.

A change of modulus you can calculate. Let ψ be the character modulo 3 that takes −1 at 2. Induce it to χ modulo 6. On the odd integers the two agree, and the change removes the even terms. Thus L(s,χ) = (1 + 2−s)L(s,ψ). The factor at 3 is one because ψ(3) = 0. When Re s > 0, the added term 2−s has absolute value strictly below one. At the boundary point s = πi/log 2 it equals −1 and the finite factor vanishes. This locates precisely where the zero-transfer argument uses strict positivity of the real part.

10.2The strip theorem for characters

Assume 0 < Re s < 1 and L(s,χ) = 0. The finite factors transfer the zero to ψ. Its completed function is obtained by multiplying by the real gamma factor appropriate to the parity of ψ. The gamma arguments have positive real part in this strip, so the factors are finite and nonzero. In particular the completed function vanishes too. The functional equation for ψ−1, evaluated at s, gives a zero of the completed function for ψ−1 at 1 − s. On units the inverse character is its complex conjugate. The arguments s and 1 − s avoid 0 and 1. Returning to the uncompleted function gives L(1 − s, ψ−1) = 0.

If Re s < ½, then Re(1 − s) > ½, contradicting right-half-plane nonvanishing for the inverse primitive character. If Re s > ½, nonvanishing for χ already contradicts the original zero. This leaves Re s = ½. It proves the strip statement for arbitrary moduli.

Follow a hypothetical zero of a complex character

Modulo 5, the residue 2 generates the unit group. The rule ψ(2) = i therefore fixes a primitive character and ψ−1(2) = −i. If L(¼ + 2i,ψ) vanished, the completed functional equation would give a zero for ψ−1 at ¾ − 2i. The modulus is still 5. The character has changed, so the right-half-plane theorem must cover the inverse as well. Conjugating this latter zero would give a zero for ψ at ¾ + 2i. This last operation explains why the same-character symmetry in a plot is a reflection across a vertical line, even though the functional equation uses 1 − s.

10.3Why classical RH excludes the negative even integers

The public zeta theorem follows a slightly different route. Specialize right-half-plane nonvanishing to the unique character of modulus one. Suppose ζ(s) = 0 with s ≠ 1 and s outside the negative even integers. The right-hand case is impossible immediately. For Re s < ½, put w = 1 − s. Since ζ(0) = −½, s ≠ 0 and w ≠ 1. We have Re w > ½, so ζ(w) ≠ 0, and w avoids all nonpositive integers. In the normalization used by this source the functional equation reads

ζ(1−w) = 2(2π)−w Γ(w) cos(πw/2) ζ(w).

The power of 2π is nonzero and Γ has no zero for Re w > 0. If the cosine vanished, w would be an odd integer, so s would be even. Positive even integers contradict Re s < ½, zero has already been excluded, and negative even integers are exactly the excluded trivial zeros. Every factor on the right is therefore nonzero, contradicting ζ(s) = 0. This proves the implication from the nonvanishing input to the exact classical target.

Why can the same argument accommodate ζ(−2) and ζ(0)?

For s = −2 one has w = 3. The gamma and zeta factors on the right are finite and nonzero, but cos(3π/2) = 0. The equation gives ζ(−2) = 0. For s = 0 one has w = 1. Now the cosine vanishes while ζ(w) has a pole, so value-by-value multiplication at w = 1 is unavailable. Writing w = 1 + h, cos(πw/2) = −πh/2 + O(h³) and ζ(w) = 1/h + O(1). Their product tends to −π/2. The remaining multiplier tends to 2(2π)−1Γ(1) = 1/π. This recovers ζ(0) = −½.
